## Definition

Fix an integer $d\ge1$. An admitted domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ is a nonempty bounded Lipschitz domain (its boundary is locally the graph of a Lipschitz function, with $\Omega$ on one side) with fixed $r_0>0$ and $0<\theta<\pi/2$ such that for every $x\in\overline\Omega$ there is an orthogonal map $Q_x$ for which
$$x+Q_x\{z\in\mathbb R^d:0<|z|<r_0,\ z_1>|z|\cos\theta\}\subset\Omega.$$
An orthogonal map is a real linear map with $Q_x^{\mathsf T}Q_x=I$, equivalently one preserving the Euclidean inner product. The map $Q_x$ may depend on $x$; no simultaneous selection of the maps is part of this definition.

A real radial kernel on $\mathbb R^d$ has the form $K(x,y)=\phi(|x-y|)$ for a function $\phi:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$. For a finite ordered list of distinct sites $X=(x_1,\ldots,x_N)$, its Gram matrix is $K_X=(K(x_i,x_j))_{i,j=1}^N$. The kernel is **strictly positive definite** if $c^{\mathsf T}K_Xc>0$ for every such $X$ and every nonzero $c\in\mathbb R^N$; the nonstrict positive-semidefinite condition replaces $>$ by $\ge$. Only strict positivity is used for the ordinary interpolation solve below.

For an integer $m\ge1$, let $\Pi_{m-1}(\mathbb R^d)$ be the real polynomials of total degree at most $m-1$, with an ordered basis $p_1,\ldots,p_J$, where $J=\dim\Pi_{m-1}(\mathbb R^d)$. The evaluation matrix on $X$ is $P_X=(p_j(x_i))_{i,j}$. The sites are **$m$-unisolvent** for this polynomial space when $P_X$ has linearly independent columns. A kernel is **strictly conditionally positive definite of order $m$** when, for every finite distinct $X$ and this evaluation matrix, $c^{\mathsf T}K_Xc>0$ for every nonzero $c\in\mathbb R^N$ satisfying $P_X^{\mathsf T}c=0$. Thus strict conditional positivity is a strict inequality on the moment-null subspace; it is stronger than the corresponding nonstrict inequality.

For data $y\in\mathbb R^N$, the strictly positive definite interpolation system is $K_Xa=y$. For an order-$m$ strictly conditionally positive definite kernel and $m$-unisolvent sites, the polynomially augmented interpolation system is
$$\begin{bmatrix}K_X&P_X\\P_X^{\mathsf T}&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}a\\b\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}y\\0\end{bmatrix}.$$
Whenever the relevant system has a unique solution, its kernel-plus-polynomial function $x\mapsto\sum_i a_iK(x,x_i)+\sum_j b_jp_j(x)$ is called the interpolant. Invertibility for the stated strict hypotheses is supplied by [[lem-rbf-augmented-system-is-invertible]].

For a finite nonempty site set $X\subset\Omega$, the **fill distance** is $h_X=\sup_{x\in\Omega}\min_{x_i\in X}|x-x_i|$. If $N\ge2$, the **separation radius** and **mesh ratio** are $q_X=\tfrac12\min_{i\ne j}|x_i-x_j|$ and $\rho_X=h_X/q_X$, respectively. These are exact geometric quantities, independent of any floating-point solver.

## Statement

Let $n\ge0$ and let $t_0,\ldots,t_n$ be distinct real numbers. For
$0\le j\le n$, define
$$L_j(x):=\prod_{k\ne j}\frac{x-t_k}{t_j-t_k}.$$
If $p(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}c_kx^k$ has degree at most $n$, then
$$p(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{n}p(t_j)L_j(x).$$
Consequently, writing $L_j(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\ell_{jk}x^k$, every coefficient
satisfies
$$|c_k|\le\left(\sum_{j=0}^{n}|\ell_{jk}|\right)\max_{0\le j\le n}|p(t_j)|.$$
The empty product convention gives $L_0=1$ when $n=0$.

1.1 Each denominator $t_j-t_k$ is nonzero, so every $L_j$ is a polynomial of degree at most $n$ and $L_j(t_i)$ is $1$ for $i=j$ and $0$ otherwise. The polynomial $p-\sum_jp(t_j)L_j$ has degree at most $n$ and vanishes at the $n+1$ distinct nodes; [F2] makes it the zero polynomial. This also covers $n=0$, when $L_0=1$. [F1, F2, given, construct, algebra]
2.1 Comparing the coefficients of $x^k$ in the identity of step 1.1 gives $c_k=\sum_jp(t_j)\ell_{jk}$. The triangle inequality yields the stated coefficient bound. [given, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For real polynomials $p,q$ with $q\ne0$, there is a reduced pair
$p_0,q_0$ representing $p/q$, and any two reduced pairs representing the same
nonzero rational function differ by a common nonzero real scalar. The zero
rational function has reduced pair $(0,1)$ up to a nonzero scalar. If a
reduced denominator is strictly positive on an interval and is normalized to
coefficient Euclidean norm $1$, then the representing pair is unique.

1.1 For a nonzero quotient, let $d=\gcd(p,q)$ from [F1] and put $p_0=p/d$, $q_0=q/d$. Then $Ap+Bq=d$ implies $Ap_0+Bq_0=1$, so no nonconstant polynomial divides both $p_0$ and $q_0$. For the zero quotient, $p=0$ and reducing by $\gcd(0,q)$ gives $(0,1)$. [given, F1, construct, algebra]

2.1 Suppose $p_0/q_0=p_1/q_1$ are nonzero reduced representations. Cross-multiplication gives $p_0q_1=p_1q_0$. By the Bézout identity $Ap_0+Bq_0=1$ from step 1.1, multiplication by $p_1$ shows $p_0$ divides $p_1$; the same argument with the denominator gives $q_0\mid q_1$. Write $p_1=h p_0$ and $q_1=k q_0$. Cross-multiplication and nonzero $p_0q_0$ give $h=k$. If $h$ were nonconstant, it would divide both $p_1$ and $q_1$, contradicting reduction. Thus $h=k$ is a nonzero constant. The zero case is the reduced pair already identified in step 1.1. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 If both positive denominators have coefficient norm $1$, their common scalar from step 2.1 is positive and its multiplication scales the coefficient norm by that scalar. The two norms being $1$ forces the scalar to be $1$, and then the numerators agree as well. [step 2.1, algebra] ∎
cases.reason: The quantified objects are numerator and denominator polynomials, with the denominator expressly nonzero; there is no node family, empty product, or empty search domain in the reduction argument.

## Statement refuted

For every real matrix $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, every integer $0\le k<n$, and every prescribed ordered list $J$ of $k$ distinct column indices, there is a matrix $T$ with $T(:,J)=I_k$, $\max_{i,j}|T_{ij}|\le1$, and
$\|A-A(:,J)T\|_2\le\sqrt{1+k(n-k)}\,\sigma_{k+1}(A)$, where $\|\cdot\|_2$ is the Euclidean operator norm and $\sigma_j(A)$ is the $j$th singular value.

1.1 Any $1\times2$ matrix satisfying $T(:,J)=1$ has the form $T=(t,1)$. The coefficient condition gives $|t|\le1$, and direct multiplication gives $A-A(:,J)T=\begin{bmatrix}10&0\\-t&0\end{bmatrix}$. Its spectral norm is the Euclidean norm of its first column, $\sqrt{100+|t|^2}\ge10$. [given, A1, algebra]

2.1 The singular values of the diagonal matrix in [A1] are $10$ and $1$, so the proposed upper bound is $\sqrt{1+1\cdot(2-1)}\,\sigma_2(A)=\sqrt2$. Since $10>\sqrt2$, no such $T$ satisfies the claim. [A1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $P^-=L^- (L^-)^T$ and $R=L_RL_R^T$, with real factors of arbitrary
rank. Let $H\in\mathbb R^{p\times n}$ and suppose
$$S=H P^-H^T+R\succ0.$$
Pad $L_R$ with zero columns to at least $p$ columns and $L^-$ with zero
columns to at least $n$ columns. Denote the resulting factors by
$L_R^{\mathrm{pad}}$ and $L^-_{\mathrm{pad}}$, and form
$$Z=\begin{bmatrix}L_R^{\mathrm{pad}}&HL^-_{\mathrm{pad}}\\0&L^-_{\mathrm{pad}}\end{bmatrix}.$$
Then $Z^T$ has at least $p+n$ rows. Take an exact reduced QR factorization
$Z^T=UR$ with $U^TU=I$ and set $L=R^T$. For each $i=1,\ldots,p$,
multiply column $i$ of $L$ by the sign of its diagonal entry. This makes the
first $p$ diagonal entries positive; the signs are well defined because
$S\succ0$. Partition the resulting $L$ as
$$L=\begin{bmatrix}L_{11}&0\\L_{21}&L_{22}\end{bmatrix}$$
at the observation and state dimensions. Then
$$L_{11}L_{11}^T=S,\qquad L_{21}L_{11}^T=P^-H^T,$$
and
$$L_{22}L_{22}^T=P^- -P^-H^TS^{-1}HP^-.$$
For innovation $v=y-Hm^-$, the exact solve $L_{11}z=v$ gives
$m^-+L_{21}z=m^-+P^-H^TS^{-1}v$. Thus the factor update has exactly the
canonical one-step mean and covariance; $L_{22}$ may be singular.

1.1 Write $\bar r_R$ and $\bar r_-$ for the padded column counts. They satisfy $\bar r_R\ge p$ and $\bar r_-\ge n$, so $Z^T$ has $\bar r_R+\bar r_-\ge p+n$ rows, as required for the reduced QR. Padding either factor with zero columns leaves its Gram matrix unchanged. Multiplication of the prearray by its transpose therefore gives $$ZZ^T=\begin{bmatrix} L_R^{\mathrm{pad}}(L_R^{\mathrm{pad}})^T+HL^-_{\mathrm{pad}}(L^-_{\mathrm{pad}})^TH^T&HL^-_{\mathrm{pad}}(L^-_{\mathrm{pad}})^T\\ L^-_{\mathrm{pad}}(L^-_{\mathrm{pad}})^TH^T&L^-_{\mathrm{pad}}(L^-_{\mathrm{pad}})^T \end{bmatrix} =\begin{bmatrix}S&HP^-\\P^-H^T&P^- \end{bmatrix}.$$ [given, algebra]

2.1 Initially set $L^0=R^T$ and partition it at dimensions $p,n$. Since $Z^T=UR$ and $U^TU=I$, $L^0(L^0)^T=R^TR=ZZ^T$. Block multiplication gives $L^0_{11}(L^0_{11})^T=S$, $L^0_{21}(L^0_{11})^T=P^-H^T$, and $L^0_{21}(L^0_{21})^T+L^0_{22}(L^0_{22})^T=P^-$. The positive-definite matrix $S=L^0_{11}(L^0_{11})^T$ makes $L^0_{11}$ invertible, so its diagonal entries are nonzero. Let $D$ be the diagonal matrix whose entries are the signs of those entries, and set $L=L^0\operatorname{diag}(D,I_n)$. This flips the first $p$ columns of $L^0$, making the diagonal of $L_{11}=L^0_{11}D$ positive. Because $\operatorname{diag}(D,I_n)$ is orthogonal, $LL^T=L^0(L^0)^T$; moreover $L_{21}=L^0_{21}D$ and $L_{22}=L^0_{22}$. Hence all three displayed block identities remain true. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Because $S\succ0$ and $S=L_{11}L_{11}^T$, the square matrix $L_{11}$ is invertible. From the cross-block identity, $L_{21}=P^-H^T L_{11}^{-T}$; hence $$L_{21}L_{21}^T=P^-H^TL_{11}^{-T}L_{11}^{-1}HP^- =P^-H^TS^{-1}HP^-.$$ Subtracting this equality from the lower-right identity in step 2.1 gives the stated posterior covariance. Since it is also $L_{22}L_{22}^T$, it is positive semidefinite even when $L_{22}$ is singular. [given, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The solve $L_{11}z=v$ gives $$L_{21}z=L_{21}L_{11}^{-1}v =P^-H^TL_{11}^{-T}L_{11}^{-1}v =P^-H^TS^{-1}v.$$ By [F2], these mean and covariance are the one-step Gaussian conditional update. The matrix calculations themselves are deterministic and use no choice beyond [A1]. [A1, F2, step 2.1, step 3.1, given, algebra] ∎
cases.evidence: The statement does not impose positive state or observation dimensions; empty blocks reduce the Gram identities to the remaining covariance factorization, with the observation solve vacuous when its block has size zero.

## Definition

A **certified enclosure** for a real value is a nonempty closed interval
$B=[a,b]$ with finite dyadic endpoints; for a complex value it is a nonempty
closed rectangle $B=[a_1,b_1]+i[a_2,b_2]$ with finite dyadic endpoints. Its
radius is half its length in the real case and half its Euclidean diagonal in
the complex case; $d(B,0)$ is the Euclidean distance from $B$ to $0$.
An evaluator item declares whether its input is an exact dyadic point or a
dyadic interval/rectangle enclosure; a successful range result contains the
exact function image of every admissible point in an input enclosure. Constants
not exactly dyadic must be supplied with certified enclosing intervals or
rectangles.

The interval backend uses the endpoint operations in
[[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]]; the soundness of finite
arithmetic expression DAGs follows from
[[thm-outward-rounded-operations-are-isotone-and-dag-sound]]. Real elementary
function ranges use [[thm-real-elementary-range-enclosures]], and complex
exponential and principal-logarithm ranges use
[[thm-complex-elementary-range-enclosures]]. An operation that returns a
non-finite status supplies no finite enclosure claim.

A finite-budget evaluator receives a branch input enclosure wholly within
the stated domain, absolute tolerance $\varepsilon_a>0$, optional relative
tolerance $\varepsilon_r>0$, finite integer work and precision caps, and the
fixed format and truncation parameters required by the backend. Its result has
one of four statuses:

- `success`: the returned enclosure contains the exact requested value and its
  radius is at most $\varepsilon_a$. If $0\notin B$ and relative tolerance was
  requested, the evaluator may also report `relative_certified: true` only when
  $\operatorname{rad}(B)/d(B,0)\le\varepsilon_r$.
- `inconclusive`: the procedure exhausted a finite cap before its requested
  enclosure test passed.
- `domain`: the input is outside the stated branch domain, violates a stated
  parameter condition, or lies on a branch cut excluded by that branch.
- `range`: a certified finite enclosure cannot be represented in the requested
  output format; the procedure returns no unsound finite interval.

If a success enclosure contains $0$, it still supplies the stated absolute
bound, but it carries no relative-accuracy claim. The work and precision caps
do not imply that success occurs for every input.
cases.evidence: Closed dyadic intervals and rectangles include their endpoint values; an enclosure touching zero can still pass absolute tolerance, but the explicit distance and exclusion test prevents a relative certificate there.

## Definition

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define the Fresnel functions and error function by

$$C(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^k(\pi/2)^{2k}z^{4k+1}}{(2k)!(4k+1)}, \qquad S(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^k(\pi/2)^{2k+1}z^{4k+3}}{(2k+1)!(4k+3)}, \qquad \operatorname{erf}(z)=\frac{2}{\sqrt\pi}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^kz^{2k+1}}{k!(2k+1)}, \qquad \operatorname{erfc}(z)=1-\operatorname{erf}(z).$$

The following local lemmas prove convergence and show that $C,S,\operatorname{erf}$
equal the standard entire integral functions with their usual normalizations.

For $a,b,c,z\in\mathbb C$ with $c\notin\{0,-1,-2,\ldots\}$ and $|z|<1$,
define

$$(a)_0=1,\qquad (a)_k=\prod_{j=0}^{k-1}(a+j),\qquad {}_2F_1(a,b;c;z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(a)_k(b)_k}{(c)_k k!}z^k.$$

Only this Gauss-series branch of ${}_2F_1$ is defined on this page; no value
outside $|z|<1$ or across a continuation cut is implicit.
cases.evidence: The rising factorial at index zero is explicitly one, so its empty product starts the hypergeometric series correctly; none of the entire-function series is an empty sum.

## Definition

Input a real function $f$ that is continuous on the interior of the selected target domain, a step $h>0$, nonnegative integers $N_-,N_+$, and exactly one domain mode. The finite rule evaluates $f$ only at interior points:

1. **Finite interval $(a,b)$, $a<b$.** Put $m=(a+b)/2$, $d=(b-a)/2$, $s(t)=\sinh t=(e^t-e^{-t})/2$, $c(t)=\cosh t=(e^t+e^{-t})/2$, and $\psi(t)=\tanh((\pi/2)s(t))$, where $\tanh u=\sinh u/\cosh u$. Set $x(t)=m+d\psi(t)$, $x'(t)=d(\pi/2)c(t)/\cosh^2((\pi/2)s(t))$, and $\Phi(t)=f(x(t))x'(t)$.
2. **Positive half-line $(0,\infty)$.** Here $f$ is continuous on $(0,\infty)$. Set $x(t)=\exp((\pi/2)s(t))$, $x'(t)=x(t)(\pi/2)c(t)$, and $\Phi(t)=f(x(t))x'(t)$.
3. **Whole line $\mathbb R$.** Here $f$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$. Set $x(t)=\sinh((\pi/2)s(t))$, $x'(t)=\cosh((\pi/2)s(t))(\pi/2)c(t)$, and $\Phi(t)=f(x(t))x'(t)$.

Return the finite sum
$$T_{h,N_-,N_+}(f)=h\sum_{k=-N_-}^{N_+}\Phi(kh).$$
The algorithm makes no accuracy claim from integrability alone. Analytic-strip and tail hypotheses required for an error certificate are stated in [[thm-double-exponential-trapezoid-error-bound]].
cases.evidence: Both truncation indices are nonnegative, so even when they vanish the quadrature sum contains the central transformed sample; an empty sum cannot occur for valid input.

## Definition

Input a real function $f$ that is continuous on the interior of the selected target domain, a step $h>0$, nonnegative integers $N_-,N_+$, and exactly one domain mode. The finite rule evaluates $f$ only at interior points:

1. **Finite interval $(a,b)$, $a<b$.** Put $m=(a+b)/2$, $d=(b-a)/2$, $s(t)=\sinh t=(e^t-e^{-t})/2$, $c(t)=\cosh t=(e^t+e^{-t})/2$, and $\psi(t)=\tanh((\pi/2)s(t))$, where $\tanh u=\sinh u/\cosh u$. Set $x(t)=m+d\psi(t)$, $x'(t)=d(\pi/2)c(t)/\cosh^2((\pi/2)s(t))$, and $\Phi(t)=f(x(t))x'(t)$.
2. **Positive half-line $(0,\infty)$.** Here $f$ is continuous on $(0,\infty)$. Set $x(t)=\exp((\pi/2)s(t))$, $x'(t)=x(t)(\pi/2)c(t)$, and $\Phi(t)=f(x(t))x'(t)$.
3. **Whole line $\mathbb R$.** Here $f$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$. Set $x(t)=\sinh((\pi/2)s(t))$, $x'(t)=\cosh((\pi/2)s(t))(\pi/2)c(t)$, and $\Phi(t)=f(x(t))x'(t)$.

Return the finite sum
$$T_{h,N_-,N_+}(f)=h\sum_{k=-N_-}^{N_+}\Phi(kh).$$
The algorithm makes no accuracy claim from integrability alone. Analytic-strip and tail hypotheses required for an error certificate are stated in [[thm-double-exponential-trapezoid-error-bound]].

## Definition

Write $\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ and $\|x\|_2=(x_1^2+x_2^2+x_3^2)^{1/2}$ for $x\in\mathbb R^3$. For $\alpha=(\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3)\in\mathbb N_0^3$, exponent $a>0$, and center $A\in\mathbb R^3$, a **primitive Cartesian Gaussian** is
$$g_{\alpha,a,A}(x)=\prod_{j=1}^3(x_j-A_j)^{\alpha_j}\exp(-a\|x-A\|_2^2),\qquad x\in\mathbb R^3.$$
A **finite Gaussian contraction** is a finite sum $\phi=\sum_{k=1}^q c_k g_{\alpha_k,a_k,A_k}$ with $q\in\mathbb N_0$, $c_k\in\mathbb C$, $a_k>0$, and $A_k\in\mathbb R^3$. The zero-term sum is the zero function. Bras are conjugated.

For a pair of contractions put $f_{\phi,\psi}(x)=\overline{\phi(x)}\psi(x)$. For pair densities $f,g$, define the **Coulomb form**
$$\mathcal C(f,g)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{\overline{f(x)}g(y)}{\|x-y\|_2}\,dy\,dx.$$
For finite contractions $\phi,\psi,\rho,\sigma$, define the overlap, kinetic, point-nucleus attraction, and two-electron Coulomb expressions by
$$S(\phi,\psi)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\overline{\phi(x)}\psi(x)\,dx,\qquad T(\phi,\psi)=-\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^3}\overline{\phi(x)}\,\Delta\psi(x)\,dx,$$
$$V_C(\phi,\psi)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{\overline{\phi(x)}\psi(x)}{\|x-C\|_2}\,dx,$$
$$G(\phi,\psi;\rho,\sigma)=\mathcal C(f_{\phi,\psi},f_{\rho,\sigma}).$$
The primitives and their finite contractions are smooth: [[thm-derivative-of-exponential]] supplies smoothness of exp, and repeated coordinatewise applications of [[lem-derivative-algebra-and-chain-rules]] supply all polynomial-product and composition derivatives. Thus the following Laplacian is well defined.

Here $\Delta\psi=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}^2\psi$ is the Cartesian Laplacian.
All displayed integrals mean Lebesgue integrals in the sense of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]. A finite nuclear attraction is any finite real linear combination of the $V_C$ terms, with its centers and weights specified. This definition alone asserts neither convergence nor a physical approximation postulate.

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ be bounded and open, and suppose its first coordinate projection is contained in an interval $(a,b)$ of width $L=b-a$. For every real $v\in H^1_0(D)$,
$$\|v\|_{L^2(D)}\le L\|\partial_1v\|_{L^2(D)}\le L\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(D)}.$$

1.1 First take $v\in C_c^\infty(D)$ and extend it by zero to $(a,b)\times\mathbb R^{d-1}$. For every $x'\in\mathbb R^{d-1}$ and $x_1\in(a,b)$, the fundamental theorem of calculus gives $v(x_1,x')=\int_a^{x_1}\partial_1v(t,x')\,dt$. Cauchy--Schwarz yields $|v(x_1,x')|^2\le L\int_a^b|\partial_1v(t,x')|^2dt$. [given, F1, F4]
2.1 Integrating the last inequality over $x_1$ gives a second factor $L$; integrating over $x'$ and using the zero extension proves $\|v\|_2^2\le L^2\|\partial_1v\|_2^2$. [F2, F3, step 1.1]

3.1 For general $v\in H^1_0(D)$, [A1, F1] supplies a sequence $v_n\in C_c^\infty(D)$ converging to $v$ in $W^{1,2}$. The two norms in step 2.1 converge by [F2], so passing to the limit gives the same inequality for $v$. Finally $|\partial_1v|\le|\nabla v|$ almost everywhere. [A1, F1, F2, F3, algebra, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty, bounded, connected and Lipschitz. Here Lipschitz means that its compact boundary has a finite atlas of rigidly moved cylinders in which $D$ is the strict epigraph $x_d>\varphi(x')$ of a Lipschitz function. There are finitely many bounded open sets $U_i\subset D$ covering $D$, each star-shaped with respect to a closed ball $\overline B_i\subset U_i$, and the graph joining $i,j$ when $U_i\cap U_j\ne\varnothing$ is connected. There are measurable sets $E_i\subset U_i$ partitioning $D$ and, for every edge of a spanning tree of this graph, a function $\psi_{ij}\in C_c^\infty(U_i\cap U_j)$ with integral one.

1.1 Fix one graph chart, with Lipschitz constant $L$, and a smaller horizontal ball $C$ whose closure lies in its base. Shrink its radius $r$ until the chart's upper height $H_{\rm chart}$ satisfies $H_{\rm chart}-\sup_C\varphi>4(L+1)r$. Choose $c$ with $\sup_C\varphi+3(L+1)r<c<H_{\rm chart}-(L+1)r$ and $0<\rho<r$. Then the closed ball $\overline B((x'_0,c),\rho)$ stays in the cylinder. Set $U=\{(x',x_d):x'\in C,\ \varphi(x')<x_d<H\}$ with $c+\rho<H<H_{\rm chart}$. [given, construct]

2.1 If $x\in U$, $z\in\overline B((x'_0,c),\rho)$, and $w=(1-t)x+tz$ with $0<t<1$, then $z'\in C$ and convexity keeps $w'\in C$. Since $|z'-x'|\le2r$, Lipschitz continuity gives $\varphi(w')\le\varphi(x')+2Lrt$. Also $c-\rho>\sup_C\varphi+2Lr$, so $w_d>(1-t)\varphi(x')+t(c-\rho)>\varphi(x')+2Lrt\ge\varphi(w')$, and $w_d<H$ by convexity of the vertical interval. Thus $w\in U$; the endpoints belong to $U$ as well, proving star-shapedness with respect to the closed ball. [given, algebra, step 1.1]

3.1 The boundary $\partial D$ is closed and bounded, hence compact by [F1]. At any $p\in\partial D$, a chart containing $p$ writes the boundary locally as $x_d=\varphi(x')$, with $p_d=\varphi(p')$ strictly below the chart's upper height. Shrinking a horizontal ball $C$ about $p'$ makes its closure lie in the chart base and makes the height-gap inequality of step 1.1 hold; the choices there then produce a patch $U=\{(x',x_d):x'\in C,\ \varphi(x')<x_d<H\}$ star-shaped with respect to its selected closed ball by step 2.1. Since $p$ lies inside the chart and inside the open set with $x'\in C$ and $x_d<H$, there is an ambient open ball $N$ about $p$ whose closure lies in that chart and open set. For every $x\in N\cap D$, the chart description gives $x_d>\varphi(x')$, so $x\in U$ and $N\cap D\subset U$. Let $\mathscr N$ be the family of all pairs $(N,U)$ obtained this way from the finite chart atlas and admissible local choices; the preceding existence argument shows that its first components cover $\partial D$, without choosing a patch simultaneously for every boundary point. Compactness supplies a finite subfamily $(N_i,U_i)$, $1\le i\le m$, whose neighborhoods cover $\partial D$. Their union is an open neighborhood of the compact boundary, so some relative collar $\{x\in D:\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial D)<\delta\}$ lies in that union and hence in $\bigcup_{i=1}^mU_i$. The remainder $K_\delta=\{x\in\overline D:\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial D)\ge\delta\}$ is closed and bounded, hence compact by [F1], and is contained in $D$ because every point of $\overline D\setminus D$ lies on $\partial D$. Finitely many balls with closures in $D$ cover $K_\delta$; each ball is convex and star-shaped with respect to a smaller concentric ball. Together these sets form a finite star-shaped cover of $D$. [F1, given, step 1.1, step 2.1]

4.1 The intersection graph is connected: if it split into two nonempty graph components, the unions of the corresponding open sets would be disjoint nonempty relatively open subsets whose union is $D$, contradicting connectedness. Order the cover and set $E_i=U_i\setminus\bigcup_{j<i}U_j$. Then the $E_i$ are disjoint measurable sets with $E_i\subset U_i$ and union $D$. A finite connected graph has a spanning tree. [given, step 3.1]

5.1 Each tree-edge intersection is nonempty and open, so it contains a ball. Choose a nonnegative smooth bump supported in that ball. Its integral is strictly positive; dividing by that integral gives $\psi_{ij}\in C_c^\infty(U_i\cap U_j)$ with integral one. [construct, step 4.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $K\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a nondegenerate open simplex. For every $u\in H^1(K;\mathbb R)$ and every $\varepsilon>0$, there is a function $u_\varepsilon$ smooth on an open neighborhood of $\overline K$ with $\|u_\varepsilon-u\|_{H^1(K)}<\varepsilon$.

1.1 Choose $c\in K$ and $s\in(0,1)$, and put $T_s(x)=c+s(x-c)$ and $U_s=T_s^{-1}(K)$. Since $K$ is convex and $c$ is interior, $T_s(\overline K)$ is a compact subset of $K$; hence $U_s$ is an open simplex containing $\overline K$ with positive distance from $\overline K$ to $U_s^c$. Define $u_s=u\circ T_s$ on $U_s$. For $\psi\in C_c^\infty(U_s)$, change variables $y=T_s(x)$ in the weak derivative identity of $u$; with $\widetilde\psi(y)=\psi(T_s^{-1}y)$ one has $D_{y_i}\widetilde\psi=s^{-1}(D_{x_i}\psi)\circ T_s^{-1}$, so the identity gives $D_i u_s=s(D_i u)\circ T_s$ distributionally. [A1, F1, F3, construct, algebra]

1.2 For any $g\in L^2(K)$, extend it by zero to $\mathbb R^d$. Given $\eta>0$, choose $\phi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$ with $\|g-\phi\|_{L^2(K)}<\eta$ by [F2]. Because $T_s(K)\subset K$, change of variables [F3] gives $\|(g-\phi)\circ T_s\|_{L^2(K)}\le s^{-d/2}\eta$, while uniform continuity of $\phi$ on $\overline K$ gives $\|\phi\circ T_s-\phi\|_{L^2(K)}\to0$ as $s\to1^-$. The triangle inequality and arbitrary $\eta$ therefore show $\|g\circ T_s-g\|_{L^2(K)}\to0$. [F2, F3, algebra, algebra]

2.1 Apply step 1.2 to $g=u$ and to every $g=D_i u$. By step 1.1, $D_i u_s=s(D_i u)\circ T_s$, and $s\to1$; hence $u_s|_K\to u$ in the full $H^1(K)$ norm as $s\to1^-$. [F1, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Choose $s$ close enough to $1$ that $\|u_s-u\|_{H^1(K)}<\varepsilon/2$, and let $r=\operatorname{dist}(\overline K,U_s^c)>0$. Choose the bump from [F4] and then $0<\delta<r$. The zero extension of $u_s$ is locally integrable by [F8], so $w_\delta=(\rho_\delta*E_0u_s)$ is smooth by [F7]. On $K$, [F6] gives $D_iw_\delta=\rho_\delta*E_0(D_i u_s)$. Each zero extension is in $L^2(\mathbb R^d)$; [F5] therefore gives $\|w_\delta-u_s\|_{H^1(K)}\to0$ as $\delta\to0^+$. Choose $\delta<r$ small enough to make this norm less than $\varepsilon/2$. Then $w_\delta$ is smooth on a neighborhood of $\overline K$, and the triangle inequality with step 2.1 gives $\|w_\delta-u\|_{H^1(K)}<\varepsilon$. [A1, F4, F5, F6, F7, F8, step 2.1, choose, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Let $n,m\ge1$, $V=M_{n\times1}(\mathbb R)$, and
$Q=M_{m\times1}(\mathbb R)$. Let $A\in M_n(\mathbb R)$ be symmetric
positive definite, let $B\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb R)$ have full row rank
(meaning $B^Tq=0$ implies $q=0$), and let
$M_Q\in M_m(\mathbb R)$ be symmetric positive definite. The saddle system
and its matrix are
$$ K=\begin{pmatrix}A&B^T\\B&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad Au+B^Tp=f,\quad Bu=g. $$
Define the positive pressure Schur matrix
$$ S:=BA^{-1}B^T. $$
In the block-LU convention of [[def-block-lu-factorisation]], the trailing
Schur complement of $A$ in $K$ is $-S$. The exact block solve first solves
$Au_0=f$, then $Sp=Bu_0-g$, and finally $Au=f-B^Tp$; the theorem
[[thm-na-saddle-point-exact-schur-solve]] verifies this procedure and
well-definedness.

For a scaling $\gamma>0$, the pressure-mass block-diagonal preconditioner is
$$ P_\gamma=\operatorname{diag}(A,\gamma M_Q). $$
It is symmetric positive definite. If $P_\gamma=CC^T$ is its Cholesky
factorization with $C$ lower triangular and positive on the diagonal, the
symmetric preconditioned system is $C^{-1}KC^{-T}y=C^{-1}r$, with the usual
change of unknown. This is the symmetric-preconditioning convention of
[[def-left-right-and-symmetric-positive-definite-preconditioning]]. No
spectral bound, Krylov iteration count, complexity estimate, or generic speed
improvement is part of this definition.

## Definition

Fix a bounded, connected polygonal open set $Ω\subset\mathbb R^2$ with a nonempty Dirichlet boundary segment. A finite **subdomain partition** is a family of connected polygonal open sets $Ω_i$, $1\le i\le N$, whose closures cover $\overline\Omega$, whose interiors are disjoint, and whose intersections are whole common sides, common vertices, or empty. The outer Dirichlet segment is a union of mesh boundary sides. The edge-adjacency graph of each triangulated subdomain is connected, and the subdomain adjacency graph is connected to the Dirichlet boundary. Each subdomain has a matching affine simplicial triangulation; the triangulations match on every shared side. The family has a fixed shape-regularity bound, quasiuniform mesh size $h_i$, uniformly bounded polygon side count, corner angles bounded below, inradius comparable to $H_i$, and a uniform interior-cone parameter. Write $H_i=\operatorname{diam}(\Omega_i)$ and $H/h=\max_i H_i/h_i$.

Use continuous piecewise-affine ($P_1$) scalar functions on each triangulation. The reference-element and face-matching conventions are those of [[def-reference-finite-element-and-unisolvent-dofs]], [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]], and [[def-broken-and-conforming-polynomial-spaces]]: local polynomials are affine, their nodal values determine them, and conforming functions have equal traces across a shared side. For each subdomain choose a coefficient $\rho_i>0$, constant on $\Omega_i$ but allowed to jump across interfaces. Its local energy is

$$a_i(v,w)=\rho_i\sum_{K\subset\Omega_i}\int_K\nabla v\cdot\nabla w\,dx.$$

The global finite-element space consists of the continuous piecewise-affine functions on the subdomain meshes that vanish on the outer Dirichlet boundary, with energy $a(v,w)=\sum_i a_i(v|_{\Omega_i},w|_{\Omega_i})$. Local interior degrees of freedom are the mesh vertices strictly inside $\Omega_i$; local boundary degrees of freedom are its remaining vertices, with outer Dirichlet values fixed to zero. A **floating local block** means the same local energy before any outer-boundary values are fixed. A **subdomain corner** is a vertex of its polygonal boundary.

All constants in later two-dimensional estimates may depend on the fixed polygon-shape, side-count, and shape-regularity bounds, but not on $h$, $H$, the number of subdomains, or the positive numbers $\rho_i$.

## Definition

Fix an integer $d\ge1$, a gas constant $R>0$, an adiabatic exponent $\gamma>1$, a constant reference entropy $s_0\in\mathbb R$, shear viscosity $\mu>0$, bulk viscosity $\zeta\ge0$, and heat conductivity $\kappa>0$. Put $c_v=R/(\gamma-1)$. A conservative state is $U=(\rho,m,E)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R$. Its **admissible state set** is

$$\mathcal G=\left\{(\rho,m,E):\rho>0,\ E>\frac{|m|^2}{2\rho}\right\}.$$

For $U\in\mathcal G$, define the velocity $u=m/\rho$, internal-energy density $\varepsilon=E-|m|^2/(2\rho)$, pressure $p=(\gamma-1)\varepsilon$, temperature $T=p/(R\rho)$, specific entropy $s(U)=c_v\log(p/\rho^\gamma)+s_0$, and mathematical entropy $\eta(U)=-\rho s(U)$. The Euler flux in coordinate direction $j$ is

$$F_j(U)=\bigl(\rho u_j,\ m u_j+p e_j,\ (E+p)u_j\bigr),\qquad j=1,\ldots,d,$$

where $e_j$ is the $j$th standard basis vector of $\mathbb R^d$. The mathematical entropy flux is $q_j(U)=\eta(U)u_j$.

For a differentiable velocity field, write $D=\operatorname{sym}\nabla u$ with $D_{ab}=(\partial_bu_a+\partial_au_b)/2$, and $D^0=D-(\operatorname{tr}D/d)I$. The Newtonian stress and Fourier viscous flux are

$$\tau=2\mu D^0+\zeta(\operatorname{tr}D)I, \qquad F_j^{\mathrm{visc}}=\bigl(0,\tau_{j1},\ldots,\tau_{jd},\ u\cdot\tau_{j\cdot}+\kappa\partial_jT\bigr).$$

The **compressible Navier–Stokes–Fourier balance law** is the conservative system

$$\partial_tU+\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_jF_j(U) =\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_jF_j^{\mathrm{visc}}(U,\nabla u,\nabla T).$$

Unless a boundary is specified separately, a periodic solution means that all fields and fluxes are periodic in each spatial coordinate. The positive parameters and the inequalities defining $\mathcal G$ imply $p>0$ and $T>0$.

Put $c_v=R/(\gamma-1)$. A conservative state is $U=(\rho,m,E)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d\times\mathbb R$. Its **admissible state set** is

$$\mathcal G=\left\{(\rho,m,E):\rho>0,\ E>\frac{|m|^2}{2\rho}\right\}.$$

For $U\in\mathcal G$, define the velocity $u=m/\rho$, internal-energy density $\varepsilon=E-|m|^2/(2\rho)$, pressure $p=(\gamma-1)\varepsilon$, temperature $T=p/(R\rho)$, specific entropy $s(U)=c_v\log(p/\rho^\gamma)+s_0$, and mathematical entropy $\eta(U)=-\rho s(U)$. The Euler flux in coordinate direction $j$ is

$$F_j(U)=\bigl(\rho u_j,\ m u_j+p e_j,\ (E+p)u_j\bigr),\qquad j=1,\ldots,d,$$

where $e_j$ is the $j$th standard basis vector of $\mathbb R^d$. The mathematical entropy flux is $q_j(U)=\eta(U)u_j$.

For a differentiable velocity field, write $D=\operatorname{sym}\nabla u$ with $D_{ab}=(\partial_bu_a+\partial_au_b)/2$, and $D^0=D-(\operatorname{tr}D/d)I$. The Newtonian stress and Fourier viscous flux are

$$\tau=2\mu D^0+\zeta(\operatorname{tr}D)I, \qquad F_j^{\mathrm{visc}}=\bigl(0,\tau_{j1},\ldots,\tau_{jd},\ u\cdot\tau_{j\cdot}+\kappa\partial_jT\bigr).$$

The **compressible Navier–Stokes–Fourier balance law** is the conservative system

$$\partial_tU+\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_jF_j(U) =\sum_{j=1}^d\partial_jF_j^{\mathrm{visc}}(U,\nabla u,\nabla T).$$

Unless a boundary is specified separately, a periodic solution means that all fields and fluxes are periodic in each spatial coordinate. The positive parameters and the inequalities defining $\mathcal G$ imply $p>0$ and $T>0$.

## Statement

On the interval $[0,2h]$ with three uniform P1 nodes and homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions, the semidiscrete heat equation with consistent mass matrix,
$$
M\dot u+\nu Ku=0,\qquad \nu>0,
$$
does not preserve nodal nonnegativity: there is a nonnegative initial vector for which the first component becomes negative immediately.

1.1 On an element $[0,h]$, the two affine basis functions are $\phi_1(x)=1-x/h$ and $\phi_2(x)=x/h$. Direct integration gives $ \int_0^h\phi_1^2\,dx=\int_0^h\phi_2^2\,dx=h/3,\quad \int_0^h\phi_1\phi_2\,dx=h/6, $ and their derivatives are $-1/h$ and $1/h$, so the element stiffness entries are $1/h,-1/h,-1/h,1/h$. Assembling the two elements yields the displayed matrices: $ M=\frac h6\begin{pmatrix}2&1&0\\1&4&1\\0&1&2\end{pmatrix}, \qquad K=\frac1h\begin{pmatrix}1&-1&0\\-1&2&-1\\0&-1&1\end{pmatrix}. $ The Neumann condition is natural in this stiffness form and adds no boundary matrix. [A1, given, algebra]

2.1 Write $M=(h/6)B$ and $K=C/h$ for the displayed integer matrices. Direct multiplication verifies $ B^{-1}=\frac1{12}\begin{pmatrix}7&-2&1\\-2&4&-2\\1&-2&7\end{pmatrix},\qquad B^{-1}C=\frac1{12}\begin{pmatrix}9&-12&3\\-6&12&-6\\3&-12&9\end{pmatrix}. $ Thus $M^{-1}K=6B^{-1}C/h^2$, so in particular $(M^{-1}K)_{13}=3/(2h^2)$. With $e_3=(0,0,1)^T$, the ODE gives $u'(0)=-\nu M^{-1}Ke_3$, whose first component is $-3\nu/(2h^2)<0$. [step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 The linear field $u\mapsto-\nu M^{-1}Ku$ is globally Lipschitz. By [F1], $e^{-t\nu M^{-1}K}e_3$ solves the IVP, and [F2] makes it the unique solution. Since $u_1(0)=0$ and $u_1'(0)<0$ by step 2.1, the right difference quotient $u_1(t)/t$ is negative for all sufficiently small $t>0$. Hence the consistent-mass P1 semidiscrete diffusion is not positivity preserving, despite the nonnegative initial nodal vector. [F1, F2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $g:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$ be $L$-Lipschitz in the Euclidean norm ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]]), where $n\ge1$. Write $B(x,r)$ for the Euclidean ball ([[def-metric-ball]]). Let
$$C=\{p\in\mathbb R^n:g(p+h)=g(p)+Dg(p)h+o(|h|)\text{ as }h\to0,\ \det Dg(p)=0\}.$$
Then $g(C)$ is null in $\mathbb R^n$.

1.1 Fix $R\ge1$ and $0<\varepsilon<1$. For each $p\in C\cap B(0,R)$, differentiability gives a nonempty set of radii $0<r_p<1$ such that $|g(p+h)-g(p)-Dg(p)h|\le\varepsilon|h|$ whenever $|h|\le5r_p$. By [A1], choose one such radius for each $p$. Divide this ball family into dyadic radius classes $[2^{-j-1},2^{-j})$, largest first. In each class use [F3] on the set of subfamilies disjoint from all previously selected balls; the union of any chain is an upper bound, so a maximal disjoint subfamily exists. The union of selected subfamilies is disjoint. It is countable by [F8]: enumerate $\mathbb Q^n$ and assign to each ball the first rational point it contains; disjoint balls get distinct points. If a rejected ball has radius $r$ and meets a selected ball of radius $R_s>r/2$, then $r<2R_s$ and every point of the rejected ball is within $2r+R_s<5R_s$ of the selected center. Thus the fivefold dilates of a countable disjoint subfamily $B(p_i,r_i)$ cover $C\cap B(0,R)$. [A1, F3, F8, given, construct]

1.2 Put $v_n=\lambda(B(0,1))$. For any selected ball $B(p_i,r_i)$, the image $g(B(p_i,5r_i))$ lies within distance $5\varepsilon r_i$ of the linear image under $Dg(p_i)$ of the radius-$5r_i$ ball. The latter lies in a disk of radius $5Lr_i$ in a subspace of dimension $q\le n-1$. In orthonormal coordinates adapted to that subspace, the tube lies in a box with $q$ side lengths at most $10Lr_i+10\varepsilon r_i$ and $n-q$ side lengths $10\varepsilon r_i$. Subdivide each side into intervals of length at most $\varepsilon r_i$. The number of resulting boxes is at most $c_n(1+L/\varepsilon)^q$; each is contained in an axis-parallel cube of side at most $c_n\varepsilon r_i$. Since $q\le n-1$ and $\varepsilon<1$, their total cube volume is at most $C_n\varepsilon(L+1)^{n-1}r_i^n$ for a finite constant $C_n\ge1$ depending only on $n$. This constructs actual null covers without a rotation-invariance theorem or an area formula. [given, construct, algebra]

2.1 The selected balls lie in $B(0,R+1)$ and are pairwise disjoint. By [F5], each has measure $v_n r_i^n$, and the containing ball has measure $v_n(R+1)^n$. Countable additivity and monotonicity [F6] give $\sum_i r_i^n\le(R+1)^n$, using $v_n>0$. The Countable Choice hypotheses of [F5] and [F6] follow from [A1]. [A1, F4, F5, F6, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The fivefold balls in step 1.1 cover $C\cap B(0,R)$, and step 1.2 supplies a finite cube cover of each corresponding image with total volume at most $C_n\varepsilon(L+1)^{n-1}r_i^n$. By [A1], choose one such finite cover for each selected ball. Index these cubes by $(i,j)$; [F7] enumerates the resulting subset of $\mathbb N^2$. Every finite partial sum is at most $C_n\varepsilon(L+1)^{n-1}\sum_i r_i^n\le C_n\varepsilon(L+1)^{n-1}(R+1)^n$ by [F9] and step 2.1. For any cover budget $\delta>0$, take $\varepsilon=\min\{1/2,\delta/[C_n(L+1)^{n-1}(R+1)^n]\}>0$; the bound is then at most $\delta$. By [F1], $g(C\cap B(0,R))$ is null. [A1, F1, F7, F9, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The set $C$ is the union of $C\cap B(0,R)$ over integers $R\ge1$. Each image in this countable union is null by step 3.1; [F2] therefore gives that $g(C)$ is null. Its Countable Choice hypothesis follows from [A1]. [A1, F2, step 3.1] ∎

## Definition

Assume the Axiom of Choice when using the well-definedness results below; it is inherited conservatively from the published $L^2$ completeness supplier. Let $d\ge1$ and $s>d/2$. Write $L^2_s(\mathbb R^d)$ for the equivalence classes modulo Lebesgue-almost-everywhere equality of measurable complex functions $g$ satisfying
$$\|g\|_{L^2_s}^2=\int_{\mathbb R^d}(1+|\xi|^2)^s|g(\xi)|^2\,d\xi<\infty.$$
For such $g$, the **inverse Fourier representative** is the function
$$U_g(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^d}g(\xi)e^{2\pi i x\cdot\xi}\,d\xi.$$
The whole-space Bessel-potential space $H^s(\mathbb R^d)$ consists of these representatives, with norm $\|U_g\|_{H^s(\mathbb R^d)}=\|g\|_{L^2_s}$. For the admitted domain $\Omega$ of [[def-rbf-kernels-sites-and-augmented-interpolation]], define $H^s(\Omega)$ to be the restrictions $U|_\Omega$ of whole-space members, with the quotient norm
$$\|u\|_{H^s(\Omega)}=\inf\{\|U\|_{H^s(\mathbb R^d)}:U|_\Omega=u\}.$$
The whole-space inner product is $\langle U_g,U_h\rangle_{H^s}=\int (1+|\xi|^2)^s g(\xi)\overline{h(\xi)}\,d\xi$, linear in the first variable as in [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]].

## Statement

Let $n\ge0$, let $f\in C([a,b],\mathbb R)$ with $a<b$, and let
$p\in\mathcal P_n([a,b])$. If $E:=\|f-p\|_{\infty,[a,b]}>0$ and there are
$n+2$ ordered nodes $x_0<\cdots<x_{n+1}$ and a sign $\sigma\in\{-1,1\}$ such
that
$$f(x_i)-p(x_i)=\sigma(-1)^iE\qquad(0\le i\le n+1),$$
then no polynomial in $\mathcal P_n([a,b])$ has smaller uniform error than
$p$. Thus the displayed residual values are an a posteriori optimality
certificate.

1.1 Suppose $q\in\mathcal P_n([a,b])$ has $\|f-q\|_{\infty,[a,b]}<E$. At a node with $f(x_i)-p(x_i)=\sigma(-1)^iE$, the strict inequality gives $|f(x_i)-q(x_i)|<E$, so $q(x_i)-p(x_i)=(f(x_i)-p(x_i))-(f(x_i)-q(x_i))$ has the same nonzero sign as $\sigma(-1)^i$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 The polynomial $q-p$ has degree at most $n$ and, by step 1.1, has nonzero alternating signs at $n+2$ ordered nodes. This contradicts [F2]. Therefore no such $q$ exists, and $p$ is a best approximant. [given, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $n\ge0$, let $f\in C([a,b],\mathbb R)$ with $a<b$, and let
$p\in\mathcal P_n([a,b])$. If $E:=\|f-p\|_{\infty,[a,b]}>0$ and there are
$n+2$ ordered nodes $x_0<\cdots<x_{n+1}$ and a sign $\sigma\in\{-1,1\}$ such
that
$$f(x_i)-p(x_i)=\sigma(-1)^iE\qquad(0\le i\le n+1),$$
then no polynomial in $\mathcal P_n([a,b])$ has smaller uniform error than
$p$. Thus the displayed residual values are an a posteriori optimality
certificate.

1.1 Suppose $q\in\mathcal P_n([a,b])$ has $\|f-q\|_{\infty,[a,b]}<E$. At a node with $f(x_i)-p(x_i)=\sigma(-1)^iE$, the strict inequality gives $|f(x_i)-q(x_i)|<E$, so $q(x_i)-p(x_i)=(f(x_i)-p(x_i))-(f(x_i)-q(x_i))$ has the same nonzero sign as $\sigma(-1)^i$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 The polynomial $q-p$ has degree at most $n$ and, by step 1.1, has nonzero alternating signs at $n+2$ ordered nodes. This contradicts [F2]. Therefore no such $q$ exists, and $p$ is a best approximant. [given, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Example

Start with the odd-length data $(0,0,1)$. Define two explicit padding rules to length four. Periodic endpoint padding appends the first entry, giving $x_P=(0,0,1,0)$. Symmetric endpoint padding repeats the final entry, giving $x_S=(0,0,1,1)$. Applying the first Haar stage to the last pair gives $(a,d)=(1/\sqrt2,1/\sqrt2)$ for $x_P$ and $(a,d)=(\sqrt2,0)$ for $x_S$. The coefficients change because the boundary rule changes the pair presented to the filter.
1.1 For the periodic padding, the last pair is $(1,0)$; substitution gives average $(1+0)/\sqrt2=1/\sqrt2$ and detail $(1-0)/\sqrt2=1/\sqrt2$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 For the symmetric padding, the last pair is $(1,1)$; substitution gives average $(1+1)/\sqrt2=\sqrt2$ and detail $(1-1)/\sqrt2=0$. The two coefficient pairs differ. [given, F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎
cases.reason: The example fixes three nonempty data entries and pads them to four; no empty data padding convention is being specified.

## Statement

For every $J\ge1$ and $x\in\mathbb R^{2^J}$, the transform $T_H$ of [[def-na-finite-periodic-haar-transform]] is an orthogonal linear map. Its inverse is $T_H^{T}$ and $\|T_Hx\|_2^2=\|x\|_2^2$.

1.1 For any real $u,v$, the two outputs of one Haar pair satisfy $((u+v)/\sqrt2)^2+((u-v)/\sqrt2)^2=u^2+v^2$ by expansion and cancellation of the cross terms. Thus the pair map has matrix $2^{-1/2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}$ whose transpose times itself is the identity; applying it to disjoint coordinate pairs preserves the squared Euclidean norm. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 At stage $r$, the approximation coordinates are replaced by their pair-map outputs, with the second outputs recorded as $d^{(r)}$ and the first outputs passed to stage $r+1$. Therefore the map from the original vector to all stored stage outputs is a composition of the orthogonal pair maps and a coordinate permutation. It is orthogonal; hence its transpose is its inverse and it preserves squared norm. [given, step 1.1, F1, algebra] ∎
cases.evidence: The stage count is at least one, hence the input length is at least two and no empty vector transform is claimed; the pair identity itself permits zero coordinate values.

## Statement

Let $m,n\ge0$, $R>0$, and
$f(z)=\sum_{k=0}^\infty c_kz^k$ for $|z|<R$, with the series convergent
there. Suppose $q_0=1,q_1,\ldots,q_n$ solve the full normalized
Padé moment equations of [[alg-pade-coefficient-matching]]. Define
$p_k=\sum_{j=0}^{\min(k,n)}q_jc_{k-j}$ for $0\le k\le m$, and
$p(z)=\sum_{k=0}^mp_kz^k$, $q(z)=\sum_{j=0}^nq_jz^j$. Then
$$
f(z)-\frac{p(z)}{q(z)}=O(z^{m+n+1})\quad\text{as }z\to0.
$$
This is a local Taylor-matching statement only; it gives no pole-location
claim and no guarantee about analytic continuation beyond the neighborhood
where $f$ is given.

Here $h(z)=O(z^M)$ as $z\to0$ means there are constants $C,\delta>0$ such
that $|h(z)|\le C|z|^M$ whenever $0<|z|<\delta$.

1.1 Multiplication of the Taylor series of $f$ by $q$ gives coefficient $\sum_{j=0}^{\min(k,n)}q_jc_{k-j}$ at degree $k$. By [F1], for each $0\le k\le m$ this coefficient is $p_k$, so the coefficients of $qf-p$ through degree $m$ vanish. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 For each $m<k\le m+n$, write $k=m+\ell$ with $1\le\ell\le n$. The moment equation in [F1] says $\sum_{j=1}^nq_jc_{k-j}=-c_k$, exactly the assertion that the degree-$k$ coefficient of $qf$ is zero, because $q_0=1$. Therefore every coefficient of $qf-p$ through degree $m+n$ vanishes. [given, F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Analyticity implies $qf-p$ has a Taylor expansion whose first possibly nonzero term has degree at least $m+n+1$, so $qf-p=O(z^{m+n+1})$. By [A1], divide by the nonvanishing $q$ near zero to obtain the asserted local order for $f-p/q$. This proof uses only the solvable coefficient equations; it makes no claim about zeros of $q$ away from $0$. [given, A1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎
cases.evidence: Zero numerator coefficients are permitted, while the denominator constant coefficient is fixed to one; the local bound follows from denominator nonvanishing at the expansion origin, not from nonzero target values.

## Statement

Let $I,J$ be nonempty finite index sets with finite cluster trees, and construct the block-cluster tree as in [[def-hlr-cluster-trees-and-geometric-admissibility]]. Its terminal rectangles $\tau\times\sigma$ are pairwise disjoint and their union is $I\times J$.

1.1 If a block node $(\tau,\sigma)$ is split on the row side, its child rectangles $(\tau_i,\sigma)$ are disjoint and cover $\tau\times\sigma$ because the $\tau_i$ partition $\tau$. If it is split on the column side, the rectangles $(\tau,\sigma_j)$ are disjoint and cover $\tau\times\sigma$ because the $\sigma_j$ partition $\sigma$. Thus every split replaces a block by a disjoint cover of that block. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Each split increases the depth of one cluster in a finite tree, so along every branch the sum of the remaining row and column depths decreases and the recursion terminates. Induct on this finite sum: a terminal node is its own terminal cover; a nonterminal node has children whose terminal covers partition their respective rectangles by the induction hypothesis, and step 1.1 shows that their union is a disjoint cover of the parent rectangle. Applying this to the root $(I,J)$ proves that the terminal rectangles partition $I\times J$. [given, F1, step 1.1, induction]

3.1 Two distinct terminal rectangles lie in different children of their first common split, whose rectangles are disjoint by step 1.1. Hence all terminal rectangles are pairwise disjoint, completing the partition claim. [step 1.1, step 2.1] ∎
cases.evidence: The root row and column sets are explicitly nonempty, while empty subdivision branches do not arise because cluster children partition their parent as declared; terminal leaves cover the full root product.

## Definition

Let $\Omega=\mathbb C\setminus(-\infty,0]$. For $z\in\Omega$, choose any
integer $m\ge0$ with $\operatorname{Re}(z+m)>0$ and set

$$\ell(z)=\ell_+(z+m)-\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}\operatorname{Log}(z+j),$$

where the sum is empty if $m=0$ and $\ell_+$ and $\operatorname{Log}$ are
defined in [[def-loggamma-right-halfplane-branch]]. The next lemma proves that
this value is independent of the admissible $m$ and that $e^{\ell(z)}=\Gamma(z)$.
This is a continued branch of log-Gamma, not a separate principal
$\operatorname{Log}(\Gamma(z))$.

## Statement

Let $a,b>0$, $A,B\in\mathbb R^3$, $p=a+b$, $\mu=ab/p$, and $P=(aA+bB)/p$. Then for every $x\in\mathbb R^3$,
$$\exp(-a\|x-A\|_2^2)\exp(-b\|x-B\|_2^2)=\exp(-\mu\|A-B\|_2^2)\exp(-p\|x-P\|_2^2).$$
For any multi-indices $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb N_0^3$, the polynomial factor $(x-A)^\alpha(x-B)^\beta$ is a finite polynomial in $x-P$ of total degree at most $|\alpha|+|\beta|$. Moreover, $P=(a/p)A+(b/p)B$ lies on the closed segment from $A$ to $B$.

1.1 Since $p=a+b>0$, expand the left exponent using $\|x-A\|^2=\|x\|^2-2A\cdot x+\|A\|^2$. The quadratic and linear terms agree with $p\|x-P\|^2$ because $pP=aA+bB$. The remaining constant satisfies $$a\|A\|^2+b\|B\|^2-p\|P\|^2=\frac{ab}{p}\|A-B\|^2=\mu\|A-B\|^2,$$ by substituting $P=(aA+bB)/p$ and expanding the inner products. Thus $a\|x-A\|^2+b\|x-B\|^2=p\|x-P\|^2+\mu\|A-B\|^2$, which gives the exponential identity. [given, F1, algebra]

1.2 Each coordinate obeys $x_j-A_j=(x_j-P_j)+(P_j-A_j)$ and $x_j-B_j=(x_j-P_j)+(P_j-B_j)$. The finite binomial theorem expands each integer power as a polynomial in $x_j-P_j$ of no larger degree; multiplying the six coordinate polynomials gives a finite polynomial of total degree at most $|\alpha|+|\beta|$. [given, F1, algebra]

## Example

For $\kappa,\varepsilon>0$, on the real line set
$$u_\varepsilon(x)=\tanh\!\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt{2\kappa}\,\varepsilon}\right).$$
This is a stationary finite-energy heteroclinic profile for the one-dimensional Allen–Cahn Euler–Lagrange equation $-\kappa u''+f_\varepsilon(u)=0$. It is a profile example on $\mathbb R$, not a boundary-value solution on a bounded no-flux interval.

1.1 Put $a=(\sqrt{2\kappa}\,\varepsilon)^{-1}$. Differentiation gives $u_\varepsilon'=a(1-u_\varepsilon^2)$ and $u_\varepsilon''=-2a^2u_\varepsilon(1-u_\varepsilon^2)=2a^2(u_\varepsilon^3-u_\varepsilon)$. Since $2\kappa a^2=\varepsilon^{-2}$, $-\kappa u_\varepsilon''+f_\varepsilon(u_\varepsilon)=0$ by [F1]. [F1, algebra]

2.1 The limits of $u_\varepsilon$ at $\pm\infty$ are $\pm1$. Also $1-u_\varepsilon^2=\operatorname{sech}^2(ax)$, so the energy density is $\frac{1}{2\varepsilon^2}\operatorname{sech}^4(ax)$, which is integrable because it decays exponentially at both ends. Hence the profile has finite energy and joins the two wells. [given, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Fix an integer $p\ge1$. Let $\xi_0=-1$, $\xi_p=1$, and let $\xi_1<\cdots<\xi_{p-1}$ be the roots of $P_p'$ in $(-1,1)$; for $p=1$ this interior list is empty. By [[lem-legendre-gauss-lobatto-nodes-are-distinct]] these $p+1$ nodes are distinct. Define $\ell_j(x)=\prod_{0\le i\le p,\ i\ne j}(x-\xi_i)/(\xi_j-\xi_i)$, set $w_j=\int_{-1}^1\ell_j(x)\,dx$, and define the **Legendre–Gauss–Lobatto rule** by $Q_p(f)=\sum_{j=0}^p w_jf(\xi_j)$.

On $[-1,1]^d$ its tensor rule is $Q_p^{\otimes d}(f)=\sum_{j_1,\ldots,j_d=0}^p(w_{j_1}\cdots w_{j_d})f(\xi_{j_1},\ldots,\xi_{j_d})$. For an affine box map $F_K(\xi)=b_K+J_K\xi$, define the transported rule by $Q_{K,p}(f)=|\det J_K|Q_p^{\otimes d}(f\circ F_K)$. The nodal basis on $K$ is the pullback of $\prod_{r=1}^d\ell_{j_r}(\xi_r)$. The local mass and stiffness forms are respectively $m_{K,p}(v,w)=Q_{K,p}(vw)$ and $a_{K,p}(v,w)=Q_{K,p}(\nabla v\cdot\nabla w)$; any sampled coefficient is evaluated at the same quadrature nodes. Global forms are assembled by summing the cell forms.

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let a bounded open set $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$, $d\in\{2,3\}$, be the union of finitely many bounded knot-cell images with disjoint interiors and a face-to-face finite piecewise $C^1$ presentation. Let $m\ge1$ and let $v: \Omega\to\mathbb R^m$ be $C^1$ on the closure of each cell, with each component's cell gradient square integrable. ## Statement

For the finite tensor-product basis and weights of [[def-nurbs-patch-map-and-rational-spline-space]], the denominator satisfies $w_-\le W(\xi)\le w_+$, the rational basis is nonnegative and sums to one, and
$$\mathcal N_h=\{s/W:s\in S_h\},\qquad S_h:=\operatorname{span}\{N_\alpha:\alpha\in\mathcal I\}.$$
On each open knot cell, the rational basis functions are differentiable and
$$\nabla R_\alpha=\frac{w_\alpha}{W}\nabla N_\alpha-\frac{w_\alpha N_\alpha}{W^2}\nabla W.$$
In particular, if $G_N:=\max_\alpha\|\nabla N_\alpha\|_{L^\infty(\text{cells})}$ and $G_W:=w_+\sum_\alpha\|\nabla N_\alpha\|_{L^\infty(\text{cells})}$, then
$$\|\nabla R_\alpha\|_{L^\infty(\text{cells})}\le \frac{w_+G_N}{w_-}+\frac{w_+G_W}{w_-^2}.$$
These derivative bounds depend on the fixed degrees and knot cells; no degree-independent bound is asserted.

1.1 Each tensor product $N_\alpha$ is nonnegative by [F1]. On any open tensor knot cell, each coordinate lies in one nonempty knot interval, so finite distributivity and [F1] give $\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal I}N_\alpha(\xi)=\prod_{r=1}^d\left(\sum_{i_r}B^{(r)}_{i_r,p_r,\Xi_r}(\xi_r)\right)=1.$ Hence $0\le N_\alpha\le1$ on the cell. The endpoint values follow by the one-sided endpoint convention in [[def-b-spline-space-and-basis]]. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Since every coefficient $w_\alpha$ is between $w_-$ and $w_+$, the identity in step 1.1 yields $w_-\sum_\alpha N_\alpha\le W=\sum_\alpha w_\alpha N_\alpha\le w_+\sum_\alpha N_\alpha,$ so $w_-\le W\le w_+$. Thus each $R_\alpha$ is well-defined and nonnegative, and $\sum_\alpha R_\alpha=\frac{\sum_\alpha w_\alpha N_\alpha}{W}=1.$ For any coefficients $c_\alpha$, $\sum_\alpha c_\alpha R_\alpha=(1/W)\sum_\alpha(c_\alpha w_\alpha)N_\alpha$. Multiplication of each coefficient by the nonzero $w_\alpha$ is a bijection on the finite coefficient space, so the span equals $S_h/W$. [F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 On the open knot cell all $N_\alpha$ and $W$ are polynomial and $W\ge w_->0$ by step 2.1. The ordinary quotient rule gives the displayed gradient formula. Also $\|\nabla W\|_\infty\le\sum_\alpha w_\alpha\|\nabla N_\alpha\|_\infty\le G_W$ and $N_\alpha\le1$ by step 1.1. Applying these bounds to the quotient rule proves the stated derivative estimate. The finite number of polynomial pieces makes each $G_N$ finite. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

$$\mathcal N_h=\{s/W:s\in S_h\},\qquad S_h:=\operatorname{span}\{N_\alpha:\alpha\in\mathcal I\}.$$
On each open knot cell, the rational basis functions are differentiable and
$$\nabla R_\alpha=\frac{w_\alpha}{W}\nabla N_\alpha-\frac{w_\alpha N_\alpha}{W^2}\nabla W.$$
In particular, if $G_N:=\max_\alpha\|\nabla N_\alpha\|_{L^\infty(\text{cells})}$ and $G_W:=w_+\sum_\alpha\|\nabla N_\alpha\|_{L^\infty(\text{cells})}$, then
$$\|\nabla R_\alpha\|_{L^\infty(\text{cells})}\le \frac{w_+G_N}{w_-}+\frac{w_+G_W}{w_-^2}.$$
These derivative bounds depend on the fixed degrees and knot cells; no degree-independent bound is asserted.

## Statement

Let $t_0\le\cdots\le t_{n+p}$ be a clamped knot vector of degree $p$ as
in [[def-b-spline-space-and-basis]], with $a=t_0$ and $b=t_{n+p}$, and
let $\xi(v)_j=v_{j-1}$ be the one-based version of any zero-based knot
vector $v$. Write $B_{i,q,v}=B_{i+1,q,\xi(v)}$ for the basis in
[[def-b-spline-space-and-basis]]. Let a B-spline curve be
$C(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}P_iB_{i,p,t}(x)$ with $d\in\mathbb N$ and
$P_i\in\mathbb R^d$. Insert
one new knot $u$ strictly inside a nonempty span by
[[alg-single-new-b-spline-knot-insertion]], obtaining knots $t'$ and
controls $Q_i$. Write $B'_{i,q}=B_{i,q,t'}$. Then, for every $x\in[a,b]$,
$$C(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{n}Q_iB_{i,p,t'}(x).$$

1.1 Since the knot vector is clamped and the insertion span is nonempty, $p\le k\le n-1$. For bookkeeping only, set $P_{-1}=P_n=0$ and write $\lambda_j=\lambda_j^{(p)}$. The copy, blend, and shift ranges in [F2] give $Q_j=\lambda_jP_j+(1-\lambda_j)P_{j-1}$ for every $0\le j\le n$: in the copy range $\lambda_j=1$, in the blend range the algorithm's $\alpha_j$ is $\lambda_j$, and in the shift range $\lambda_j=0$. This also covers $p=0$, when the blend range is empty. Therefore the finite refined sum is $\sum_{j=0}^n Q_jB'_{j,p}=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}P_i[\lambda_iB'_{i,p}+(1-\lambda_{i+1})B'_{i+1,p}]$: the first control sum uses $P_n=0$, and in the second the change of index $i=j-1$ drops the $P_{-1}=0$ term. [A1, F1, F2, F3, algebra, construct]

2.1 By [F3], each bracketed basis combination in step 1.1 equals $B_{i,p,t}$. Substitution in that finite sum gives $\sum_{j=0}^nQ_jB_{j,p,t'}=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}P_iB_{i,p,t}=C(x)$. The recurrence and control algebra hold at interior knots under the right-cell convention, and at $b$ they hold by the prescribed left limits. Hence the refined expansion equals the original curve for every $x\in[a,b]$. [A1, F1, F3, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

defect $d=d_{m,n}(r)$, and put $N=m+n-d$. Then
$$\{u q-p v:u\in\mathcal P_m,\ v\in\mathcal P_n\}=\mathcal P_N.$$
For $r=0$ with the convention $p=0,q=1,d=n,N=m$, the same equality holds.

1.1 Define $\Phi:\mathcal P_m\times\mathcal P_n\to\mathbb R[x]$ by $\Phi(u,v)=uq-pv$. It is linear. If $r=0$, [F1] gives $p=0,q=1,d=n,N=m$, so $\Phi(u,v)=u$ and its image is exactly $\mathcal P_m=\mathcal P_N$. [F1, F5, construct]

2.1 Suppose $r\ne0$. If $(u,v)\in\ker\Phi$, then $uq=pv$. Multiply the Bézout identity in [F2] by $u$: $u=Apu+Bqu=Apu+Bpv=p(Au+Bv)$, so $u=hp$ for $h:=Au+Bv$. Substitution into $uq=pv$ and cancellation of the nonzero polynomial $p$ give $v=hq$. Conversely, every $(hp,hq)$ lies in the kernel. [F1, F2, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The degree bounds on $u=hp$ and $v=hq$, together with [F4], are equivalent to $\deg h\le\min(m-\deg p,n-\deg q)=d$; the zero polynomial $h$ is included. Thus the kernel has basis $(p,q),(xp,xq),\ldots,(x^dp,x^dq)$ and dimension $d+1$. By [F3] and [F5], the image dimension is $(m+n+2)-(d+1)=m+n+1-d=N+1$. [F1, F3, F4, F5, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 For all $u,v$, the degree of $uq-pv$ is at most $\max(m+\deg q,n+\deg p)=m+n-d=N$ by [F1] and [F4]. Hence the image is a subspace of $\mathcal P_N$, whose dimension is $N+1$ by [F5]. Its dimension from step 3.1 is also $N+1$, so the two spaces are equal. [F1, F4, F5, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Input: a finite $s\times s$ matrix $M$ of exact dyadic rationals with $s\ge1$. Output: the
sign of its exact determinant, including zero.

1. In row $i$, write each nonzero entry in reduced form
   $M_{ij}=a_{ij}/2^{b_{ij}}$ in reduced form with $b_{ij}\ge0$ and
   $a_{ij}$ odd when $b_{ij}>0$; write a zero entry with $b_{ij}=0$. Set
   $k_i=\max_j b_{ij}$ and form
   $N_{ij}=2^{k_i}M_{ij}$, an integer matrix.
2. Compute $\sum_{\pi\in S_s}\operatorname{sgn}(\pi)\prod_iN_{i,\pi(i)}$
   using arbitrary-precision integer arithmetic.
3. Return the sign of this integer sum.

The row scalings are positive, so [[lem-dyadic-determinant-integer-clearance-preserves-sign]]
shows that step 3 returns the sign of $\det M$.
cases.evidence: The matrix size is explicitly positive, so every row maximum is over a nonempty finite column list; no determinant of an empty matrix needs an additional convention.

## Statement
For $\tau>0$, integer $L\ge1$, and $x\in[0,1]$, put
$$\phi_{\tau,L}(x)=\sum_{n=-L}^{L}\exp\!\left(-\frac{\pi(x+n)^2}{\tau}\right),\qquad R_{\tau,L}=\frac{2\exp(-\pi L^2/\tau)}{1-\exp(-\pi L/\tau)}.$$
Then $0\le\phi_\tau(x)-\phi_{\tau,L}(x)\le R_{\tau,L}$, and the denominator defining $R_{\tau,L}$ is positive.

1.1 Let $q=\exp(-\pi L/\tau)\in(0,1)$ by [F2]–[F3]. For positive omitted indices write $n=L+h$ with $h\ge1$. Since $0\le x\le1$, $(x+n)^2\ge n^2=(L+h)^2\ge L^2+Lh$, so their sum is at most $\exp(-\pi L^2/\tau)\sum_{h\ge1}q^h$. By [F4] this is at most $\exp(-\pi L^2/\tau)/(1-q)$. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, algebra]

1.2 For negative omitted indices write $n=-(L+1+h)$ with $h\ge0$. Then $|x+n|=L+1+h-x\ge L+h$, and $(L+h)^2\ge L^2+Lh$. Their sum is at most $\exp(-\pi L^2/\tau)\sum_{h\ge0}q^h=\exp(-\pi L^2/\tau)/(1-q)$ by [F4]. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, algebra]

2.1 The two omitted tails are nonnegative and exhaust the indices outside $[-L,L]$. Adding steps 1.1 and 1.2 gives the claimed remainder $R_{\tau,L}$; [F3] also proves its denominator is positive. [step 1.1, step 1.2, F1, F3, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $T=(t_{i-j})_{0\le i,j<n}$ be any square Toeplitz matrix, and let $Z=Z_n$ be the lower shift of [[def-displacement-rank-generators-and-lower-shift]]. With $e_0=(1,0,\ldots,0)^T$ and $t_0=T_{00}$,
$$T-ZTZ^*=e_0(e_0^*T-t_0e_0^*)+(Te_0)e_0^*.$$
Consequently, its displacement rank is at most two. A width-two generator is
$$G=[\,e_0\ \ Te_0\,],\qquad H^*=\begin{bmatrix}e_0^*T-t_0e_0^*\\ e_0^*\end{bmatrix}.$$

1.1 For $i,j\ge1$, $(ZTZ^*)_{ij}=T_{i-1,j-1}=t_{(i-1)-(j-1)}=t_{i-j}=T_{ij}$ by [F2]. If $i=0$ or $j=0$, the corresponding entry of $ZTZ^*$ is zero because the first row of $Z$ and the first column of $Z^*$ are zero. Thus $T-ZTZ^*$ agrees with $T$ on its first row and first column and is zero in the interior. The displayed expression has exactly these entries: its first row is $e_0^*T$, its first column is $Te_0$, and its $(0,0)$ entry is $t_0$. [F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 The factorization in the statement multiplies to the displayed expression from step 1.1. It has two columns, so the rank of $T-ZTZ^*$ is at most two by the definition of rank and a product through $\mathbb C^2$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice and a neutral finite point-source configuration on the
cell $A\mathbb Z^3$ of
[[def-ewald-three-dimensional-periodic-source-data]]. Put
$$\widehat u(0)=0,\qquad \widehat u(k)=\frac{4\pi}{V|\kappa_k|^2} \sum_{i=1}^nq_i e^{-i\kappa_k\cdot x_i}\quad(k\ne0).$$
The polynomially bounded sequence $\widehat u(k)$ defines a periodic
distribution $u$ by Fourier pairing. It is the unique mean-zero periodic
distribution satisfying $-\Delta u=4\pi\rho$.

1.1 Define $\widehat u$ by the displayed coefficients. For $k\ne0$, $|\widehat u(k)|\le\frac{4\pi Q}{V|\kappa_k|^2},\qquad Q=\sum_i|q_i|,$ so the sequence is polynomially bounded. Under Countable Choice [A1], [F2] therefore defines a continuous periodic distribution $u$ with exactly these coefficients; its zero Fourier coefficient is zero by construction. [given, A1, F1, F2, algebra]

1.2 For a smooth periodic $\varphi$, use Countable Choice [A1], [F3], and the coefficient pairing of [F2] to compute $\langle u,-\Delta\varphi\rangle =V\sum_{k\ne0}\widehat u(k)|\kappa_k|^2\widehat\varphi(-k) =4\pi\sum_iq_i\sum_{k\ne0}e^{-i\kappa_k\cdot x_i}\widehat\varphi(-k).$ The sums converge absolutely by [F2]. Reindex the full Fourier series by $j=-k$; [F2] gives $\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}e^{-i\kappa_k\cdot x_i}\widehat\varphi(-k)=\varphi(x_i)$. The omitted zero term contributes $\widehat\varphi(0)\sum_iq_i=0$ by neutrality. Hence $\langle u,-\Delta\varphi\rangle=4\pi\sum_iq_i\varphi(x_i)=4\pi\langle\rho,\varphi\rangle$, proving $-\Delta u=4\pi\rho$. [given, A1, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 If $u_1,u_2$ are two mean-zero periodic distribution solutions, let $h=u_1-u_2$. Testing $-\Delta h=0$ against each character gives $|\kappa_k|^2\widehat h(k)=0$ for every $k\ne0$. Thus all nonzero Fourier coefficients of $h$ vanish, and its zero coefficient vanishes because both solutions have mean zero. Under [A1], the smooth Fourier partial sums converge in every smooth seminorm by [F2]; continuity of $h$ as a distribution then makes $h$ vanish on every smooth test function. Therefore $u_1=u_2$. [A1, F2, F3, algebra] ∎
cases.evidence: A single source can satisfy neutrality only with zero charge, giving zero nonzero-frequency coefficients and hence the zero mean-zero solution; lattice dimension stays fixed at three.

## Statement

Let $R>0$, $\lambda>0$, $\sigma\in\{-1,1\}$, and $H\in C_c^1((-R,R);\mathbb C)$. Then
$$\left|\int_{-R}^RH(u)e^{i\sigma\lambda u^2/2}\,du\right|\le\frac{6\|H\|_\infty+R\|H'\|_\infty}{\sqrt\lambda}.$$

1.1 Rescale $u=Rt$, put $\Lambda=\lambda R^2$, and define $\widetilde H(t)=H(Rt)$. If $\Lambda<1$, the integral is at most $2R\|H\|_\infty\le2\|H\|_\infty/\sqrt\lambda$, so the claim holds. Assume $\Lambda\ge1$, put $\delta=\Lambda^{-1/2}$, and split $[-1,1]$ into $[-\delta,\delta]$, $[\delta,1]$, and $[-1,-\delta]$. The central integral in the rescaled variable is at most $2\delta\|H\|_\infty$. [given, construct, algebra]

2.1 On $[\delta,1]$, [F1] and [F2] integrate by parts using $(i\sigma\Lambda t)^{-1}$ and $\widetilde H$; the boundary at $1$ vanishes because $\widetilde H$ is compactly supported in $(-1,1)$. ## Example

Take
$A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&1\\0&1&1\\1&1&2\end{bmatrix}$,
and select $I=J=(1,2)$. The resulting skeleton CUR factors reconstruct $A$ exactly.

1.1 Direct extraction gives $C=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&1\\1&1\end{bmatrix}$, $R=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&1\\0&1&1\end{bmatrix}$, and $W=I_2$. Since $I_2$ satisfies the four Penrose equations [F3], uniqueness [F4] gives $W^\dagger=I_2$; [F1] therefore gives the reconstruction $CR$. [given, A1, F1, F3, F4, algebra]

2.1 Multiplication yields $CR=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&1\\0&1&1\\1&1&2\end{bmatrix}=A$. The identity $I_2$ satisfies the Penrose equations [F3], hence equals $W^\dagger$ by uniqueness [F4]. The third row of $A$ is the sum of the first two, and the first two are independent, so $\operatorname{rank}(A)=2=\operatorname{rank}(W)$. Hence [F2] also applies and confirms the exact skeleton CUR identity. [A1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For the P2M, M2M, M2L, L2L and L2P formulas of [[alg-planar-laplace-fmm-fixed-order]], P2M gives the source moments about a leaf center, M2M gives exactly the same moments about a parent center, and the finite M2L coefficients are the degree-$0$ through degree-$p$ Taylor coefficients of the order-$p$ source multipole polynomial about the target center. L2L is exact re-centering of the resulting degree-$p$ polynomial, and L2P evaluates it exactly. For every $n\ge0$ define $M_n(C)=\sum_{j\in I_C}q_j(z_j-c_C)^n$; the algorithm stores only $n\le p$. For a far pair $(C,D)$ and $z$ in the target cell, the fixed-branch source potential also has the absolutely convergent outer expansion $M_0(C)L_{CD}(z-c_C)-\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}M_n(C)/(n(z-c_C)^n)$.

1.1 For $|w|<1$, the geometric series $1/(1+t)=\sum_{r=0}^{\infty}(-t)^r$ converges uniformly on each closed disk $|t|\le r_0<1$. Integrating it from $0$ to $w$ gives the analytic branch identity $\log(1+w)=\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}(-1)^{m+1}w^m/m$. [given, F1, algebra]

1.2 For a nonempty child cell $E$ of $C$, write $z_j-c_C=(z_j-c_E)+(c_E-c_C)$ and apply the finite binomial theorem to its $n$th power. Summing over the sources in each nonempty child and then over the nonempty children gives $M_n(C)=\sum_E\sum_{r=0}^n\binom nr(c_E-c_C)^{n-r}M_r(E)$ for every $n\le p$; empty children contribute zero. This is exactly the M2M pass. [F2, algebra]

1.3 If a parent local polynomial is $\sum_{k=0}^pL_k(z-c_D)^k$, put $z-c_D=(z-c_E)+(c_E-c_D)$ and expand each power. The coefficient of $(z-c_E)^j$ is $\sum_{k=j}^p\binom kjL_k(c_E-c_D)^{k-j}$; hence L2L exactly re-centers the polynomial without adding truncation error. [F2, algebra]

2.1 For a far pair $(C,D)$, put $z-c_C=D_0+x$ with $D_0=c_D-c_C$ and $|x|\le a_D$. Then $|D_0+x|\ge R-a_D>a_C$. Substituting $w=-(z_j-c_C)/(z-c_C)$ into the branch-normalized series from step 1.1 and summing the finite source set gives $M_0(C)L_{CD}(z-c_C)-\sum_{n\ge1}M_n(C)/[n(z-c_C)^n]$. The branch is $L_{CD}$ because both $z-c_C$ and $z-z_j$ lie in its disk and the difference of their logarithms is the series that vanishes at $z_j=c_C$. The convergence is absolute because $|z_j-c_C|/|z-c_C|<1$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 For a far pair put $D=c_D-c_C$, $x=z-c_D$ and $y=z_j-c_C$. By [F1], $|x-y|\le|x|+|y|<R=|D|$. The branch-normalized logarithm therefore has expansion $L_{CD}(D+x-y)=L_{CD}(D)+\sum_{m\ge1}(-1)^{m+1}(x-y)^m/(mD^m)$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Expand $(x-y)^m$ by the binomial theorem and set $m=n+k$. For $n\ge1,k\ge0$, the coefficient of $x^ky^n$ is $(-1)^{k+1}\binom{n+k-1}{k}/(nD^{n+k})$, since $\binom{n+k}{k}/(n+k)=\binom{n+k-1}{k}/n$. The terms with $n=0$ are $M_0L_{CD}(D)$ for $k=0$ and $(-1)^{k+1}M_0/(kD^k)$ for $k\ge1$; the terms with $k=0,n\ge1$ are $-M_n/(nD^n)$. Summing $y^n$ over sources replaces it by $M_n$, and retaining $0\le n,k\le p$ yields precisely the M2L formulas in [F2]. [F2, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 Substitution of a target point into the re-centered degree-$p$ polynomial is exactly L2P, and termwise differentiation gives its derivative formula. These are finite polynomial identities and require no additional convergence assumption. [F2, step 1.3, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Every overlap, kinetic, point-nucleus attraction, and two-electron Coulomb integral defined in [[def-cartesian-gaussian-primitives-and-contractions]] exists absolutely for finite Cartesian Gaussian contractions. The same holds after any fixed finite number of spatial derivatives or one derivative with respect to a primitive center or positive exponent. With nuclear positions fixed, if primitive centers remain in compact sets and all exponents remain in a compact subset of $(0,\infty)$, these differentiated integrands have a common integrable majorant. Thus differentiation with respect to primitive centers or exponents may be passed under any of these integrals.

1.1 Repeated product-rule differentiation shows that every fixed spatial or primitive-parameter derivative is a finite sum of polynomial-Gaussian terms. If centers $A$ range over compact sets and exponents satisfy $a\ge a_0>0$, then $\|x-A\|^2\ge\tfrac12\|x\|^2-\|A\|^2$. Each such term is therefore bounded by $K(1+\|x\|)^N e^{-a_0\|x\|^2/2}$ for finite $K,N$ uniform on those parameter sets. This majorant is integrable by [F2], so each pair product is in $L^1\cap L^\infty$; products involving $\Delta\psi$ have the same form. [given, F1, F2, algebra, L9]

2.1 The overlap and kinetic integrands are polynomial-Gaussian products and are absolutely integrable by step 1.1. For a nuclear center $C$, the pair product is bounded on $\|x-C\|<1$. To check local kernel integrability without a radial-coordinate formula, partition $0<\|z\|<1$ into $A_k=\{2^{-(k+1)}\le\|z\|<2^{-k}\}$: on $A_k$, $\|z\|^{-1}\le2^{k+1}$ and $A_k$ lies in a cube of volume $8\cdot2^{-3k}$, so $\int_{A_k}\|z\|^{-1}dz\le16\cdot4^{-k}$. The sum is $64/3$. Outside this unit ball the kernel is at most one, so the remaining integral is bounded by the pair product's $L^1$ norm. This proves absolute convergence of the point-nucleus attraction. [given, F1, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Let $f,g$ be two pair products from finite contractions; by step 1.1 they belong to $L^1\cap L^\infty$. On $\|x-y\|<1$, Tonelli [F3] and $z=y-x$ give the bound $\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty\int_{\|z\|<1}\|z\|^{-1}dz\le(64/3)\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty$ by the shell calculation in step 2.1. On the complement, $\|x-y\|^{-1}\le1$, giving bound $\|f\|_1\|g\|_1$. Hence the two-electron integrand is absolutely integrable, and [F4] supplies its product and iterated integral meanings. [given, F1, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Primitive-center and exponent derivatives only increase the polynomial degrees of the Gaussian factors; the singular centers $C$ and diagonal $x=y$ are fixed. The near-nucleus and near-diagonal estimates in steps 2.1 and 3.1 therefore apply uniformly to their difference quotients: [L8] bounds each quotient by the corresponding next parameter derivative, whose compact-uniform Gaussian majorant is given in step 1.1. Applying [F5] passes each derivative through the integral. Finite linearity extends every result from primitives to contractions. [given, F1, F3, F5, L8, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra, L9] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $(\mathcal U_m,
\mathcal Q_m)$ be reconstructions from
[[def-finite-volume-space-time-reconstruction]] for schemes using a continuous
consistent flux $F$ for a continuous physical flux $f$ as in
[[def-conservative-finite-volume-scheme]]. Suppose $h_m\to0$,
$\mathcal U_m\to u$ strongly in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R\times(0,T))$, and
for every bounded interval $I\subset\mathbb R$ and $T'<T$ there is
$M_{I,T'}<\infty$ such that $|\mathcal U_m|\le M_{I,T'}$ almost everywhere on
$I\times[0,T']$ for every $m$. Then $u$ is locally essentially bounded up to
the initial face and, for every bounded interval $I$ and $T'<T$,
$$ \|\mathcal Q_m-f(u)\|_{L^1(I\times(0,T'))}\longrightarrow0. $$

1.1 Fix a closed bounded interval $I$ and $T'<T$, with common state bound $M$ on $I\times[0,T']$. For $0<\epsilon<T'$, let $K=I\times[\epsilon,T']$. If $E=\{(x,t)\in K:|u(x,t)|>M\}$ had positive measure, then $E=\bigcup_{r\ge1}E_r$, where $E_r=\{(x,t)\in K:|u(x,t)|\ge M+1/r\}$. By countable subadditivity in [F3], some $E_r$ has positive measure. Since $|\mathcal U_m|\le M$ almost everywhere on $K$, it follows that $\|\mathcal U_m-u\|_{L^1(K)}\ge r^{-1}|E_r|>0$ for every $m$, contradicting strong $L^1$ convergence on $K$. Thus $|u|\le M$ almost everywhere on $K$. Taking $\epsilon=1/r$ for sufficiently large integers $r$ covers $I\times(0,T')$; any bounded interval is contained in a closed bounded one, so $u$ is locally essentially bounded up to $t=0$. [F3, given, algebra]

2.1 Fix $0<\epsilon<T'$ and a compact rectangle $K\subset\mathbb R\times[\epsilon,T']$. Enlarge its spatial interval by $1$; step 1.1 bounds $u$ there. The cutoff $v=u$ on this enlarged bounded rectangle and $v=0$ elsewhere is bounded and measurable, so [F3] makes $v\in L^1(\mathbb R^2)$. For all large $m$, $h_m<1$. By [F2], $\|u(\cdot+h_m,\cdot)-u\|_{L^1(K)}\to0$: the cutoff agrees with $u$ on $K$ and on $K+h_m$. Also $K+h_m$ is contained in one fixed compact enlargement $K'$ for all large $m$, so strong local convergence gives $\|\mathcal U_m(\cdot+h_m,\cdot)-u(\cdot+h_m,\cdot)\|_{L^1(K)}=\|\mathcal U_m-u\|_{L^1(K+h_m)}\le\|\mathcal U_m-u\|_{L^1(K')}\to0$. The triangle inequality gives $\mathcal U_m(\cdot+h_m,\cdot)\to u$ in $L^1(K)$. [A1, F2, F3, given, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Let $K$ be as in step 2.1, and choose a common bound $M$ on the enlarged rectangle. The square $S=[-M,M]^2$ is a nonempty closed box, hence compact by [F4]. Continuity of $F$ and [F5] bound $F$ on $S$; [F6] makes it uniformly continuous there. Put $a_m=\mathcal U_m(x,t)$ and $b_m=\mathcal U_m(x+h_m,t)$. Steps 1.1–2.1 show both converge to $u$ in measure on $K$, and all three values lie in $[-M,M]$ almost everywhere. For $\delta>0$, the set where either input error is at least $\delta$ has measure at most $\delta^{-1}$ times the sum of the two $L^1$ errors. Uniform continuity makes $|F(a_m,b_m)-F(u,u)|$ arbitrarily small off this set, while boundedness of $F$ controls it on the set. Thus $F(a_m,b_m)\to F(u,u)=f(u)$ in $L^1(K)$. By [F1], $\mathcal Q_m\to f(u)$ in $L^1(K)$. [A1, F1, F4, F5, F6, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 On $I\times(0,\epsilon)$, the local state bound on the interval enlarged by $1$ bounds both flux inputs, while step 1.1 bounds $u$. Continuity of $F$ and $f$ bounds $\mathcal Q_m$ and $f(u)$ there by one constant independent of $m$. Hence the integral of $|\mathcal Q_m-f(u)|$ over this strip is at most a constant times $|I|\epsilon$. Step 3.1 gives convergence on $I\times[\epsilon,T']$. Letting first $m\to\infty$ and then $\epsilon\downarrow0$ proves convergence on $I\times(0,T']$. [F1, F5, step 1.1, step 3.1, given, algebra] ∎

[[def-monotone-finite-volume-entropy-scheme]], with cell-time slabs
$I_j\times[t_n,t_{n+1})$ and $t_n=n\tau$. The **piecewise-linear time
interpolant** $W_{h,\tau}$ is constant in $x$ on each cell and, for
$t\in[t_n,t_{n+1})$, is
$$W_{h,\tau}(x,t):=(1-\theta)U_j^n+\theta U_j^{n+1},\qquad \theta:=\frac{t-t_n}{\tau},\qquad x\in I_j.$$
The piecewise-constant state $\mathcal U_{h,\tau}$ and face flux
$\mathcal Q_{h,\tau}$ use the convention of
[[def-finite-volume-space-time-reconstruction]]. Values on mesh boundaries
are irrelevant to the corresponding Lebesgue classes.

The interpolant is affine in time on each slab and has the scheme values at
both time endpoints. Its purpose here is to obtain time-uniform local compactness
and the strong initial trace; the weak-limit supplier is applied to
$\mathcal U_{h,\tau}$ after proving that the two reconstructions have the same
strong local limit.

## Definition

Fix $\gamma>1$ and admissible left/right primitive states
$(\rho_K,u_K,p_K)$, $K\in\{L,R\}$, with $\rho_K,p_K>0$ and
$c_K=\sqrt{\gamma p_K/\rho_K}$. Set
$$A_K=\frac{2}{(\gamma+1)\rho_K},\qquad B_K=\frac{\gamma-1}{\gamma+1}p_K.$$
For a trial star pressure $p>0$, the wave pressure response from side $K$ is
$$f_K(p)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{2c_K}{\gamma-1}\left[\left(\dfrac p{p_K}\right)^{(\gamma-1)/(2\gamma)}-1\right],&0<p\le p_K,\\(p-p_K)\sqrt{\dfrac{A_K}{p+B_K}},&p\ge p_K.\end{cases}$$
The two formulas agree at $p=p_K$. The **star-pressure residual** is
$$\Phi(p)=f_L(p)+f_R(p)+u_R-u_L,\qquad p>0.$$
This is a scalar root equation; it does not itself define a Riemann solution.
cases.evidence: The two wave sides are explicitly the left and right states, each with positive density and pressure; their response sum cannot be an empty side family.

## Statement

For any supplied Roe matrix, the Roe flux is consistent:
$\widehat f_{\rm Roe}(u,u)=f(u)$. For a finite periodic array define
$$U_j^{new}=U_j-\nu\bigl(\widehat f_{j+1/2}-\widehat f_{j-1/2}\bigr),$$
where $\widehat f_{j+1/2}=\widehat f_{\rm Roe}(U_j,U_{j+1})$ and indices are
modulo $n$, with $n\ge1$. For any scalar $\nu$, the update preserves the sum of cell states. The
Roe jump property is the defining matrix identity in
[[def-roe-linearization-and-flux]] and is not an entropy assertion.
1.1 If $u_L=u_R=u$, the jump is zero, so [F1] gives $\widehat f_{\rm Roe}(u,u)=\tfrac12(f(u)+f(u))=f(u)$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 Substituting the displayed periodic update into the sum of all cells gives $-\nu\sum_j(\widehat f_{j+1/2}-\widehat f_{j-1/2})$. Each interface flux occurs once with each sign, so the sum is zero. The Roe jump identity is not used in this telescoping argument and no entropy inequality follows from it. [given, F1, algebra] ∎
cases.evidence: The periodic cell count is explicitly at least one; at its minimum value both neighboring flux indices coincide and the single update conserves that cell state.
