## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $V,Q$ be real Hilbert spaces and let $F\in V\prime$, $G\in Q\prime$ be bounded data. Suppose bounded bilinear forms $a,b$ and $(u,p)\in V\times Q$ satisfy
$$a(u,v)+b(v,p)=F(v),\qquad b(u,q)=G(q)$$
for all $v\in V,q\in Q$. Let $V_h\subset V$, $Q_h\subset Q$ be finite-dimensional conforming subspaces, with $Q_h\ne\{0\}$ and discrete inf-sup constant $\beta_h:=\inf_{q_h\ne0}\sup_{v_h\ne0}b(v_h,q_h)/(\|v_h\|_V\|q_h\|_Q)>0$. Assume the **discrete** kernel coercivity $a(v_h,v_h)\ge\alpha_*\|v_h\|_V^2$ for every $v_h\in Z_h:=\{w_h:b(w_h,q_h)=0\text{ for all }q_h\in Q_h\}$, where $\alpha_*>0$. Put $M_a=\|a\|$, $M_b=\|b\|$. The Galerkin system with the same $F,G$ has a unique solution $(u_h,p_h)$. For any $w_h\in V_h$, $r_h\in Q_h$, define $\delta_u=\|u-w_h\|_V$, $\delta_p=\|p-r_h\|_Q$, $R_h=\beta_h^{-1}M_b\delta_u$, and
$$U_h=\delta_u+\alpha_*^{-1}\{M_a(\delta_u+R_h)+M_b\delta_p\}+R_h,$$
$$P_h=\delta_p+\beta_h^{-1}\{M_a(U_h+\delta_u)+M_b\delta_p\}.$$
Then $\|u-u_h\|_V\le U_h$ and $\|p-p_h\|_Q\le P_h$. In particular the pressure bound retains $\beta_h^{-1}$ explicitly; taking infima over $w_h,r_h$ gives the corresponding best-approximation bound.

1.1 Apply [F1] to $V_h,Q_h$ with the assumed $Z_h$-coercivity and discrete inf-sup constant $\beta_h$. Since the restricted forms are bounded, the Galerkin system with the same $F,G$ has a unique solution $(u_h,p_h)$. [A1, F1, given]

2.1 Fix $w_h,r_h$ and set $\theta_u=w_h-u_h$, $\theta_p=r_h-p_h$, $\eta_u=u-w_h$, $\eta_p=p-r_h$. Subtracting the discrete equations from the continuous equations gives $a(\theta_u,v_h)+b(v_h,\theta_p)=-a(\eta_u,v_h)-b(v_h,\eta_p)$ and $b(\theta_u,q_h)=-b(\eta_u,q_h)$. [A1, given, step 1.1]
3.1 The second identity implies $\|B_h\theta_u\|_Q\le M_b\delta_u$. By [F2] choose $r_u\in V_h$ with $B_hr_u=B_h\theta_u$ and $\|r_u\|_V\le R_h$. Then $z_h=\theta_u-r_u\in Z_h$. [A1, F2, step 2.1]

4.1 Test the first identity of step 2.1 with $z_h$. Since $b(z_h,\theta_p)=0$, $a(z_h,z_h)=-a(\eta_u,z_h)-b(z_h,\eta_p)-a(r_u,z_h)$. Discrete-kernel coercivity and boundedness imply, when $z_h\ne0$, $\|z_h\|\le\alpha_*^{-1}\{M_a(\delta_u+R_h)+M_b\delta_p\}$; if $z_h=0$ this bound is immediate. Therefore $\|u-u_h\|\le\|\eta_u\|+\|z_h\|+\|r_u\|\le U_h$. [given, step 2.1, step 3.1]

5.1 For any $v_h$, the first identity of step 2.1 gives $|b(v_h,\theta_p)|\le[M_a(\|\theta_u\|+\delta_u)+M_b\delta_p]\|v_h\|$. Taking the supremum and applying the discrete inf-sup yields $\|\theta_p\|\le\beta_h^{-1}\{M_a(U_h+\delta_u)+M_b\delta_p\}$. Hence $\|p-p_h\|\le\delta_p+\|\theta_p\|\le P_h$. [A1, F2, algebra, step 2.1, step 4.1] ∎
cases.evidence: The pressure subspace is expressly nonzero and a positive discrete inf-sup prevents an empty set of nonzero velocity tests; approximation competitors still include zero vectors in both linear spaces.

## Statement refuted

For a fixed tetrahedral edge $e$, the canonical edge-circulation functional $u\mapsto\int_eu\cdot t_e\,ds$ extends to a bounded linear functional on $H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$.

1.1 By [F4] with $r=1/2$ and $R=1$, choose $\eta\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3)$ with $\eta(0)=1$ and support in the unit ball. Choose $\varepsilon>0$ small enough that $b
otin a+\varepsilon\operatorname{supp}\eta$. Define $\psi_\varepsilon(x)=\eta((x-a)/\varepsilon)$ on $\Omega$ and $u_\varepsilon=
abla\psi_\varepsilon$. Then $\operatorname{curl}u_\varepsilon=0$ distributionally because distributional mixed derivatives commute, so [F1] gives $\|u_\varepsilon\|_{H(\operatorname{curl})}=\|u_\varepsilon\|_2$. A change of variables on $\mathbb R^3$ bounds $\|u_\varepsilon\|_2^2\le\varepsilon\|
abla\eta\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^3)}^2	o0$. [A1, F1, F4, construct, algebra]

2.1 By [F3] along $e$, $\ell_e(u_\varepsilon)=\psi_\varepsilon(b)-\psi_\varepsilon(a)=0-1=-1$ for every such $\varepsilon$. If a bounded extension existed, [F2] would give $|\ell_e(u_\varepsilon)|\le C\|u_\varepsilon\|_{H(\operatorname{curl})}$, which tends to zero by step 1.1, contradicting the fixed value $1$. Thus the edge moment is not bounded on the energy space; canonical interpolation cannot be applied to arbitrary H(curl) fields by these moments alone. [A1, F2, F3, step 1.1, contradiction] ∎

Mollification with radius less than $t/(2(1+L))$ produces a smooth function compactly supported in $\Omega$. The limit is the zero extension of its $L^2$ limit and proves the converse. Lipschitz boundaries have three-dimensional measure zero, since every graph has zero vertical section measure, so support in $\overline\Omega$ causes no additional $L^2$ term. ## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice.

Let $Q=(0,T)\times\Omega$ have finite measure, $1<p<\infty$, and let
$a(x,\xi)$ be a Carathéodory flux with the monotonicity and $p$-growth
hypotheses of [[def-pe12-monotone-diffusion-flux]], independent of time.
Suppose $\xi_n\rightharpoonup\xi$ in $L^p(Q;\mathbb R^d)$,
$q_n=a(x,\xi_n)\rightharpoonup q$ in $L^{p'}(Q;\mathbb R^d)$, and
$$\limsup_{n\to\infty}\int_Q q_n\cdot\xi_n \le\int_Qq\cdot\xi.$$
Then $q(x,t)=a(x,\xi(x,t))$ for almost every $(t,x)\in Q$.

1.1 Fix arbitrary $\eta\in L^p(Q;\mathbb R^d)$. By [F1]–[F3], monotonicity gives the finite nonnegative integrals $$0\le\int_Q(q_n-a(x,\eta))\cdot(\xi_n-\eta).$$ Expanding them and using the two weak convergences for the three terms linear in a weakly convergent factor, the limsup hypothesis yields $$0\le\int_Q(q-a(x,\eta))\cdot(\xi-\eta).$$ Indeed the expanded nonnegative sequence has limsup at most the displayed right-hand side, so that right-hand side cannot be negative. [F1, F2, F3, given, algebra]

2.1 Let $\zeta\in L^p(Q;\mathbb R^d)$ and $0<\varepsilon\le1$. Substitute $\eta=\xi+\varepsilon\zeta$ and $\eta=\xi-\varepsilon\zeta$ into step 1.1. After dividing by $\varepsilon$, the two inequalities give $$\int_Q(q-a(x,\xi+\varepsilon\zeta))\cdot\zeta\le0,\qquad \int_Q(q-a(x,\xi-\varepsilon\zeta))\cdot\zeta\ge0.$$ For either sign, the absolute value of the flux factor times $|\zeta|$ is bounded by $$C\bigl(g(x)+|\xi|^{p-1}+|\zeta|^{p-1}\bigr)|\zeta|,$$ which is integrable by [F3]; here $g(x)$ is viewed as constant in time and $Q$ has finite time length. Carathéodory continuity gives pointwise $a(x,\xi\pm\varepsilon\zeta)\to a(x,\xi)$ as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. Dominated convergence [F4] in both inequalities proves $\int_Q(q-a(x,\xi))\cdot\zeta=0$ for every $\zeta\in L^p(Q;\mathbb R^d)$. [F1, F3, F4, step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 Put $w=q-a(x,\xi)\in L^{p'}(Q;\mathbb R^d)$ and choose $\zeta=|w|^{p'-2}w$, defined as zero where $w=0$. Since $(p'-1)p=p'$, this $\zeta$ belongs to $L^p$, and step 2.1 gives $0=\int_Qw\cdot\zeta=\int_Q|w|^{p'}$. Thus $w=0$ almost everywhere, which is the claimed flux identification. [F3, step 2.1, algebra] ∎
cases.evidence: On a cylinder of zero measure the almost-everywhere conclusion and all integral inequalities are vacuous; on positive measure the test family contains zero and the signed perturbations needed in step 2.1.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice, any anchor set $D\subseteq V$ as in
[[def-anchored-finite-metric-graph-h1-space]], a mesh
$\mathcal T_h$ of [[def-metric-graph-p1-edge-mesh]], positive constants
$\kappa_e$ on the edges, and edgewise $u_e\in H^2(0,\ell_e)$ as in
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], with the
trace matching and anchor conditions of $V_D$. Let $I_hu$ be the edgewise
nodal linear interpolant. Then $I_hu\in V_h$ and
$$\left(\sum_{e\in E}\kappa_e\|(u_e-I_hu_e)'\|_{L^2(e)}^2\right)^{1/2} \le h\left(\sum_{e\in E}\kappa_e\|u''_e\|_{L^2(e)}^2\right)^{1/2}.$$

1.1 Fix an edge cell $K=[a,b]$ of length $h_K=b-a$. By [F1] and [F2], the continuous representative of $u_e$ has endpoint values and the representative of $u'_e$ is absolutely continuous. Thus the slope of the nodal interpolant on $K$ is $$s_K=\frac{u_e(b)-u_e(a)}{h_K} =\frac1{h_K}\int_a^b u'_e(y)\,dy.$$ The fundamental theorem in [F2] justifies this equality. [F1, F2, F4, A1, given]

2.1 For any $x\in K$, [F2] and [F3] give $$|u'_e(x)-s_K| \le\frac1{h_K}\int_a^b|u'_e(x)-u'_e(y)|\,dy \le\frac1{h_K}\int_a^b\sqrt{h_K}\|u''_e\|_{L^2(K)}\,dy =\sqrt{h_K}\|u''_e\|_{L^2(K)}.$$ Squaring and integrating over $x\in K$ yields $$\|(u_e-I_hu_e)'\|_{L^2(K)}^2 =\|u'_e-s_K\|_{L^2(K)}^2 \le h_K^2\|u''_e\|_{L^2(K)}^2.$$ The first equality holds because the derivative of the nodal interpolant is the constant slope $s_K$ on K. ## Definition

Assume Countable Choice. For $u\in H^1(K)$, use the facet traces of
[[lem-crouzeix-raviart-simplex-traces-and-green-identity]] and define its local
face-average interpolant by
$$I_K^{CR}u:=\sum_{F\subset\partial K}\left(\frac1{|F|}\int_Fu\,dS\right)\phi_{K,F},$$
where $\phi_{K,F}$ is the explicit polynomial in
[[def-crouzeix-raviart-local-p1-element]]. On a finite matching mesh, define
$I_h^{CR}u$ cellwise by $(I_h^{CR}u)|_K=I_K^{CR}(u|_K)$. For a global
$u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$, the cell traces agree on interior facets and vanish on
boundary facets, so this formula has the intended global Crouzeix–Raviart
degrees of freedom. The local estimate item proves its fractional
approximation bounds.

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice for the $L^2$ projection convention.

Suppose the three-generation marked refinement call completes and returns $\mathcal T_*\ge\mathcal T$, and let $\operatorname{osc}_\mathcal T(K)^2=h_K^2\|f-\Pi_K^0f\|_2^2$. For a Dörfler set $M_O$ with parameter $\theta_O\in(0,1]$,
$$\operatorname{osc}_{\mathcal T_*}^2\le\gamma_O\operatorname{osc}_{\mathcal T}^2,\qquad \gamma_O=1-\frac34\theta_O<1.$$

1.1 For each parent $K\in\mathcal T$, let $K'$ range over its descendants in $\mathcal T_*$, including $K'=K$ if it is unrefined. Nestedness of the piecewise-constant spaces gives $\sum_{K'\subset K}\|f-\Pi_{K'}^0f\|_{L^2(K')}^2\le\|f-\Pi_K^0f\|_{L^2(K)}^2.$ Indeed, the childwise projection space contains the parent constant space, and the $L^2$ orthogonal projection minimizes squared error. If $K\in M_O$, the completed call supplies three generations, so [F1] gives $h_{K'}^2\le h_K^2/4$ and the sum of descendant oscillations is at most one quarter of the parent oscillation. For every other parent, containment gives $h_{K'}\le h_K$, so its descendant oscillations sum to at most its original contribution. An unrefined cell retains its contribution exactly. [A1, F1, given, algebra]

2.1 Summing step 1.1 over refined parents gives $\operatorname{osc}_{\mathcal T_*}^2\le\operatorname{osc}_{\mathcal T}^2-\frac34\sum_{K\in M_O}\operatorname{osc}_{\mathcal T}(K)^2.$ Apply the bulk inequality [F2] to obtain the stated $\gamma_O$. If all oscillations vanish, both sides are zero and the same inequality holds. [A1, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎
cases.evidence: When the total oscillation is zero an empty bulk-marked set is allowed, and step 2.1 explicitly states the resulting zero inequality; positive total oscillation and positive bulk fraction require a nonempty marked set.

Suppose the three-generation marked refinement call completes and returns $\mathcal T_*\ge\mathcal T$, and let $\operatorname{osc}_\mathcal T(K)^2=h_K^2\|f-\Pi_K^0f\|_2^2$. For a Dörfler set $M_O$ with parameter $\theta_O\in(0,1]$,
$$\operatorname{osc}_{\mathcal T_*}^2\le\gamma_O\operatorname{osc}_{\mathcal T}^2,\qquad \gamma_O=1-\frac34\theta_O<1.$$

1.1 For each parent $K\in\mathcal T$, let $K'$ range over its descendants in $\mathcal T_*$, including $K'=K$ if it is unrefined. Nestedness of the piecewise-constant spaces gives $\sum_{K'\subset K}\|f-\Pi_{K'}^0f\|_{L^2(K')}^2\le\|f-\Pi_K^0f\|_{L^2(K)}^2.$ Indeed, the childwise projection space contains the parent constant space, and the $L^2$ orthogonal projection minimizes squared error. If $K\in M_O$, the completed call supplies three generations, so [F1] gives $h_{K'}^2\le h_K^2/4$ and the sum of descendant oscillations is at most one quarter of the parent oscillation. For every other parent, containment gives $h_{K'}\le h_K$, so its descendant oscillations sum to at most its original contribution. An unrefined cell retains its contribution exactly. [A1, F1, given, algebra]

2.1 Summing step 1.1 over refined parents gives $\operatorname{osc}_{\mathcal T_*}^2\le\operatorname{osc}_{\mathcal T}^2-\frac34\sum_{K\in M_O}\operatorname{osc}_{\mathcal T}(K)^2.$ Apply the bulk inequality [F2] to obtain the stated $\gamma_O$. If all oscillations vanish, both sides are zero and the same inequality holds. [A1, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Example

Let $\Gamma=S_1$ be the unit circle, let $s>0$, and scale the curve to $S_s$. For a smooth density $\lambda$ on $S_1$, set $\lambda_s(sy)=s^{-1}\lambda(y)$. Then
$$\operatorname{cap}(S_s)=s\operatorname{cap}(S_1),\qquad V_{S_s}\lambda_s(sx)=V_{S_1}\lambda(x)-\frac{\log s}{2\pi}\int_{S_1}\lambda\,ds.$$
In particular, the change in the layer trace depends only on the total charge, so it is a rank-one constant-mode term. For $\lambda=1/(2\pi)$ on $S_1$ and $s=e$, the total charge is one and the trace changes by $-1/(2\pi)$.

1.1 Apply [F1] with $K=S_1$ and $\Gamma=S_1$ to obtain both scaling identities in the Example. The functional $\lambda\mapsto\int_{S_1}\lambda ds$ has one-dimensional range, and its output is a constant function, so the trace correction is rank at most one. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 For $\lambda=1/(2\pi)$ on the unit circle, $\int_{S_1}\lambda ds=(1/(2\pi))(2\pi)=1$. Substituting $s=e$ into the correction gives $-(\log e)/(2\pi)=-1/(2\pi)$. Any zero-total-charge density has no scale correction by the same formula. [step 1.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Definition

For the finite system of [[def-na-finite-state-discounted-bellman-system]],
order each finite set $A_i$ by its declared indices and put
$P=\prod_{i\in S}|A_i|$. The procedure takes an evaluation budget $K\ge1$
(default $K=P$) and proceeds as follows.

1. Initialize $\pi_0(i)$ to the least-index action in $A_i$.
2. For the current policy $\pi_k$, solve exactly
   $A^{\pi_k}V^k=r^{\pi_k}$.
3. Form the strict-improvement set
   $$J_k=\left\{i:\max_{a\in A_i}(Q_i^aV^k+r_i^a)>Q_i^{\pi_k(i)}V^k+r_i^{\pi_k(i)}\right\},$$
   where $Q_i^aV=\sum_jq^a_{ij}V_j$.
4. If $J_k=\varnothing$, return $(\texttt{converged},\pi_k,V^k)$.
5. If $J_k\ne\varnothing$ and $k+1=K$, return
   $(\texttt{budget\_exhausted},\pi_k,V^k)$; this status makes no Bellman-solution
   claim.
6. Otherwise, at each $i\in J_k$ switch to the least-index maximizing action
   in $A_i$; retain $\pi_k(i)$ at every state outside $J_k$ and continue.

The policy matrix solve is well-defined by
[[lem-na-discounted-bellman-policy-matrix-inverse-positive]]. A budget of $P$
policy evaluations is sufficient by the theorem below.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $k\ge1$, $n_i\ge1$, let $U_i\subseteq\mathbb R^{n_i}$ be open, and let $u_i:U_i\to\mathbb R$ be upper semicontinuous, meaning $\limsup_{y\to x}u_i(y)\le u_i(x)$ at each $x\in U_i$. Suppose $\phi$ is $C^2$ near $z=(z_1,\ldots,z_k)\in\prod_iU_i$ and $\sum_i u_i(x_i)-\phi(x)$ has a local maximum at $z$. Set $A=D^2\phi(z)$, and let $\|A\|$ be its Euclidean operator norm ([[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]]). For every $\varepsilon>0$ there are $X_i\in\mathbb S^{n_i}$ such that
$$(D_i\phi(z),X_i)\in\overline J^{2,+}u_i(z_i),$$
and
$$-\left(\varepsilon^{-1}+\|A\|\right)I\ \le\ \operatorname{diag}(X_1,\ldots,X_k)\ \le\ A+\varepsilon A^2.$$
Here all jets are full Euclidean jets. In particular one may take each $U_i$ to be a space-time domain of dimension $d+1$. For a lower semicontinuous function $v$, applying the theorem to $-v$ and then negating its jet gives the corresponding closed subjet for $v$.

1.1 First prove the quadratic compactly localized case. Translate to $z=0$, subtract $u_i(0)$ and the affine terms $D_i\phi(0)\cdot x_i$, and suppose $u_i(0)=0$ and $w(x):=\sum_i u_i(x_i)\le x^{\mathsf T}Ax/2$ on compact neighborhoods $K_i$ of zero. Extend the restrictions by $-\infty$ off $K_i$, set $\lambda=\varepsilon^{-1}+\|A\|>0$ and $B=A+\varepsilon A^2$, and write $h=x-\xi$. The identity $|\varepsilon^{-1/2}h-\varepsilon^{1/2}A\xi|^2\ge0$ gives $x^{\mathsf T}Ax\le\xi^{\mathsf T}B\xi+\lambda|x-\xi|^2$. Define $\widehat u_i$ by [F2] and $f(\xi)=\sum_i\widehat u_i(\xi_i)$. The supremum separates over the finite compact product, so $f(\xi)=\sup_x\{w(x)-\lambda|x-\xi|^2/2\}\le\xi^{\mathsf T}B\xi/2$. Each $\widehat u_i(0)\ge0$, while $f(0)\le0$, so all are zero; also $f+\lambda|\xi|^2/2$ is convex. [F2, F4, algebra, construct]

2.1 The function $F(\xi)=f(\xi)-\xi^{\mathsf T}B\xi/2-|\xi|^4$ has a strict maximum at zero and is locally semiconvex, since the Hessian of the subtracted polynomial is bounded on every fixed ball. Apply [F3] outside the null set where $f$ lacks a Peano expansion: for each $n$, [A1] selects $|\xi_n|<1/n$, $|q_n|\le1/n$ so $F+q_n\cdot\xi$ has a local maximum at $\xi_n$ and $f$ has expansion $(p_n,Z_n)$ there. Restricting to lines gives $p_n=B\xi_n+4|\xi_n|^2\xi_n-q_n$ and $Z_n\le B+8\xi_n\xi_n^{\mathsf T}+4|\xi_n|^2I$; convexity of $f+\lambda|\xi|^2/2$ gives $Z_n\ge-\lambda I$. Thus $p_n\to0$ and $Z_n$ is bounded. AC supplies the countable selections and is inherited from [F3]. [A1, step 1.1, F3, algebra, choose]

3.1 Separability makes $Z_n$ block diagonal: each coordinate restriction gives the corresponding Peano expansion of $\widehat u_i$, and summing those expansions gives a second expansion of $f$ with Hessian $\operatorname{diag}(Z_{n,11},\ldots,Z_{n,kk})$. Uniqueness follows because a quadratic form that is $o(|h|^2)$ vanishes on every direction and hence by polarization. Set $X_{n,i}=Z_{n,ii}$. The transfer in [F2] gives $y_{n,i}=\xi_{n,i}+p_{n,i}/\lambda$, $(p_{n,i},X_{n,i})\in J^{2,+}u_i(y_{n,i})$, and $u_i(y_{n,i})=\widehat u_i(\xi_{n,i})+|p_{n,i}|^2/(2\lambda)$. Since $y_{n,i}\to0$, they eventually lie inside $K_i$; continuity of $\widehat u_i$ gives $u_i(y_{n,i})\to0=u_i(0)$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, F1, F2, algebra]

$$(D_i\phi(z),X_i)\in\overline J^{2,+}u_i(z_i),$$
and

## Statement

Let $a<b$, $s\ge1$, $\omega\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$, $f\in C^s[a,b]$, and $g\in C^{s+1}[a,b]$ be real with $|g'|\ge c>0$. Use a nonsingular collocation system from [[alg-na-levin-collocation-quadrature]]. Write $A_{jk}=L_\omega\psi_k(x_j)$, $y_j=f(x_j)$, $c=A^{-1}y$, $p=\sum_kc_k\psi_k$, $Q=p(b)e^{i\omega g(b)}-p(a)e^{i\omega g(a)}$, and $r=f-L_\omega p$. Assume $\psi_k\in C^{s+1}[a,b]$. Then
$$I_\omega(f,g;[a,b])-Q=I_\omega(r,g;[a,b])=\sum_{j=0}^{s-1}\frac{(-1)^j}{(i\omega)^{j+1}}\left[\frac{T_g^jr(x)}{g'(x)}e^{i\omega g(x)}\right]_a^b+\frac{(-1)^s}{(i\omega)^s}I_\omega(T_g^sr,g;[a,b]).$$
Put $E_j=|T_g^jf(a)/g'(a)|+|T_g^jf(b)/g'(b)|$, $V_j=\|v_j(a)\|_2+\|v_j(b)\|_2$ for $v_{j,k}(x)=T_g^j(L_\omega\psi_k)(x)/g'(x)$, and $K_s=(\sum_k\|T_g^s(L_\omega\psi_k)\|_\infty^2)^{1/2}$. Then
$$|I_\omega(f,g)-Q|\le\sum_{j=0}^{s-1}\frac{E_j+\|A^{-1}\|_2\|y\|_2V_j}{|\omega|^{j+1}}+\frac{b-a}{|\omega|^s}\left(\|T_g^sf\|_\infty+\|A^{-1}\|_2\|y\|_2K_s\right).$$
If an approximate coefficient vector $\widehat c$ has exact residual $\rho=A\widehat c-y$ and endpoint vector $d_k=\psi_k(b)e^{i\omega g(b)}-\psi_k(a)e^{i\omega g(a)}$, its output satisfies
$$|Q(\widehat c)-Q|\le\|d\|_2\|A^{-1}\|_2\|\rho\|_2=\|d\|_2\frac{\kappa_2(A)}{\|A\|_2}\|\rho\|_2.$$
If $B_s$ denotes the right-hand side of the preceding collocation bound, then
$$|I_\omega(f,g)-Q(\widehat c)|\le B_s+\|d\|_2\|A^{-1}\|_2\|\rho\|_2.$$
All vector norms are Euclidean, $\|A\|_2=\sup_{\|v\|_2=1}\|Av\|_2$ is the induced matrix norm, and $\kappa_2(A)=\|A\|_2\|A^{-1}\|_2$.
Thus a small nodal residual alone does not provide an integral-error bound; the smooth residual terms and inverse solve amplification are also required.

1.1 For any $p\in C^1[a,b]$, [F2] gives $(pe^{i\omega g})'=(L_\omega p)e^{i\omega g}$. Apply [F3] to the real and imaginary components of $p$ and $e^{i\omega g}$; the product rule and cancellation of the two $i\omega g'p$ terms yield $I_\omega(L_\omega p,g)=[pe^{i\omega g}]_a^b$. With $p$ from [F1] and $r=f-L_\omega p$, linearity gives $I_\omega(f,g)-Q=I_\omega(r,g)$. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

1.2 The coefficient equations imply $A(\widehat c-c)=\rho$, so $\widehat c-c=A^{-1}\rho$. The endpoint formula is linear in the coefficient vector, hence $Q(\widehat c)-Q=d^\top A^{-1}\rho$. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 The hypotheses on $f,g,\psi_k$ make $r\in C^s[a,b]$. Apply [F4] to $r$ to obtain the displayed exact expansion and bound its integral remainder by $(b-a)|\omega|^{-s}\|T_g^sr\|_\infty$. [given, F4, step 1.1]

2.2 By [F5], $|d^\top A^{-1}\rho|\le\|d\|_2\|A^{-1}\|_2\|\rho\|_2$. The definition $\kappa_2(A)=\|A\|_2\|A^{-1}\|_2$ and nonsingularity give the displayed condition-number form. [F1, F5, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Since $c=A^{-1}y$, $\|c\|_2\le\|A^{-1}\|_2\|y\|_2$. Linearity of $T_g$ gives $T_g^jr=T_g^jf-\sum_kc_kT_g^j(L_\omega\psi_k)$. At each endpoint, [F5] bounds the corresponding divided sum by $\|c\|_2\|v_j(a)\|_2$ or $\|c\|_2\|v_j(b)\|_2$; on the interval it bounds $\|\sum_kc_kT_g^s(L_\omega\psi_k)\|_\infty$ by $\|c\|_2K_s$. Substitution in the expansion from step 2.1 gives the stated $E_j,V_j,K_s$ bound. [given, F4, F5, step 2.1, algebra]
4.1 The triangle inequality combines the exact-collocation bound in step 3.1 with step 2.2, giving the stated integral bound for $Q(\widehat c)$. [step 3.1, step 2.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For every finite full-dimensional dyadic planar site set, a dyadic supertriangle can be chosen to contain every input site strictly and to have all three vertices strictly outside every circumcircle through a noncollinear input triple. If the input has no three collinear and no four cocircular sites, the supertriangle can additionally be chosen so the augmented set has no three collinear sites and no four cocircular sites.

1.1 For each noncollinear triple $(a,b,c)$ from $P$, its center $o$ is uniquely determined by
$$2o\cdot(b-a)=\|b\|^2-\|a\|^2,\qquad 2o\cdot(c-a)=\|c\|^2-\|a\|^2.$$

## Example

This example shows why the operation theorem records tree depth, node count, and list counts explicitly. In the square $[-1/2,1/2]^2$, place two distinct unit charges at $z_1=0$ and $z_2=2^{-M}$ for an integer $M\ge3$, and refine a dyadic quadtree until every leaf has occupancy at most $1$.

1.1 At depth $h$ the cell along the corner path containing $0$ has side length $2^{-h}$. For every $h<M$, $2^{-M}<2^{-h}$, so both $0$ and $2^{-M}$ lie in that same cell; at the next split the second point is on the midpoint boundary and is assigned to the upper child, while $0$ is assigned to the lower child. Therefore the tree has a nonempty path through depth $M$ and at least $M+1$ nonempty cells, although $N=2$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 With fixed $p=1$, $Np^2=2$ is constant as $M$ varies, whereas the tree-node count and per-node pass visits grow at least linearly in $M$. Thus no work bound with a constant depending only on $N$ and $p$ follows for arbitrarily clustered inputs; the explicit linear-size level-restriction required in [F2] fails uniformly across this family. [given, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let a finite open-boundary TT have order $d\ge2$ and be in the following mixed gauge about a one-site or two-site center window $J=[k,k+w-1]$, where $w\in\{1,2\}$: every core strictly left of $J$ is left-isometric and every core strictly right of $J$ is right-isometric. The center coefficient array has shape $r_{k-1}\times n_k\times\cdots\times n_{k+w-1}\times r_{k+w-1}$, with boundary ranks interpreted as one, and $x$ is its vectorization in the fixed lexicographic order. Hold every core outside $J$ fixed. Contracting the fixed prefix and suffix defines a linear embedding $E$ from center coefficients to the full tensor space. Then $E^*E=I$, so $\|Ex\|_F=\|x\|_2$. For every finite Hermitian Hamiltonian input $H$, the effective matrix
$$H_{\mathrm{eff}}:=E^*HE$$
is Hermitian and satisfies
$$\langle Ex,HEx\rangle_F=x^*H_{\mathrm{eff}}x.$$

1.1 Let $L_j$ be the prefix interface through site $j$, with rows indexed by $(i_1,\ldots,i_j)$ and columns by $\alpha_j$. Put $L_0=[1]$. For $j<k$, its recurrence is $L_j=(L_{j-1}\otimes I_{n_j})G_j^{(L)}$, where $G_j^{(L)}$ is the left matricization from [F3]. If $L_{j-1}^*L_{j-1}=I$, then $(L_{j-1}\otimes I)^*(L_{j-1}\otimes I)=I\otimes I$ and hence $L_j^*L_j=G_j^{(L)*}G_j^{(L)}=I$ by [F3]. Induction gives $L_{k-1}^*L_{k-1}=I$. For the suffix, put $R_{d+1}=[1]$ and contract from right to left: for $j>k+w-1$, $R_j=G_j^{(R)}(I_{n_j}\otimes R_{j+1})$, with rows indexed by $\alpha_{j-1}$ and columns by $(i_j,\ldots,i_d)$. Since $R_{j+1}R_{j+1}^*=I$ implies $(I\otimes R_{j+1})(I\otimes R_{j+1})^*=I\otimes I$, the right-isometry in [F3] gives $R_jR_j^*=G_j^{(R)}G_j^{(R)*}=I$. Induction yields $R_{k+w}R_{k+w}^*=I$. [given, F3, induction, algebra]

2.1 By [F1], the full array entries are the finite contractions of the fixed cores with the center coefficients. Expand $\langle Ex,Ey\rangle_F$ using the conjugate-first finite sum in [F2], and first sum over the physical prefix and suffix indices. Those sums replace the interface factors by $L^*L=I$ and $RR^*=I$ from step 1.1. The remaining finite sum is exactly $\langle x,y\rangle_F$. Hence $E^*E=I$ and $\|Ex\|_F=\|x\|_2$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 By [F1], $H^*=H$. Therefore $H_{\mathrm{eff}}^*=(E^*HE)^*=E^*H^*E=E^*HE=H_{\mathrm{eff}}$. Associativity of finite matrix multiplication gives $\langle Ex,HEx\rangle_F=x^*E^*HEx=x^*H_{\mathrm{eff}}x$, as claimed. [F1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the continuous stabilizability and detectability hypotheses of [[thm-care-stabilizing-psd-solution-and-value]], and start exact mode of [[alg-finite-budget-newton-kleinman-policy-iteration]] from a supplied stabilizing $K_0$. Every closed loop $A_j=A-BK_j$ is Hurwitz, every exact Lyapunov matrix $X_j$ is positive semidefinite, and $X_{j+1}\preceq X_j$. The sequence converges to the unique stabilizing CARE solution $X_*$. Once $j$ is sufficiently large, there is a finite constant $C$ such that
$$\|X_{j+1}-X_*\|_F\le C\|X_j-X_*\|_F^2.$$

## Statement

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $b\in C^2(\mathbb R)$ and consider a sequence of full-line uniform hydrostatic HLL grids from [[def-pe05-hydrostatic-hll-scheme]] with widths $d_k\to0$ and time steps $\tau_k\to0$. Set $I_i^k=[id_k,(i+1)d_k)$, $x_i^k=(i+\tfrac12)d_k$, $t_n^k=n\tau_k$, and $J_n^k=[t_n^k,t_{n+1}^k)$, and sample $b_i^k=b(x_i^k)$. On $I_i^k\times J_n^k$, let $\mathcal U_k=(h_k,m_k)$ and $u_k$ be the piecewise-constant state and primitive-velocity reconstructions, with $m_k=h_ku_k$, $u_k=0$ on dry cells, and $U_i^{k,n}\in K$. Define $\mathcal F_k=\widehat F_{i+1/2}^{k,n}$ and $\mathcal S_k=S_i^{k,n}$ on that same slab, using the sampled bed. Assume that on every compact rectangle in $\mathbb R\times[0,T)$, including the initial layer, the depths and velocities are uniformly bounded; that on every compact rectangle in $\mathbb R\times(0,T)$, $h_k\to h$ and $u_k\to u$ strongly in $L^1$ and $m_k\to m=hu$ strongly in $L^1$; that $u=0$ almost everywhere where $h=0$; and that the initial reconstructions converge locally in $L^1$ to $U_0=(h_0,m_0)$. Then $U=(h,m)$ satisfies, for every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R\times[0,T);\mathbb R^2)$,
$$\int_0^T\int_{\mathbb R}\left(U\cdot\varphi_t+F(U)\cdot\varphi_x+(0,-ghb_x)\cdot\varphi\right)\,dx\,dt+\int_{\mathbb R}U_0(x)\cdot\varphi(x,0)\,dx=0.$$
Thus the limit is a locally bounded distributional weak solution of the shallow-water balance law in [[def-pe05-shallow-water-balance-law]]. Strong convergence, primitive-velocity convergence and the source-quadrature hypotheses are assumptions; this theorem proves no compactness, entropy inequality or convergence rate.

1.1 By [F5], applied to the nonnegative bulk and initial depths, the strong local convergences, $m=hu$, the dry-velocity convention and the local initial velocity bound, both $U$ and $U_0$ belong to $K$ almost everywhere. Thus $F(U)$ in the weak formulation is defined. [F5, given]

1.2 Fix $\varphi$ and choose $N_k$ so that $\varphi$ vanishes for $t\ge t_{N_k-1}^k$ for all sufficiently large $k$. Apply [F2] to the actual states, shared face fluxes and source terms of the scheme; its exact finite sum is zero for each such $k$. [F1, F2, given, choose]

1.3 The initial term in [F2] tends to $\int_{\mathbb R}U_0(x)\cdot\varphi(x,0)\,dx$. Indeed, on each cell-time slab touching $t=0$, the averaged test differs from $\varphi(x,0)$ by at most $C_\varphi(d_k+\tau_k)$, and the uniform state bound including the initial layer makes the sum of these quadrature errors tend to zero on the fixed compact support. The initial reconstruction convergence then gives the claimed limit. [F2, given, algebra]

1.4 The time-difference sum in [F2] differs from $\int_0^T\int \mathcal U_k\cdot\varphi_t$ by $O(\tau_k)$. Taylor's formula in time makes each difference of adjacent cell-time test averages equal to the integral of $\varphi_t$ over the current slab, up to $C_\varphi\tau_k^2$ after spatial averaging; the uniform state bound and the $O(d_k^{-1}\tau_k^{-1})$ cells/slabs meeting the support give total error $O(\tau_k)$. The omitted initial-slab integral is also $O(\tau_k)$. [F2, given, algebra]

1.5 The face-flux sum in [F2] differs from $\int_0^T\int\mathcal F_k\cdot\varphi_x$ by $O(d_k)$. For each cell, the difference of adjacent test averages is the spatial average of $\int_0^{d_k}\varphi_x(x+s,t)\,ds$; replacing this average by $\varphi_x(x,t)$ has error at most $C_\varphi d_k^2\tau_k$ per cell-time slab. The local depth and velocity bounds give $h^*\le H$, $|u^*|\le M$, and wave speeds at most $M+\sqrt{gH}$. The physical fluxes and reconstructed states are bounded; in the middle HLL branch its equivalent convex-combination formula has coefficient $\alpha\beta/(\alpha+\beta)\le\max(\alpha,\beta)$, so the face fluxes are uniformly bounded as well. The number of cells/slabs meeting the support then gives the stated total error. The source sum in [F2] is exactly $\int_0^T\int\mathcal S_k\cdot\varphi$ because $\mathcal S_k$ is constant on each slab. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 Choose a compact spatial interval containing the test support and all cells meeting it for sufficiently large $k$, and choose $T_0<T$ beyond the temporal support. On this compact rectangle the hypotheses give uniform bounds for $h_k,u_k$ through $t=0$; the interior strong limits inherit the same essential bounds. Hence $\mathcal U_k$, $U$, $F(U)$ and the products with the fixed test derivatives are uniformly bounded. Step 1.5 supplies a uniform bound for $\mathcal F_k$. For sufficiently large $k$, $d_k\le1$, and [F6] together with the local bounds on $b'$ and the depths gives a uniform bound for $\mathcal S_k$; the limit source $(0,-ghb_x)$ is bounded too. Thus the contributions of all state, flux and source integrals from the initial layer $[0,\varepsilon]$ are bounded by $C\varepsilon$, uniformly in sufficiently large $k$ and for the limit integrands. On the remaining compact rectangle with $t\ge\varepsilon$, the assumed strong convergence gives convergence of the state integral, [F4] gives convergence of the face-flux integral, and [F3] gives convergence of the source integral. Taking $k\to\infty$ for fixed $\varepsilon>0$ and then $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ proves convergence of these full integrals. Step 1.3 supplies the initial term, steps 1.4–1.5 identify the limits of the discrete sums, step 1.2 supplies the exact discrete identity, and step 1.1 its state admissibility. Passing to the limit proves the displayed weak formulation. [A1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 1.4, step 1.5, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded Lipschitz open set. There are bounded real linear maps $R:H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)\to H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ and $Q:H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)\to H_0^1(\Omega)$ such that
$$u=Ru+\nabla Qu,\qquad \|Ru\|_{H^1}+\|Qu\|_{H^1}\le C_\Omega\|u\|_{H(\operatorname{curl})}.$$
No contractibility, connected boundary, or mesh hypothesis is required. The scalar estimate uses the full H(curl) norm; no estimate by curl alone is asserted.

1.1 Fix a ball $B$ with $\overline\Omega\Subset B$, let $U$ be the zero extension of $u$ by [F1], and use [F2] with support $\overline\Omega$. Then $U=w+\nabla p$, $\|w\|_{H^1}\le C\|u\|_{H(\operatorname{curl})}$, and $\|p\|_{H^1}\le C_\Omega\|u\|_2$. The exterior open set $D=B\setminus\overline\Omega$ has Lipschitz boundary: near $\partial\Omega$ use the same graph with the opposite side, and near $\partial B$ use the smooth sphere; these boundary sets are a positive distance apart. It may have several components, which [F3] permits. On $D$, $U=0$, so $\nabla p=-w$. Hence $p|_D\in H^2(D)$, with $\|p\|_{H^2(D)}\le C_\Omega\|u\|_{H(\operatorname{curl})}$. This follows directly from the definition of second weak derivatives: $D_iD_jp=-D_iw_j\in L^2(D)$. [F1, F2, construct, algebra, F3]

2.1 Extend $p|_D$ by [F3] to $a=E_D(p|_D)\in H^2(\mathbb R^3)$. Choose one fixed $\chi\in C_c^\infty(B)$ equal to one near $\overline\Omega$, and define whole-space fields $Z=\chi(w+
abla a)$ and $P=\chi(p-a)$. Both are in $H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ with norms bounded by $C_\Omega\|u\|_{H(\operatorname{curl})}$. On $D$, $a=p$ and $
abla a=
abla p=-w$ almost everywhere, so $Z=P=0$ there; outside $B$ their cutoff makes them zero. Thus they vanish almost everywhere outside $\overline\Omega$. By [F1], $z=Z|_\Omega\in H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ and $q=P|_\Omega\in H_0^1(\Omega)$. On $\Omega$, $\chi=1$ and its gradient is zero, giving $z+
abla q=w+
abla a+
abla p-
abla a=u$. Fixed zero extension, Fourier multipliers, $E_D$, and cutoff make the maps $R:u\mapsto z$, $Q:u\mapsto q$ linear; their estimates have just been proved. Only the geometry of $\Omega,B$, not a mesh or a topological assumption, enters the constants. [F1, F3, step 1.1, construct, algebra, F4] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice for the graph spaces and real $L^2$ product as in [[def-na-curl-curl-kernel-quotient-gauge]]. Let $V_h$ be that finite-dimensional real edge space, $K_h=\ker(\operatorname{curl}|_{V_h})$, and $Z_h=V_h\cap K_h^\perp$. Here $V_h^*=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb R}(V_h,\mathbb R)$ is the algebraic dual of [[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]]. For every $f\in V_h^*$ there is a unique pair $(u_h,p_h)\in Z_h\times K_h$ satisfying
$$ (\operatorname{curl}u_h,\operatorname{curl}v_h)_{L^2}+(p_h,v_h)_{L^2}=f(v_h)\quad(v_h\in V_h),\qquad (u_h,q_h)_{L^2}=0\quad(q_h\in K_h).$$
The gauge multiplier is the $L^2$ Riesz representative of $f|_{K_h}$. The quotient solution satisfies the exact stability identity
$$\|\operatorname{curl}u_h\|_{L^2}=\|f|_{Z_h}\|_{(Z_h,\|\operatorname{curl}(\cdot)\|_{L^2})^*},\qquad \|p_h\|_{L^2}=\|f|_{K_h}\|_{(K_h,\|\cdot\|_{L^2})^*}.$$
The constraint form $b(v,q)=(v,q)_{L^2}$ has inf-sup constant one when $K_h\ne\{0\}$, $V_h$ has the $H(\operatorname{curl})$ graph norm and $K_h$ has the $L^2$ norm; if $K_h=\{0\}$ the constraint is vacuous. The curl form is coercive with constant one on $Z_h$ in the quotient curl norm. No mesh-uniform estimate in the full graph norm is claimed here.

1.1 On $Z_h$, the bilinear form $a_h(u,v)=(\operatorname{curl}u,\operatorname{curl}v)_{L^2}$ is an inner product: if $a_h(u,u)=0$, then $u\in K_h$ and $u\in K_h^\perp$, hence $u=0$. The finite-dimensional Riesz theorem [F3] applied to $f|_{Z_h}$ gives a unique $u_h\in Z_h$ with $a_h(u_h,z_h)=f(z_h)$ for every $z_h\in Z_h$. Applying [F3] to the $L^2$ inner product on the finite-dimensional $K_h$ gives a unique $p_h\in K_h$ with $(p_h,q_h)_{L^2}=f(q_h)$ for all $q_h\in K_h$. The zero subspace cases are included in [F3]. [A1, F1, F3, F4, given, construct]

2.1 Restrict the $L^2$ inner product to the finite-dimensional space $V_h$. Its orthogonal complement of $K_h$ is $V_h\cap K_h^\perp=Z_h$ by [F1], so [F2] gives $V_h=Z_h\oplus K_h$. Thus each $v_h$ has a unique orthogonal decomposition $v_h=z_h+q_h$. Since $\operatorname{curl}q_h=0$ and $(p_h,z_h)=0$, the two identities of step 1.1 give $a_h(u_h,v_h)+(p_h,v_h)=f(z_h)+f(q_h)=f(v_h)$. Also $u_h\in Z_h$ gives the gauge equation. Any solution must restrict to the unique Riesz problems on $Z_h$ and $K_h$, proving uniqueness. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For any real inner product $c(\cdot,\cdot)$ and any nonzero $w$, positivity of $c(v-tw,v-tw)$ at $t=c(v,w)/c(w,w)$ gives $|c(v,w)|^2\le c(v,v)c(w,w)$; if $w=0$ the inequality is immediate. Thus the norm of the functional $z\mapsto c(u,z)$ is at most $\|u\|_c$, and when $u\ne0$ equality is attained at $z=u$; when $u=0$ both sides vanish. Applying this argument to $a_h$ and the $L^2$ product, together with the Riesz identities of step 1.1, proves both exact dual-norm identities. For the constraint, if $q_h\ne0$ choose $v_h=q_h$; then $\operatorname{curl}q_h=0$, $\|v_h\|_{H(\operatorname{curl})}=\|q_h\|_2$, and $b(v_h,q_h)=\|q_h\|_2^2$, so the inf-sup constant is at least one. For the upper bound, the same positive-square argument with the $L^2$ inner product gives $|b(v_h,q_h)|\le\|v_h\|_2\|q_h\|_2\le\|v_h\|_{H(\operatorname{curl})}\|q_h\|_2$. On $Z_h$, $a_h(v_h,v_h)=\|[v_h]\|_{\operatorname{curl}}^2$, which gives coercivity constant one in the declared quotient norm. [A1, F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice for the graph spaces and real $L^2$ product as in [[def-na-curl-curl-kernel-quotient-gauge]]. Let $V_h$ be that finite-dimensional real edge space, $K_h=\ker(\operatorname{curl}|_{V_h})$, and $Z_h=V_h\cap K_h^\perp$. Here $V_h^*=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb R}(V_h,\mathbb R)$ is the algebraic dual of [[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]]. For every $f\in V_h^*$ there is a unique pair $(u_h,p_h)\in Z_h\times K_h$ satisfying
$$ (\operatorname{curl}u_h,\operatorname{curl}v_h)_{L^2}+(p_h,v_h)_{L^2}=f(v_h)\quad(v_h\in V_h),\qquad (u_h,q_h)_{L^2}=0\quad(q_h\in K_h).$$
The gauge multiplier is the $L^2$ Riesz representative of $f|_{K_h}$. The quotient solution satisfies the exact stability identity
$$\|\operatorname{curl}u_h\|_{L^2}=\|f|_{Z_h}\|_{(Z_h,\|\operatorname{curl}(\cdot)\|_{L^2})^*},\qquad \|p_h\|_{L^2}=\|f|_{K_h}\|_{(K_h,\|\cdot\|_{L^2})^*}.$$
The constraint form $b(v,q)=(v,q)_{L^2}$ has inf-sup constant one when $K_h\ne\{0\}$, $V_h$ has the $H(\operatorname{curl})$ graph norm and $K_h$ has the $L^2$ norm; if $K_h=\{0\}$ the constraint is vacuous. The curl form is coercive with constant one on $Z_h$ in the quotient curl norm. No mesh-uniform estimate in the full graph norm is claimed here.

1.1 On $Z_h$, the bilinear form $a_h(u,v)=(\operatorname{curl}u,\operatorname{curl}v)_{L^2}$ is an inner product: if $a_h(u,u)=0$, then $u\in K_h$ and $u\in K_h^\perp$, hence $u=0$. The finite-dimensional Riesz theorem [F3] applied to $f|_{Z_h}$ gives a unique $u_h\in Z_h$ with $a_h(u_h,z_h)=f(z_h)$ for every $z_h\in Z_h$. Applying [F3] to the $L^2$ inner product on the finite-dimensional $K_h$ gives a unique $p_h\in K_h$ with $(p_h,q_h)_{L^2}=f(q_h)$ for all $q_h\in K_h$. The zero subspace cases are included in [F3]. [A1, F1, F3, F4, given, construct]

2.1 Restrict the $L^2$ inner product to the finite-dimensional space $V_h$. Its orthogonal complement of $K_h$ is $V_h\cap K_h^\perp=Z_h$ by [F1], so [F2] gives $V_h=Z_h\oplus K_h$. Thus each $v_h$ has a unique orthogonal decomposition $v_h=z_h+q_h$. Since $\operatorname{curl}q_h=0$ and $(p_h,z_h)=0$, the two identities of step 1.1 give $a_h(u_h,v_h)+(p_h,v_h)=f(z_h)+f(q_h)=f(v_h)$. Also $u_h\in Z_h$ gives the gauge equation. 3.1 For any real inner product $c(\cdot,\cdot)$ and any nonzero $w$, positivity of $c(v-tw,v-tw)$ at $t=c(v,w)/c(w,w)$ gives $|c(v,w)|^2\le c(v,v)c(w,w)$; if $w=0$ the inequality is immediate. On $Z_h$, $a_h(v_h,v_h)=\|[v_h]\|_{\operatorname{curl}}^2$, which gives coercivity constant one in the declared quotient norm. [A1, F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For the linear Galerkin V/W-cycle procedure of [[alg-finite-galerkin-v-cycle]],
on any level $j$ and for all $x,a,b\in\mathbb R^{n_j}$,
$$\operatorname{Cycle}(j,x+a,b+A_ja)=a+\operatorname{Cycle}(j,x,b).$$
The identity is in exact arithmetic and uses the same hierarchy, smoothing
matrices, sweep counts, and cycle count on both sides.
1.1 At level $j=0$, [F1] returns $A_0^{-1}b$. Since $A_0$ is invertible, $A_0^{-1}(b+A_0a)=A_0^{-1}b+a,$ so the identity holds at the base level. [given, F1, algebra]

1.2 At a noncoarsest level, if the current state is shifted from $x$ to $x+a$ and the right side from $b$ to $b+A_ja$, then the residual is unchanged because $(b+A_ja)-A_j(x+a)=b-A_jx$. Each pre-smoothing update in [F1] therefore preserves the shift by $a$ and gives the same fine residual in the two executions. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 With identical fine residuals, both executions start the coarse correction at $e=0$ and call the same deterministic recursive procedure with the same right side $P_j^{\mathsf T}r$. Thus every call returns the same coarse correction $e$, including every repeated W-cycle call. Prolongation adds the same $P_je$ to both shifted states, and the post-smoothing residuals are again identical, so every post-update preserves the shift. [F1, step 1.2, algebra]
3.1 The base calculation and the noncoarsest calculation establish the stated identity for every level of the finite hierarchy. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

Let f∈C³(R^d) have bounded third derivative and define D_εf(x)=∫f(y)∇W_ε(x−y)dy. Then for every ε>0 and x∈R^d,

$$|D_\varepsilon f(x)-\nabla f(x)|\le \frac{m_3}{6}\varepsilon^2\|D^3f\|_\infty,$$

where ||D³f||∞ is the supremum of the operator norm of the trilinear derivative.

1.1 The scalar components of f(x−z)∇W_ε(z) are continuous and compactly supported, so [F5] makes them Riemann integrable on a bounding box. Apply [F4] with z=εu componentwise to rewrite D_εf(x)=ε^(−1)∫f(x−εu)∇W(u)du. [F1, F4, F5]
1.2 For each x,u, [F3] gives f(x−εu)=f(x)−ε∇f(x)·u+(ε²/2)D²f(x)[u,u]+R(x,u), with |R(x,u)|≤(ε³/6)||D³f||∞|u|³. [given, F3]

2.1 Integrate the expansion of step 1.2 against ε^(−1)∇W(u). Linearity [F6] and [F2] make the constant and quadratic terms vanish; the linear term in coordinate k equals −∂_kf(x)Σ_j∫u_j∂_kW(u)du=∂_kf(x). Thus the integrated polynomial part is ∇f(x). [F2, F6, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Put G(u)=R(x,u)∇W(u), a continuous compactly supported vector function, and v=∫G componentwise. If v≠0 set a=v/||v||₂; then ||a||₂=1 and ||v||₂=∫⟨a,G(u)⟩≤∫|⟨a,G(u)⟩|≤∫||G(u)||₂ by linearity, monotonicity, and [F7]. If v=0 the same upper bound is immediate. The pointwise remainder estimate in step 1.2 and [F2] therefore give ||v||₂≤(ε³/6)||D³f||∞∫|u|³|∇W(u)|du=(ε³m₃/6)||D³f||∞. Multiplication by ε^(−1) from step 1.1 proves the stated bound. [F2, F5, F6, F7, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC and the data of [[def-volume-integral-scattering-model]] with $0<|D|<\infty$. Then $K_k:L^2(D;\mathbb C)\to L^2(D;\mathbb C)$ is compact and
$$\|K_k\|\le\|G_k(x-y)q(y)\|_{L^2(D\times D)}\le\|q\|_\infty\sqrt{\frac{|D|\operatorname{diam}(D)}{4\pi}}.$$

The proof supplies both the finite-measure Hilbert–Schmidt rescaling route required by the kernel interface and the singular-truncation/Schur route specified for this volume kernel. No uniqueness or outgoing-scattering solvability is asserted here.

1.1 By [F11] and AC, $X=L^2(D;\mathbb C)$ is a Banach space. Normalize $D$ to the probability measure $d\nu=dx/M$. By [F2], the operator $K_k$ is unitarily equivalent to the integral operator on $L^2(D,\nu)$ with kernel $\widetilde a=M a$. Its kernel norm equals $\|a\|_{L^2(D\times D,dx\,dy)}$ by [F2]. Applying [F3] to this probability-space kernel gives compactness of the normalized operator and its norm bound; unitary equivalence transfers both to $K_k$. [given, F1, F2, F3, F11]

1.2 We also verify the singular-truncation route. Choose a measurable representative $q_0$ and set it to zero on the measurable null set where $|q_0|>\|q\|_\infty$. This does not change the operator, since the kernel changes only on a product-null set, and now $|q_0(y)|\le\|q\|_\infty$ for every $y$. For $\varepsilon>0$, put $\chi_\varepsilon(r)=0$ for $r\le\varepsilon$, $\chi_\varepsilon(r)=(r-\varepsilon)/\varepsilon$ for $\varepsilon<r<2\varepsilon$, and $\chi_\varepsilon(r)=1$ for $r\ge2\varepsilon$. Let $K_\varepsilon$ have kernel $\chi_\varepsilon(|x-y|)G_k(x-y)q_0(y)$. The difference kernel is supported where $|x-y|<2\varepsilon$ and bounded in modulus by $\|q\|_\infty/(4\pi|x-y|)$. By [F9] its row and column integrals, for every fixed row and column, are at most $A=B\le(\|q\|_\infty/(4\pi))4\pi\int_0^{2\varepsilon}r\,dr=2\|q\|_\infty\varepsilon^2$. For each $x$, weighted Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|T_hv(x)|^2\le(\int|h(x,y)|dy)(\int|h(x,y)||v(y)|^2dy)$; integrating and using Tonelli yields $\|T_hv\|_2^2\le AB\|v\|_2^2$. Hence $\|K-K_\varepsilon\|\le2\|q\|_\infty\varepsilon^2$. [given, F1, F9, algebra]

1.3 Fix $\varepsilon>0$. Extend the everywhere-bounded representative $q_0$ by zero to $\mathbb R^3$; it lies in $L^2(\mathbb R^3)$ because $q\in L^\infty(D)$ and $|D|<\infty$. By [F5], choose $q_j\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ with $\|q_j-q_0\|_{L^2(D)}\to0$. The kernel $g_{\varepsilon,j}(x,y)=\chi_\varepsilon(|x-y|)G_k(x-y)q_j(y)$ extends continuously to the compact set $\overline D\times\overline D$ by assigning zero on $x=y$; the cutoff vanishes near the diagonal. For $\|v\|_2\le1$, its integral outputs obey $|T_{\varepsilon,j}v(x)|\le\sqrt{|D|}\|g_{\varepsilon,j}\|_\infty$ and $|T_{\varepsilon,j}v(x)-T_{\varepsilon,j}v(x')|\le\sqrt{|D|}\sup_y|g_{\varepsilon,j}(x,y)-g_{\varepsilon,j}(x',y)|$. Uniform continuity of $g_{\varepsilon,j}$ makes these outputs uniformly bounded and equicontinuous. Applying [F6] separately to real and imaginary parts gives compact closures $C_R,C_I$ in $C(\overline D;\mathbb R)$. The product $C_R\times C_I$ is compact by finite-product compactness. Under the homeomorphism $w\mapsto(\operatorname{Re}w,\operatorname{Im}w)$, the closure of the complex output family is a closed subset of this compact product, hence compact in $C(\overline D;\mathbb C)$. The inclusion into $L^2(D)$ is continuous, so $T_{\varepsilon,j}:L^2(D)\to L^2(D)$ is compact. [given, F5, F6, F10, construct]

2.1 Since $|\chi_\varepsilon G_k|\le(4\pi\varepsilon)^{-1}$, the square norm of the kernel difference between $K_\varepsilon$ and $T_{\varepsilon,j}$ is at most $|D|(16\pi^2\varepsilon^2)^{-1}\|q-q_j\|_{L^2(D)}^2$. [F8] therefore gives $\|K_\varepsilon-T_{\varepsilon,j}\|\to0$. By [F7], $K_\varepsilon$ is compact. [given, F5, F7, F8, step 1.3, algebra]

3.1 As $\varepsilon\downarrow0$, step 1.2 gives $\|K-K_\varepsilon\|\le2\|q\|_\infty\varepsilon^2\to0$. Applying [F7] again shows $K$ is compact. Step 1.1 independently gives the displayed norm estimate and compactness with the finite-measure Hilbert–Schmidt normalization. [F1, F2, F3, F7, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC and the data of [[def-volume-integral-scattering-model]] with $0<|D|<\infty$. Then $K_k:L^2(D;\mathbb C)\to L^2(D;\mathbb C)$ is compact and
$$\|K_k\|\le\|G_k(x-y)q(y)\|_{L^2(D\times D)}\le\|q\|_\infty\sqrt{\frac{|D|\operatorname{diam}(D)}{4\pi}}.$$

The proof supplies both the finite-measure Hilbert–Schmidt rescaling route required by the kernel interface and the singular-truncation/Schur route specified for this volume kernel. No uniqueness or outgoing-scattering solvability is asserted here.

1.1 By [F11] and AC, $X=L^2(D;\mathbb C)$ is a Banach space. Normalize $D$ to the probability measure $d\nu=dx/M$. By [F2], the operator $K_k$ is unitarily equivalent to the integral operator on $L^2(D,\nu)$ with kernel $\widetilde a=M a$. Its kernel norm equals $\|a\|_{L^2(D\times D,dx\,dy)}$ by [F2]. Applying [F3] to this probability-space kernel gives compactness of the normalized operator and its norm bound; unitary equivalence transfers both to $K_k$. [given, F1, F2, F3, F11]

1.2 We also verify the singular-truncation route. Choose a measurable representative $q_0$ and set it to zero on the measurable null set where $|q_0|>\|q\|_\infty$. This does not change the operator, since the kernel changes only on a product-null set, and now $|q_0(y)|\le\|q\|_\infty$ for every $y$. For $\varepsilon>0$, put $\chi_\varepsilon(r)=0$ for $r\le\varepsilon$, $\chi_\varepsilon(r)=(r-\varepsilon)/\varepsilon$ for $\varepsilon<r<2\varepsilon$, and $\chi_\varepsilon(r)=1$ for $r\ge2\varepsilon$. Let $K_\varepsilon$ have kernel $\chi_\varepsilon(|x-y|)G_k(x-y)q_0(y)$. The difference kernel is supported where $|x-y|<2\varepsilon$ and bounded in modulus by $\|q\|_\infty/(4\pi|x-y|)$. By [F9] its row and column integrals, for every fixed row and column, are at most $A=B\le(\|q\|_\infty/(4\pi))4\pi\int_0^{2\varepsilon}r\,dr=2\|q\|_\infty\varepsilon^2$. For each $x$, weighted Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|T_hv(x)|^2\le(\int|h(x,y)|dy)(\int|h(x,y)||v(y)|^2dy)$; integrating and using Tonelli yields $\|T_hv\|_2^2\le AB\|v\|_2^2$. Hence $\|K-K_\varepsilon\|\le2\|q\|_\infty\varepsilon^2$. [given, F1, F9, algebra]

1.3 Fix $\varepsilon>0$. Extend the everywhere-bounded representative $q_0$ by zero to $\mathbb R^3$; it lies in $L^2(\mathbb R^3)$ because $q\in L^\infty(D)$ and $|D|<\infty$. By [F5], choose $q_j\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ with $\|q_j-q_0\|_{L^2(D)}\to0$. The kernel $g_{\varepsilon,j}(x,y)=\chi_\varepsilon(|x-y|)G_k(x-y)q_j(y)$ extends continuously to the compact set $\overline D\times\overline D$ by assigning zero on $x=y$; the cutoff vanishes near the diagonal. For $\|v\|_2\le1$, its integral outputs obey $|T_{\varepsilon,j}v(x)|\le\sqrt{|D|}\|g_{\varepsilon,j}\|_\infty$ and $|T_{\varepsilon,j}v(x)-T_{\varepsilon,j}v(x')|\le\sqrt{|D|}\sup_y|g_{\varepsilon,j}(x,y)-g_{\varepsilon,j}(x',y)|$. Uniform continuity of $g_{\varepsilon,j}$ makes these outputs uniformly bounded and equicontinuous. Applying [F6] separately to real and imaginary parts gives compact closures $C_R,C_I$ in $C(\overline D;\mathbb R)$. The product $C_R\times C_I$ is compact by finite-product compactness. Under the homeomorphism $w\mapsto(\operatorname{Re}w,\operatorname{Im}w)$, the closure of the complex output family is a closed subset of this compact product, hence compact in $C(\overline D;\mathbb C)$. The inclusion into $L^2(D)$ is continuous, so $T_{\varepsilon,j}:L^2(D)\to L^2(D)$ is compact. [given, F5, F6, F10, construct]

2.1 Since $|\chi_\varepsilon G_k|\le(4\pi\varepsilon)^{-1}$, the square norm of the kernel difference between $K_\varepsilon$ and $T_{\varepsilon,j}$ is at most $|D|(16\pi^2\varepsilon^2)^{-1}\|q-q_j\|_{L^2(D)}^2$. [F8] therefore gives $\|K_\varepsilon-T_{\varepsilon,j}\|\to0$. By [F7], $K_\varepsilon$ is compact. [given, F5, F7, F8, step 1.3, algebra]

3.1 As $\varepsilon\downarrow0$, step 1.2 gives $\|K-K_\varepsilon\|\le2\|q\|_\infty\varepsilon^2\to0$. Applying [F7] again shows $K$ is compact. Step 1.1 independently gives the displayed norm estimate and compactness with the finite-measure Hilbert–Schmidt normalization. [F1, F2, F3, F7, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement refuted

For each integer $n\ge1$, set $\varepsilon_n=2^{-n}$ and take the four unweighted sites with distinct stable identifiers $1,2,3,4$ at $p_1=(0,0,0)$, $p_2=(1,0,0)$, $p_3=(0,1,0)$, and $p_4=(1/4,1/4,\varepsilon_n)$. All coordinates are dyadic. They span one tetrahedron. Its circumsphere is empty of other sites because there are no other sites, so it is a Delaunay tetrahedron, while its inradius tends to zero and its diameter is at least $1$ as $n\to\infty$.

1.1 For every $n\ge1$, $\varepsilon_n\in\mathbb D$ and the four sites therefore satisfy the dyadic-coordinate input condition of [F1]. The first three points are noncollinear in $z=0$ and $p_4$ has positive height, so the four points are affinely independent and form a nondegenerate tetrahedron. Its volume is one third of base area $1/2$ times height $\varepsilon_n$, namely $V_n=\varepsilon_n/6$. With only these four sites, its circumsphere contains no other site in its interior, so [F1] makes it an empty-sphere Delaunay tetrahedron. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 The total face area $S_n$ is at least the base area $1/2$ and is bounded above uniformly in $n$, since every edge length is at most $2$ and each of the four face areas is at most half the product of two such edge lengths; in particular $S_n\le8$. The inradius is $r_n=3V_n/S_n=\varepsilon_n/(2S_n)$, so $\varepsilon_n/16\le r_n\le\varepsilon_n$ and $r_n\to0$. The diameter is at least $|p_1-p_2|=1$. Thus empty-sphere Delaunay membership imposes no positive uniform inradius-to-diameter bound in three dimensions. [F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎
cases.evidence: There are exactly four sites and no other sites, so the circumsphere exclusion condition is genuinely vacuous; this empty-other-sites case still defines a full-dimensional Delaunay tetrahedron.

## Statement

Let $Q=Y=(0,1)^d$, $\epsilon_n\to0$, and $(u_n)$ be bounded in $H^1_0(Q)$. There are a subsequence, $u\in H^1_0(Q)$, and $u_1\in L^2(Q;V_\#)$ such that $u_n\rightharpoonup u$ in $H^1_0(Q)$, $u_n\to u$ in $L^2(Q)$, and
$$\nabla u_n\overset{2}{\rightharpoonup}\nabla_xu(x)+\nabla_yu_1(x,y).$$

1.1 By [F1]–[F2], first extract a subsequence converging weakly in $H^1_0(Q)$ to some $u\in H^1_0(Q)$, and then a further subsequence converging strongly in $L^2(Q)$ to the same $u$. By [F3], extract successive further subsequences on which each of the $d$ components of $\nabla u_n$ two-scale converges; since there are finitely many components, one subsequence works for all. Write its vector limit as $G(x,y)$. [F1, F2, F3, A1, algebra]

2.1 For every allowed product test $\phi(x)\psi(y)$, strong $L^2$ convergence and the uniform sampled-test bound in [F4] show that replacing $u_n$ by $u$ in its pairing changes the limit by zero. Weak $L^2$ averaging in [F4], applied to $\psi(x/\epsilon_n)$ against $u\phi\in L^2(Q)$, then gives limit $\int_Q u\phi\int_Y\psi$. Thus the two-scale limit of $u_n$ is the $y$-independent function $u(x)$. [F4, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 For a smooth compactly supported $\phi(x)$ and constant vector $c$, test gradient convergence with $\phi c$. Ordinary weak $H^1$ convergence gives $\int_{Q\times Y}G\cdot\phi c=\int_Q\nabla u\cdot\phi c$. Hence $H:=G-\nabla_xu$ has zero $y$-mean for almost every $x$. [F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Let $\Phi(x,y)=\sum_r\phi_r(x)\Psi_r(y)$ be a smooth periodic vector field, compactly supported in $x$, with $\operatorname{div}_y\Phi=0$. The weak-derivative identity [F7], applied for each fixed $y$, and Tonelli [F8] give $\int_{Q\times Y}G\cdot\Phi=-\int_{Q\times Y}u\,\operatorname{div}_x\Phi=\int_{Q\times Y}\nabla_xu\cdot\Phi,$ because the two-scale limit of $u_n$ is $u(x)$ by step 2.1 and the $x$-derivative of each test is still an allowed test. Therefore $H$ is orthogonal to every such divergence-free field. [F7, F8, step 2.1, F3, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 For every nonzero $k\in\mathbb Z^d$ and every real $c\perp k$, use slow tests $\phi(x)c\cos(2\pi k\cdot y)$ and $\phi(x)c\sin(2\pi k\cdot y)$ in step 3.1. They are divergence-free in $y$. Since the resulting integrals vanish for every $\phi\in C_c^\infty(Q)$, the Fourier coefficient $\widehat H(x,k)$ is parallel to $k$ for almost every $x$. There are countably many $k$ and a finite basis of each $k^\perp$, so [A1] permits one null set outside which this holds for all $k$; the zero coefficient is zero by step 2.2. [step 3.1, A1, step 2.2, F6, algebra]

5.1 For $k\ne0$ define $\widehat u_1(x,k)=(\widehat H(x,k)\cdot k)/(2\pi i|k|^2)$ and set $\widehat u_1(x,0)=0$. The parallel property from step 4.1 gives $2\pi i k\widehat u_1(x,k)=\widehat H(x,k)$. Moreover $|\widehat u_1(x,k)|\le |\widehat H(x,k)|/(2\pi|k|)$, so Parseval [F6] implies $\int_Q\sum_k(1+|k|^2)|\widehat u_1(x,k)|^2dx\le C_d\|H\|_{L^2(Q\times Y)}^2.$ The partial Fourier sums therefore converge in $L^2(Q;H^1_\#(Y))$; conjugate symmetry makes their limit real, its mean is zero, and its $y$-gradient is $H$. This supplies the claimed $u_1$ and proves the decomposition. [step 4.1, F6, F5, A1, algebra] ∎

Let $Q=Y=(0,1)^d$, $\epsilon_n\to0$, and $(u_n)$ be bounded in $H^1_0(Q)$. There are a subsequence, $u\in H^1_0(Q)$, and $u_1\in L^2(Q;V_\#)$ such that $u_n\rightharpoonup u$ in $H^1_0(Q)$, $u_n\to u$ in $L^2(Q)$, and
$$\nabla u_n\overset{2}{\rightharpoonup}\nabla_xu(x)+\nabla_yu_1(x,y).$$

1.1 By [F1]–[F2], first extract a subsequence converging weakly in $H^1_0(Q)$ to some $u\in H^1_0(Q)$, and then a further subsequence converging strongly in $L^2(Q)$ to the same $u$. By [F3], extract successive further subsequences on which each of the $d$ components of $\nabla u_n$ two-scale converges; since there are finitely many components, one subsequence works for all. Write its vector limit as $G(x,y)$. [F1, F2, F3, A1, algebra]

2.1 For every allowed product test $\phi(x)\psi(y)$, strong $L^2$ convergence and the uniform sampled-test bound in [F4] show that replacing $u_n$ by $u$ in its pairing changes the limit by zero. Weak $L^2$ averaging in [F4], applied to $\psi(x/\epsilon_n)$ against $u\phi\in L^2(Q)$, then gives limit $\int_Q u\phi\int_Y\psi$. Thus the two-scale limit of $u_n$ is the $y$-independent function $u(x)$. [F4, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 For a smooth compactly supported $\phi(x)$ and constant vector $c$, test gradient convergence with $\phi c$. Ordinary weak $H^1$ convergence gives $\int_{Q\times Y}G\cdot\phi c=\int_Q\nabla u\cdot\phi c$. Hence $H:=G-\nabla_xu$ has zero $y$-mean for almost every $x$. [F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Let $\Phi(x,y)=\sum_r\phi_r(x)\Psi_r(y)$ be a smooth periodic vector field, compactly supported in $x$, with $\operatorname{div}_y\Phi=0$. The weak-derivative identity [F7], applied for each fixed $y$, and Tonelli [F8] give $\int_{Q\times Y}G\cdot\Phi=-\int_{Q\times Y}u\,\operatorname{div}_x\Phi=\int_{Q\times Y}\nabla_xu\cdot\Phi,$ because the two-scale limit of $u_n$ is $u(x)$ by step 2.1 and the $x$-derivative of each test is still an allowed test. Therefore $H$ is orthogonal to every such divergence-free field. [F7, F8, step 2.1, F3, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 For every nonzero $k\in\mathbb Z^d$ and every real $c\perp k$, use slow tests $\phi(x)c\cos(2\pi k\cdot y)$ and $\phi(x)c\sin(2\pi k\cdot y)$ in step 3.1. They are divergence-free in $y$. Since the resulting integrals vanish for every $\phi\in C_c^\infty(Q)$, the Fourier coefficient $\widehat H(x,k)$ is parallel to $k$ for almost every $x$. There are countably many $k$ and a finite basis of each $k^\perp$, so [A1] permits one null set outside which this holds for all $k$; the zero coefficient is zero by step 2.2. [step 3.1, A1, step 2.2, F6, algebra]

5.1 For $k\ne0$ define $\widehat u_1(x,k)=(\widehat H(x,k)\cdot k)/(2\pi i|k|^2)$ and set $\widehat u_1(x,0)=0$. The parallel property from step 4.1 gives $2\pi i k\widehat u_1(x,k)=\widehat H(x,k)$. Moreover $|\widehat u_1(x,k)|\le |\widehat H(x,k)|/(2\pi|k|)$, so Parseval [F6] implies $\int_Q\sum_k(1+|k|^2)|\widehat u_1(x,k)|^2dx\le C_d\|H\|_{L^2(Q\times Y)}^2.$ The partial Fourier sums therefore converge in $L^2(Q;H^1_\#(Y))$; conjugate symmetry makes their limit real, its mean is zero, and its $y$-gradient is $H$. This supplies the claimed $u_1$ and proves the decomposition. [step 4.1, F6, F5, A1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

Use the model and coefficient notation of [[def-na-first-order-hjb-cauchy-problem]] and the periodic grid of [[def-na-periodic-grid-and-tensor-multilinear-interpolation]]. Choose a time step $\tau>0$ and a finite nonempty control set $A_k\subset A$. For a finite control model take $A_k=A$; for compact controls use a sequence of finite sets with the stated uniform Hamiltonian error. For each control and grid node put
$$b_{a,j}^+=\max\{b_{a,j},0\},\qquad b_{a,j}^- =\max\{-b_{a,j},0\},$$
and define the explicit row
$$G^a_i(V)=V_i+\tau\left[\sum_{j=1}^d\left(\frac{b_{a,j}^+(x_i,t_n)}{h_j}(V_{i+e_j}-V_i)+\frac{b_{a,j}^-(x_i,t_n)}{h_j}(V_{i-e_j}-V_i)\right)+\ell_a(x_i,t_n)\right].$$
The periodic HJB upwind update is
$$U_i^{n+1}=\min_{a\in A_k}G_i^a(U^n).$$
Require the CFL condition
$$\tau\max_{a,i}\sum_{j=1}^d\frac{|b_{a,j}(x_i,t_n)|}{h_j}\le1$$
at every step. Initialize $U_i^0=u_0(x_i)$ and repeat the update for the specified finite number of time steps. Since the transport velocity in [[def-periodic-one-way-advection-schemes]] is $-b_a$ for this Hamiltonian sign convention, the displayed one-sided direction is its sign-reflected upwind row.

## Example

Assume Countable Choice. For fixed $d\ge1$, $\nu>0$, and $a>0$, let $X_m$ be the midpoint grid in $\Omega=(0,1)^d$ for each odd $m\ge3$. There are $0<\delta_m<1/(4m^2)$ such that the augmented sets $Z_m=X_m\cup\{x_0+\delta_me_1\}$, with $x_0=(1/2,\ldots,1/2)$, satisfy $h_{Z_m}\to0$, $\rho_{Z_m}\to\infty$, and $\kappa_2(K_{Z_m})\to\infty$ for the normalized Matérn kernel.

1.1 The cube is bounded and Lipschitz. At a boundary point $p$, let $I$ be the nonempty set of active coordinates ($p_j=0$ or $1$), with inward signs $\sigma_j=1$ at $0$ and $-1$ at $1$. Put $u_j=\sigma_j/\sqrt{|I|}$ for $j\in I$ and $u_j=0$ otherwise. In the orthogonal coordinates $x=p+y+tu$ with $y\perp u$, a sufficiently small neighborhood has no constraints from inactive coordinates, and the active inequalities reduce to $$t>\max_{j\in I}(-\sqrt{|I|}\,\sigma_j y_j).$$ This is the epigraph of a finite maximum of linear functions, hence a local Lipschitz graph with the cube on one side. The cube also satisfies the uniform cone condition. For $x\in[0,1]^d$, choose signs $\sigma_j=1$ if $x_j\le1/2$ and $-1$ otherwise, and put $u=(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_d)/\sqrt d$. If $u=e_1$ take $Q_x=I$; otherwise put $v=(e_1-u)/|e_1-u|$ and $Q_x=I-2vv^{\mathsf T}$, which is orthogonal and sends $e_1$ to $u$. Choose $0<\theta<\pi/2$ with $\cos\theta/\sqrt d-\sin\theta>0$, and set $r_0=1/2$. For any cone vector $z$, $z_1>|z|\cos\theta$ and $|z-z_1e_1|<|z|\sin\theta$. Hence $\sigma_j(Q_xz)_j\ge z_1/\sqrt d-|z-z_1e_1|>|z|(\cos\theta/\sqrt d-\sin\theta)>0$ for each coordinate. Each coordinate moves toward the cube's interior by less than $r_0$, so $x+Q_xz\in(0,1)^d$. [F1, given, construct, algebra]

1.2 Distinct midpoint sites have fill distance at most $\sqrt d/(2m)$. Since $m$ is odd, $x_0\in X_m$. By continuity in [F2], choose $\epsilon_m>0$ so that $|1-k(\delta e_1)|<1/m$ whenever $0<\delta<\epsilon_m$, then choose $0<\delta_m<\min\{\epsilon_m,1/(4m^2)\}$. Strict positive definiteness for $x_0$ and $x_0+\delta_me_1$ makes $1-k(\delta_me_1)>0$, so $0<1-k(\delta_me_1)<1/m$. Put $Z_m=X_m\cup\{x_0+\delta_me_1\}$. The new site is inside the cube because $\delta_m<1/(4m^2)<1/2$. Every other grid site is at distance at least $1/m$ from $x_0$, while $\delta_m<1/(4m^2)<1/(2m)$, so the new site is distinct from all grid sites. At the boundary corner $0$, the nearest grid point is $\left(1/(2m),\ldots,1/(2m)\right)$, at distance $\sqrt d/(2m)$; the new site has squared distance $d/4+\delta_m+\delta_m^2>d/(4m^2)$, so $\min_{z\in Z_m}|z|=\sqrt d/(2m)$. For $D_m(x)=\min_{z\in Z_m}|x-z|$, the triangle inequality gives $|D_m(x)-D_m(y)|\le|x-y|$. Since $x_n=(1/n,\ldots,1/n)\in\Omega$ for $n\ge2$ and $x_n\to0$, $D_m(x_n)\to D_m(0)$; the fill-distance supremum therefore satisfies $h_{Z_m}\ge\sqrt d/(2m)\ge1/(2m)$. Adding a site cannot increase fill distance, so also $h_{Z_m}\le\sqrt d/(2m)\to0$. The separation radius satisfies $0<q_{Z_m}\le\delta_m/2<1/(8m^2)$; consequently $\rho_{Z_m}=h_{Z_m}/q_{Z_m}>4m\to\infty$. [F1, F2, F3, given, choose, algebra]

2.1 Let $u$ be the unit vector with entries $1/\sqrt2$ and $-1/\sqrt2$ at the new site and $x_0$, and zero elsewhere. The corresponding Rayleigh quotient is $$u^{\mathsf T}K_{Z_m}u=\tfrac12(1+1-2k(\delta_me_1))=1-k(\delta_me_1).$$ Hence [F3] gives $0<\lambda_{\min}(K_{Z_m})\le1-k(\delta_me_1)<1/m$. By [F3] choose an orthonormal eigenbasis $Q$ and write $K_{Z_m}=Q\Lambda Q^{\mathsf T}$. Since every diagonal entry is $1$, $$\operatorname{tr}K_{Z_m}=|Z_m|=\sum_{i,j}q_{ij}^2\lambda_j=\sum_j\lambda_j,$$ so $\lambda_{\max}(K_{Z_m})$ is at least the average eigenvalue, namely $1$. For a unit vector $v=Qc$, orthogonality gives $\|K_{Z_m}v\|_2^2=\sum_j\lambda_j^2c_j^2\le\lambda_{\max}(K_{Z_m})^2$, with equality at a top eigenvector; the same calculation for $K_{Z_m}^{-1}$ gives induced 2-norm $1/\lambda_{\min}(K_{Z_m})$. Thus [F4] gives $\kappa_2(K_{Z_m})=\lambda_{\max}(K_{Z_m})/\lambda_{\min}(K_{Z_m})>m$. Together with step 1.2, this gives $h_{Z_m}\to0$, $\rho_{Z_m}\to\infty$, and condition number tending to infinity. [F2, F3, F4, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

## Example

Let the sample set be $Z=(0,1)$ and, for any $M>0$, let
$f_M(t)=Mt(1-t)$ on $[0,1]$. Exact AAA with support budget $B=1$, sweep
budget $S=0$, and tolerance zero starts at the constant mean of the two
samples and returns immediately with zero sampled residual, but its uniform
error is $M/4$.
For a continuous $q$ on $[0,1]$, write
$\|q\|_{\infty,[0,1]}:=\sup_{t\in[0,1]}|q(t)|$.

1.1 The sample values are $f_M(0)=f_M(1)=0$, so their mean is zero and the initial candidate $r_0$ is the zero function. Its residual at both sample points is zero, hence the tolerance-zero stopping rule in [F1] returns $r_0$ before selecting any support node. [given, F1, algebra]

## Statement

For the CARE case, suppose the exact Hamiltonian stable invariant subspace has a basis $U=\begin{bmatrix}U_1\\U_2\end{bmatrix}$ with $U_1$ invertible, and set $X=U_2U_1^{-1}$. If $X=X^*$, then $X$ solves the CARE and the restriction matrix on the graph is $A-GX$.

For the DARE case, suppose an exact stable deflating basis for the pencil $(N,M)$ is $U=\begin{bmatrix}U_1\\U_2\end{bmatrix}$ with $U_1$ invertible, and set $X=U_2U_1^{-1}$. If $X=X^*$ and $R+B^*XB\succ0$, then $X$ solves the DARE and the restriction matrix is $A_c=(I+GX)^{-1}A=A-B(R+B^*XB)^{-1}B^*XA$.

1.1 In either case, $U_2=XU_1$, so $U=[I;X]U_1$. If $H U=U T$ in the CARE case, right multiplication by $U_1^{-1}$ gives $H[I;X]=[I;X](U_1TU_1^{-1})$. The top block fixes the restriction matrix as $A-GX$; the bottom block reads $-Q-A^*X=X(A-GX)$, which is exactly $A^*X+XA-XGX+Q=0$. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 If $NU=MU T$ in the DARE case, the same normalization gives $N[I;X]=M[I;X](U_1TU_1^{-1})$. The top block is $A=(I+GX)(U_1TU_1^{-1})$, so invertibility of $I+GX$ gives restriction matrix $(I+GX)^{-1}A$. The lower block is $X-Q=A^*X(I+GX)^{-1}A$, which is the DARE by [F3]. No claim survives an unverified leading-block inverse or a subsequent nonzero symmetry residual. [F2, F3, algebra] ∎
cases.reason: The graph construction assumes a leading square basis block with an inverse and fixed Riccati data; no empty-dimensional stable-subspace convention is stated here.

## Statement refuted

The continuous Q1 velocity / cellwise P0 pressure pair is uniformly inf-sup stable on every Cartesian mesh.

1.1 Define $q=+1$ on the lower-left and upper-right cells and $q=-1$ on the other two. Equal cell areas show $\int_Dq=0$, and $q\ne0$. Let $\eta$ be the one-dimensional hat with values $0,1,0$ at $0,1/2,1$. The only interior Q1 node is the center, so each scalar velocity is a multiple of $\phi(x,y)=\eta(x)\eta(y)$. [given, construct]

2.1 Let $I_L=[0,1/2]$, $I_R=[1/2,1]$, and similarly $J_B,J_T$. Direct integration gives $\int_{I_L}\eta'=1$, $\int_{I_R}\eta'=-1$, and $\int_{J_B}\eta=\int_{J_T}\eta=1/4$. The alternating signs factor, so $\int_Dq\,\partial_x\phi=(1-(-1))(1/4-1/4)=0$. Interchanging $x,y$ gives $\int_Dq\,\partial_y\phi=0$. [algebra, step 1.1]

3.1 Every admissible velocity is $(a\phi,b\phi)$ for constants $a,b$, so step 2.1 gives $b(v,q)=0$ for every velocity while $q$ is a nonzero mean-zero pressure. Its supremum in the discrete inf-sup quotient is zero; nonnegativity of that quotient forces the discrete inf-sup constant to be $0$. Thus this family is not uniformly inf-sup stable. [given, F1, discharge-construct, step 2.1] ∎

## Statement

For a finite conforming simplicial mesh of bounded $D$, define $P_0:L^2(D)\to\mathbb P_0(\mathcal T_h)$ cellwise by
$$ (P_0g)|_K=|K|^{-1}\int_Kg. $$
Then $P_0$ is linear, equals the identity on piecewise constants, is the $L^2$-orthogonal projection onto that space, satisfies $\|P_0g\|_2\le\|g\|_2$, and preserves the integral $\int_DP_0g=\int_Dg$.

1.1 The cell integral is linear, so the formula defines a linear piecewise-constant map. If $g$ is constant on each cell, its cell average is the same constant, so $P_0g=g$. For any piecewise constant $q_h$, $\int_D(g-P_0g)q_h=\sum_Kq_K\left(\int_Kg-|K|\,|K|^{-1}\int_Kg\right)=0.$ Thus the range is orthogonal to the residual and $P_0$ is the orthogonal projection onto $\mathbb P_0(\mathcal T_h)$. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 By [F2], $|K|\,|(P_0g)|_K|^2=|K|^{-1}|\int_Kg|^2\le\int_K|g|^2$. Summing over cells gives $\|P_0g\|_2^2\le\|g\|_2^2$. Summing the defining averages multiplied by cell measures gives $\int_DP_0g=\sum_K\int_Kg=\int_Dg$. [F1, F2, algebra] ∎
cases.evidence: The mesh cells have positive finite measure, so each average divides by a nonzero measure; if the entire measured domain were null the resulting zero space would only give the trivial projection.

## Example

On the reference tetrahedron with vertices $x_0=0$, $x_1=e_1$, $x_2=e_2$, $x_3=e_3$, take the Whitney edge field $\phi_{01}=\lambda_0\nabla\lambda_1-\lambda_1\nabla\lambda_0$ and orient the face $[0,1,2]$ by the vertex order shown. Compute the circulation on $[0,1]$ and the curl flux through $[0,1,2]$.

1.1 In the reference coordinates, $\lambda_1=x_1$, $\lambda_0=1-x_1-x_2-x_3$, so $\phi_{01}=(1-x_2-x_3,x_1,x_1)$. Along $[0,1]$, parameterized by $x(t)=(t,0,0)$, this field has tangent component $1$; therefore its oriented circulation is $\int_0^1 1\,dt=1$. [F1, construct, algebra]

2.1 Differentiating the displayed polynomial gives $\operatorname{curl}\phi_{01}=(0,-2,2)$. The oriented face $[0,1,2]$ lies in $x_3=0$ with normal $e_3$ and area $1/2$, so its curl flux is $2\cdot(1/2)=1$. Its oriented boundary is $[1,2]-[0,2]+[0,1]$; by [F2], the first two circulations vanish and the last is one, agreeing with the flux by [F3]. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Example

On the reference tetrahedron with vertices $x_0=0$, $x_1=e_1$, $x_2=e_2$, $x_3=e_3$, take the Whitney edge field $\phi_{01}=\lambda_0\nabla\lambda_1-\lambda_1\nabla\lambda_0$ and orient the face $[0,1,2]$ by the vertex order shown. Compute the circulation on $[0,1]$ and the curl flux through $[0,1,2]$.

1.1 In the reference coordinates, $\lambda_1=x_1$, $\lambda_0=1-x_1-x_2-x_3$, so $\phi_{01}=(1-x_2-x_3,x_1,x_1)$. Along $[0,1]$, parameterized by $x(t)=(t,0,0)$, this field has tangent component $1$; therefore its oriented circulation is $\int_0^1 1\,dt=1$. [F1, construct, algebra]

2.1 Differentiating the displayed polynomial gives $\operatorname{curl}\phi_{01}=(0,-2,2)$. The oriented face $[0,1,2]$ lies in $x_3=0$ with normal $e_3$ and area $1/2$, so its curl flux is $2\cdot(1/2)=1$. Its oriented boundary is $[1,2]-[0,2]+[0,1]$; by [F2], the first two circulations vanish and the last is one, agreeing with the flux by [F3]. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement refuted

Keeping the same finite neighbor pattern in units of ε while refining ε alone guarantees consistency of a meshfree particle derivative. The following explicit periodic family refutes this claim for an affine field.

1.1 The adjacent gaps in one period are 3ε/5, 7ε/5, 3ε/2, and ε/2, so the fill radius is h=3ε/4. The four Voronoi-cell lengths per period are 11ε/20, ε, 29ε/20, and ε; hence every volume is at most 2h. If a cell meets B(x,r), its node lies in B(x,r+h). Nodes are separated by at least ε/2, so at most 1+4(r+h)/ε such nodes can lie in that interval. Each cell volume is at most 29ε/20, and r+h≥3ε/4; therefore the total active volume is at most (29/20)ε+(29/5)(r+h)≤(116/15)(r+h)≤8(r+h). The local-volume bound holds with C_L=8. In particular, the cells at −ε/2 and 3ε/5 are [−5ε/4,−ε/4] and [3ε/10,13ε/10], each of volume ε. [given, F2, algebra]

2.1 The nearest-node intervals tile R, repeat with period 4ε, and have gaps between their endpoints only at shared cell boundaries. Every compact support meets finitely many intervals. For any compactly supported continuous g, choose a finite consecutive block of cells containing supp(g); [F4] makes g integrable on its compact union, and repeated [F5] splits that integral into the cell integrals. Cells outside the block have zero integral because they do not meet supp(g). Thus the integration-compatibility identity in [F2] holds for every compactly supported continuous g. [F2, F4, F5, step 1.1, choose]

3.1 On |s|<1, W′(s)=−(105/16)s(1−s²)². For f(y)=y at x=0, set g(y)=y\,\partial_xW_\varepsilon(x-y)|_{x=0}. By [F1], g vanishes outside [−ε,ε], and [F2] defines its particle sum as Q_hg=Σ_jV_jg(x_j). The node at 0 contributes zero; only y=−ε/2 and y=3ε/5 contribute, with values −W′(1/2)/2=945/1024 and −(3/5)W′(3/5)=3024/3125. Thus Q_hg=945/1024+3024/3125, independent of ε. [F1, F2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Here f′(0)=1 and f‴=0, so [F3] gives D_εf(0)=1 exactly. Since each summand in the value from step 3.1 exceeds 1/2, that value is greater than 1 for every ε. The derivative error therefore does not tend to zero although h/ε=3/4 remains fixed. [F3, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. For every $\phi\in H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$, the affine class $\mathcal A_\phi$ in [[def-bem-double-layer-transmission-space]] has a unique minimum-energy pair $D\phi=(u^-,u^+)$. It is harmonic on both sides, satisfies
$$\gamma^-D\phi-\gamma^+D\phi=-\phi,\qquad \partial_n^-D\phi=\partial_n^+D\phi,$$
and obeys
$$\|\nabla u^-\|_{L^2(\Omega^-)}+\|\nabla u^+\|_{L^2(\Omega^+)}\le C\|\phi\|_{H^{1/2}(\Gamma)}.$$
Consequently the average trace $K\phi=(\gamma^-D\phi+\gamma^+D\phi)/2$ is in $H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$ and the common conormal $q_\phi=\partial_n^-D\phi=\partial_n^+D\phi$ is in $H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)$, with both maps bounded. For every $\phi\in H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$, the weak potential agrees away from $\Gamma$, with smooth representatives, with the absolutely convergent integral $\int_\Gamma\partial_{n_y}G_3(x,y)\phi(y)dS_y$. No vanishing condition at polyhedral edges or vertices is required.

1.1 The affine class is nonempty: choose a bounded interior trace lift $L\phi$ from [F1] and take $(u_0^-,u_0^+)=(-L\phi,0)$. Its trace jump is $-\phi$ and its energy is at most $C\|\phi\|_{H^{1/2}}^2$. Let $Z=\mathcal A_0$, the linear space of matching-trace pairs. [F1, given, choose]

2.1 Equip $Z$ with $a_Z(v,w)=\int_{\Omega^-}
abla v^-\cdot
abla w^-+\int_{\Omega^+}
abla v^+\cdot
abla w^+$. A matching pair glues to a function $v$ on $\mathbb R^3$. In each Lipschitz graph chart, integration by parts for smooth approximants gives the distributional derivative of the glued function as the two piecewise derivatives plus the interface term $(\gamma^+v^+ -\gamma^-v^-)n_j$; trace continuity from [F1] passes this identity to $H^1$ functions, and the interface term vanishes. The glued function is in $L^6$: the exterior part is by definition in $L^6$, and the bounded interior part has a bounded $H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ extension from [F1], to which [A1] applies after a bounded-support cutoff. Its global weak gradient is the two piecewise gradients. First show that any such $L^6$ function with global gradient in $L^2$ belongs to $\dot H^1$: take cutoffs $\chi_R=1$ on $B_R$, supported in $B_{2R}$, with $|
abla\chi_R|\le C/R$. The gradient tail tends to zero, and Hölder gives $R^{-1}\|v\|_{L^2(B_{2R}\setminus B_R)}\le C\|v\|_{L^6(B_{2R}\setminus B_R)}	o0$. Thus $\chi_Rv	o v$ in gradient norm; each compactly supported H1 cutoff is approximated in H1 by smooth compactly supported functions. Hence $v\in\dot H^1$, and [A1] gives $\|v\|_6\le C\|
abla v\|_2$. A Cauchy sequence in $Z$ now glues to a Cauchy sequence in $\dot H^1$; its limit restricts to an interior H1 function and an exterior $E^+$ function, and bounded traces preserve the matching condition. Hence $Z$ is complete in $a_Z$. Also $a_Z(v,v)=0$ forces the glued $L^6$ function to be a constant and therefore zero, so $a_Z$ is a Hilbert inner product. [A1, F1, step 1.1, given, algebra]

4.1 The trace jump is the affine constraint. For any $g\in H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$, restrict the bounded global lift $Lg$ of [F1] to both sides; the resulting matching pair lies in $Z$. Stationarity in step 3.1 and the weak conormal conventions [F4] give $\langle\partial_n^-u^- -\partial_n^+u^+,gangle=0$. Thus the conormals agree. The exterior energy trace bound [F2] and energy bound in step 3.1 bound $\gamma^+u^+$; the identity $\gamma^-u^-=\gamma^+u^+-\phi$ then bounds the interior trace and their average. For the common conormal use the interior lift alone: $|\langle q_\phi,gangle|=|\int_{\Omega^-}
abla u^-\cdot
abla L^-g|\le C\|
abla u^-\|_2\|g\|_{H^{1/2}}$, so $q_\phi\in H^{-1/2}$ with the asserted bound. [F1, F2, F4, step 3.1, given, algebra]

5.1 Step 3.1 supplies stationarity against every matching-trace finite-energy pair, in particular restrictions of every global smooth compactly supported function. The pair belongs to $H^1(\Omega^-)\times E^+(\Omega^+)$ and has trace jump $-\phi$ by construction. Thus [F5] identifies it, with smooth representatives off $\Gamma$, with the absolutely convergent double-layer kernel integral for every $\phi\in H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$. This includes facewise smooth densities reaching edges whenever they satisfy the global trace-space hypothesis. [F3, F5, step 3.1, step 4.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For any dimension $d$, phase $\theta\in\mathbb R^d$, and positive integer $m$, let $b(y)=a(\theta+my)$ on $Y$. Let $w_p\in V_\#$ be the unique mean-zero minimizer of $\int_Yb(y)|p+\nabla v(y)|^2dy$ and define $A_{\theta,m}^{\rm ex}p=\int_Yb(y)(p+\nabla w_p(y))dy$. Then $A_{\theta,m}^{\rm ex}=A^*$ for every $p\in\mathbb R^d$. Thus a micro side length $\delta=m\epsilon$ has zero continuum sampling/resonance error, regardless of phase; a separate finite micro-space error can remain.

1.1 Since $m k\in\mathbb Z^d$ for each $k\in\mathbb Z^d$, periodicity of $a$ gives $b(y+k)=b(y)$ a.e.; the exceptional null sets pull back to null sets by [F6]. Bounds are preserved by the same affine pullback [F1]. Hence the generic cell-corrector result [F2] applies to $b$ and gives its unique mean-zero cell solution; energy expansion around that solution shows it is the unique minimizer in the Statement. Set $v_m(y)=m^{-1}\chi_p(	heta+my)-c$, where $c$ is its mean on $Y$. Periodic smooth approximants to $\chi_p$ converge on every bounded union of cells, and affine pullback [F5] shows $v_m\in V_\#$ with $
abla_yv_m=
abla\chi_p(	heta+my)$. The flux $q(z)=a(z)(p+
abla\chi_p(z))$ is periodic and divergence-free by the cell equation. Its Fourier coefficients satisfy $k\cdot\widehat q(k)=0$. For a Fourier polynomial, $q(	heta+my)$ has only frequencies $mk$, with coefficients multiplied by phases, and each remains perpendicular to $mk$; hence it is divergence-free. For any periodic $h\in L^2(Y)$, affine change of variables [F6] gives $\int_Y|h(	heta+my)|^2dy=m^{-d}\int_{	heta+mY}|h(z)|^2dz$. The latter box meets at most $(m+2)^d$ unit lattice cells, so periodicity bounds this by $m^{-d}(m+2)^d\|h\|_{L^2(Y)}^2$. Thus composition with $y\mapsto	heta+my$ is bounded on periodic $L^2$, and the divergence-free identity passes from Fourier polynomials to $q$ in $L^2$. Therefore $\int_Yb(y)(p+
abla v_m)\cdot
