## Statement

For the continuous first-order Hamiltonian of
[[def-na-first-order-hjb-cauchy-problem]], requiring the subsolution or
supersolution inequality only for smooth ($C^\infty$) local test functions is
equivalent to requiring it for all $C^1$ tests. For the diagonal second-order
operator of [[def-na-periodic-diagonal-controlled-diffusion-hjb-problem]], the
same equivalence holds between smooth tests and all $C^{1,2}$ tests in
[[def-na-second-order-parabolic-viscosity-solution]]. The result is local in
space-time and applies to upper semicontinuous subsolutions and lower
semicontinuous supersolutions.

1.1 Start with an upper contact at $z_0=(x_0,t_0)$ for a $C^1$ or $C^{1,2}$ test $\phi$. On a closed Euclidean space-time ball $K$ contained in the interior cylinder, define $\widetilde\phi(z)=\phi(z)+\varepsilon(|x-x_0|^4+|t-t_0|^4)$ for $\varepsilon>0$. The added term and all derivatives relevant to the chosen test class vanish at $z_0$, while $u-\widetilde\phi$ is strictly smaller than $u(z_0)-\phi(z_0)$ at every other point of the contact neighborhood. Thus the original and strictified tests have the same PDE residual at $z_0$. [F4, algebra]

2.1 Choose a nonnegative unit-mass mollifier $\rho_\delta$ supported in the ball of radius $\delta$ from [F1], with $\delta$ small enough that its convolution samples only points in the contact neighborhood. Choose a smooth cutoff equal to one on a neighborhood of $K$ and supported inside that contact neighborhood using [F1], multiply $\widetilde\phi$ by it, and extend the product by zero. Convolve this compactly supported function with $\rho_\delta$ to obtain $\phi_\delta$. Rewriting the convolution with the smooth kernel as $\int g(y)\rho_\delta(z-y)\,dy$ shows by uniform difference quotients on the compact support that $\phi_\delta$ is $C^\infty$. On $K$ it coincides with convolution of $\widetilde\phi$ alone. For a $C^1$ function $g$, [F5] gives $$\frac{g(z+h e_j)-g(z)}h=\int_0^1\partial_jg(z+\theta h e_j)\,d\theta$$ when the indicated derivative exists. Uniform continuity of $\partial_jg$ on the compact neighborhood makes these difference quotients converge uniformly as $h\to0$. Integrating this uniform limit against $\rho_\delta$ proves $\partial_j(\rho_\delta*g)=\rho_\delta*\partial_jg$. For a second spatial derivative, apply this identity first to $g=\widetilde\phi$ and then to $g=\partial_j\widetilde\phi$; this uses only the continuous second derivative, not a third derivative. Apply it once for time and once for each first spatial derivative. Thus $D^\alpha\phi_\delta= \rho_\delta*D^\alpha\widetilde\phi$ for exactly the derivatives required in the $C^1$ or $C^{1,2}$ class. By [F2], $$\sup_{z\in K'}|D^\alpha\phi_\delta(z)-D^\alpha\widetilde\phi(z)| \le\sup_{z\in K',\ |y|\le\delta}|D^\alpha\widetilde\phi(z-y)-D^\alpha\widetilde\phi(z)|\longrightarrow0$$ on each smaller compact ball $K'$. Hence the approximants converge in $C^1$ or $C^{1,2}$, respectively. [F1, F2, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The upper semicontinuous function $u-\phi_\delta$ attains a maximum on $K$ by [F3]. The strict gap from step 1.1 and uniform convergence from the preceding approximation step imply that, for every fixed neighborhood of $z_0$, all maximizing points lie in that neighborhood once $\delta$ is sufficiently small; the boundary of $K$ is excluded for the same reason. At any such maximizing point $z_\delta$, adding the constant $u(z_\delta)-\phi_\delta(z_\delta)$ makes $\phi_\delta$ a smooth upper test. Apply the assumed smooth-test inequality there. [F3, step 1.1, step 2.1]

4.1 The maximizing points in step 3.1 approach $z_0$ uniformly over the maximizing set, and the required derivatives of $\phi_\delta$ converge uniformly to those of $\widetilde\phi$ on $K'$ by step 2.1. Continuity of the PDE residual [F4] therefore lets the smooth-test inequalities pass to the residual of $\widetilde\phi$ at $z_0$, which equals that of $\phi$ by step 1.1. This proves the upper-test implication. For a lower contact, replace maxima by minima and reverse the inequalities; the same uniform gap and derivative convergence apply. Since smooth tests are themselves in both larger test classes, the reverse implications are immediate. [F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

## Example

Consider the nonnegative table $(x_i,y_i)=((0,1),(1,0),(2,0),(3,1))$. On the three unit cells, with $t=x-i$ on cell $[i,i+1]$, define
$$S_0(t)=1-\frac65t+\frac15t^3,\qquad S_1(t)=-\frac35t(1-t),\qquad S_2(t)=\frac35t+\frac35t^2-\frac15t^3.$$
These pieces form a natural cubic spline interpolating the table, but $S_1(t)<0$ for $0<t<1$. PCHIP on the same data has a flat middle segment at zero and remains between the nonnegative cell endpoints.

1.1 Each displayed piece has endpoint values $S_0(0)=1$, $S_0(1)=0$, $S_1(0)=S_1(1)=0$, $S_2(0)=0$, and $S_2(1)=1$, so the pieces interpolate the given table. By [F4], their first derivatives are $S_0'=-6/5+3t^2/5$, $S_1'=-3/5+6t/5$, and $S_2'=3/5+6t/5-3t^2/5$; the derivative values match at both shared knots. Their second derivatives are $S_0''=6t/5$, $S_1''=6/5$, and $S_2''=6/5-6t/5$; these match at shared knots, and $S_0''(0)=S_2''(1)=0$. By [F1], this is a natural cubic spline. [given, F1, F4, algebra]
2.1 For $0<t<1$, $S_1(t)=-3t(1-t)/5<0$, although every tabulated value is nonnegative. Thus the natural cubic spline undershoots the data range on the middle cell. [given, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The secants are $d_0=-1$, $d_1=0$, and $d_2=1$. By [F2], the interior slopes at nodes $1$ and $2$ are both zero because each neighboring pair includes a zero secant; the Hermite piece joining the two zero values with zero slopes is constant zero. By [F3], the first and last PCHIP pieces remain between $1$ and $0$, and between $0$ and $1$, respectively. Hence PCHIP is nonnegative throughout the interval and does not reproduce the natural spline's undershoot. [F2, F3, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice used by the weak Dirichlet Poisson existence supplier. Let $\Omega$ be a bounded polygon, $\mathcal T_0$ a compatible shape-regular 2D NVB mesh, and $u\in H_0^1(\Omega)$ solve $-\Delta u=f$ with $f$ piecewise constant on $\mathcal T_0$. Run the exact P1 algorithm with three-generation refinement; assume each per-call budget suffices for every refinement through iteration $k$. Write $U_k$ for the unique exact P1 Galerkin solution on $\mathcal T_k$, estimator bulk parameter $0<\theta_E\le\min(1,(1-\lambda^2)/(C_{\rm loc}C_{\rm eff}))$ for a fixed $0<\lambda<1$, as in [[lem-afem-dorfler-marking-cardinality]], and any fixed oscillation parameter $\theta_O\in(0,1]$. If $u\in\mathbb A_s$ from [[def-afem-p1-approximation-class]] for $0<s\le\frac12$, then
$$\|\nabla(u-U_k)\|_2\le C|u|_{\mathbb A_s}(1+\#\mathcal T_k-\#\mathcal T_0)^{-s},$$
where $C$ depends on the initial mesh, marking parameters and estimator constants. This is an optimal-complexity theorem only for the Laplacian and P0 initial data.

1.1 By [F5] the weak solution exists uniquely under the stated choice assumptions. Since $f$ is piecewise constant on $\mathcal T_0$, every descendant cell has $\operatorname{osc}_K=0$. By [F1] there are $0<\alpha<1$ and $C_0$ such that $e_{k+1}^2\le\alpha e_k^2$; hence, with $q=\sqrt{\alpha}<1$, $e_j\le q^{j-k}e_k$ for $j\ge k$. If $|u|_{\mathbb A_s}=0$, then $E_0(u)=0$ and all nested Galerkin errors vanish. Assume $|u|_{\mathbb A_s}>0$. [A1, F1, F5, given, algebra]

1.2 For each $k$ with $e_k>0$, put $\epsilon_k=\lambda e_k$ for the fixed $\lambda\in(0,1)$ in the statement. By [F4], if $N_k=\left\lceil(2|u|_{\mathbb A_s}/\epsilon_k)^{1/s}ightceil$, then $E_{N_k}(u)\le\epsilon_k/2$: this follows directly from $(N_k+1)^sE_{N_k}\le|u|_{\mathbb A_s}$ and $N_k+1\ge(2|u|_{\mathbb A_s}/\epsilon_k)^{1/s}$. By the definition of an infimum there is a conforming comparison mesh with at most $N_k$ added cells and best-approximation error at most $\epsilon_k$. For a symmetric Galerkin solution, [F6] and expansion of $\|
abla(u-v_T)\|_2^2=\|
abla(u-U_T)\|_2^2+\|
abla(U_T-v_T)\|_2^2$ show its exact Galerkin error is the best error, so this comparison mesh reduces the Galerkin error to at most $\epsilon_k$. If $e_k=0$, the target conclusion is already true. [F4, F6, given, choose, algebra]

2.1 The comparison mesh from step 1.2 reduces the error by the factor $\lambda$. By [F2], the marked set therefore satisfies $\#M_k\le N_k\le1+(2/\lambda)^{1/s}|u|_{\mathbb A_s}^{1/s}e_k^{-1/s}.$ Summing and applying [F3] gives $\#\mathcal T_n-\#\mathcal T_0\le C\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\#M_k\le C'\,|u|_{\mathbb A_s}^{1/s}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}e_k^{-1/s}.$ The additive $1$ is absorbed into the right side because $e_k\le e_0=E(\mathcal T_0;u)\le|u|_{\mathbb A_s}$ by [F4] at $N=0$. [F2, F3, F4, F6, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Geometric contraction from step 1.1 implies $e_k^{-1/s}\le q^{(n-k)/s}e_n^{-1/s}$ for $k<n$. Thus the sum in step 2.1 is at most $e_n^{-1/s}\sum_{j\ge1}q^{j/s}$, a finite geometric series. Rearranging yields $e_n\le C''|u|_{\mathbb A_s}(\#\mathcal T_n-\#\mathcal T_0)^{-s}$ whenever the added-cell count is positive. If it is zero, [F4] at $N=0$ gives $e_n=e_0\le|u|_{\mathbb A_s}$. Enlarging $C''$ replaces the count by $1+\#\mathcal T_n-\#\mathcal T_0$. [F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Example

Take $d=1$, $R=1$, $\gamma=2$, $c_v=1$, $s_0=0$, and three periodic nodes with $H=I_3$ and

$$D=\frac12\begin{pmatrix}0&1&-1\\-1&0&1\\1&-1&0\end{pmatrix}.$$

Use states $U_1=(1,0,1)$, $U_2=(1,0,2)$, and $U_3=(1,0,1)$. The Euler-only entropy-conservative operator has zero total mathematical-entropy rate at this state; adding the model viscous term gives the exact rate $-\kappa/8$.

1.1 The displayed $D$ is skew-symmetric, and each row sums to zero, so with $H=I_3$ it satisfies [F1]. The states have $\rho_i=1$, $p_i=E_i>0$, and $T_i=E_i$, hence are admissible. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 Formula [F2] gives $v_{E}=(-1,-1/2,-1)$ and $v_m=(0,0,0)$. Multiplication by $D$ gives $Dv_E=(1/4,0,-1/4)$ and $Dv_m=0$. Since $u_i=0$, the strain array $G$ in [F3] vanishes at every node. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 For the Euler-only operator, its entropy derivative is $-2\sum_{i,\ell}D_{i\ell}v_i^TF^{\mathrm{ec}}(U_i,U_\ell)$. Skew-symmetry and [F2] rewrite this as $-\sum_{i,\ell}D_{i\ell}(\psi(U_i)-\psi(U_\ell))=0$, since both row and column sums of $D$ vanish. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For the viscous term, matrix skew-symmetry gives $v^TDW=-(Dv)^TW$ for the nodal flux array $W_i=K_{11}(U_i)(Dv)_i$, so its entropy derivative is $-\sum_i(Dv_i)^TK_{11}(U_i)(Dv_i)$. The zero strain and $T=(1,2,1)$ from step 1.1 reduce [F3] to $-\kappa\sum_iT_i^2(Dv_{E,i})^2=-\kappa(1/16+0+1/16)=-\kappa/8$. Thus adding viscosity changes the Euler-only rate from zero to the stated negative value. [F1, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $U_i(t)\in\mathcal G$, $i\in\mathcal I$, be any differentiable solution of [[def-periodic-sbp-compressible-viscous-scheme]]. Then every component of the weighted conservative state $\sum_iH_{ii}U_i(t)$ is constant, and

$$\frac{d}{dt}\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}H_{ii}\eta(U_i(t)) =-\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}H_{ii}\sum_{j,k=1}^d(D_jv_i)^TK_{jk}(U_i)(D_kv_i)\le0.$$

The exact entropy production is the finite nodal sum displayed above.
1.1 For each direction set $Q_j=HD_j$. Then [F1] gives $Q_j^T=-Q_j$ and $Q_j\mathbf1=HD_j\mathbf1=0$. Skew-symmetry also gives $\mathbf1^TQ_j=-(Q_j\mathbf1)^T=0$. [F1, algebra]

2.1 Multiply the semidiscrete equation by $H_{ii}$ and sum in $i$. For the Euler term, each component of $\sum_{i,\ell}(Q_j)_{i\ell}F_j^{\mathrm{ec}}(U_i,U_\ell)$ is zero: swapping $i$ and $\ell$ changes the sign of $Q_j$ by step 1.1 and leaves the flux unchanged by [F2]. The viscous term sums to $\mathbf1^THD_jW=\mathbf1^TQ_jW=0$ for each nodal flux array $W$. Thus the weighted sum of each conservative component has derivative zero. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 By the chain rule, the Euler contribution to the entropy derivative is $-2\sum_{j,i,\ell}(Q_j)_{i\ell}v_i^TF_j^{\mathrm{ec}}(U_i,U_\ell)$. Skew-symmetry and flux symmetry [F2], after swapping the two indices in one copy of the sum, rewrite this as $-\sum_{j,i,\ell}(Q_j)_{i\ell}(v_i-v_\ell)^TF_j^{\mathrm{ec}}(U_i,U_\ell)$. The entropy-potential identity [F2] changes the summand to $(Q_j)_{i\ell}(\psi_j(U_i)-\psi_j(U_\ell))$. Both its row sum and column sum vanish by step 1.1, so the total Euler contribution is zero. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For each viscous direction, $v^THD_jW=-(D_jv)^THW$ by $D_j^TH=-HD_j$. Applying this to $W_i=\sum_kK_{jk}(U_i)(D_kv)_i$ shows that the remaining entropy derivative is exactly the negative sum in the Statement. Each nodal quadratic form is nonnegative by [F3], and each weight $H_{ii}$ is positive; hence the derivative is nonpositive. [F1, F3, algebra] ∎

## Example

Since $h_0^{(1)}(z)=-ie^{iz}/z$, its logarithmic derivative is $h_0'(z)/h_0(z)=i-z^{-1}$. Therefore the degree-zero exact spherical DtN multiplier at radius $R$ is $\tau_0(k,R)=ik-1/R$.

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$, $d\in\{2,3\}$, be bounded, connected, and Lipschitz, and let $V=H^1_0(D;\mathbb R)$ with norm $\|v\|_V=\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(D)}$. Let $A:D\to\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ be measurable and symmetric, with constants $0<\alpha\le\beta<\infty$ such that
$$\zeta\cdot A(x)\zeta\ge\alpha|\zeta|^2\quad\text{and}\quad\|A(x)\|_{\rm op}\le\beta\quad\text{for a.e. }x\in D,\ \zeta\in\mathbb R^d.$$
For $f\in V'$, define $a(u,v)=\int_D A\nabla u\cdot\nabla v$ and $F(v)=f(v)$. Let $V_h\subset V$ be any finite conforming isogeometric subspace on the exact admissible patch geometry. Then the weak problem and its Galerkin restriction have unique solutions $u$ and $u_h$, and
$$\|u-u_h\|_V\le\frac{\beta}{\alpha}\inf_{v_h\in V_h}\|u-v_h\|_V.$$
This is an exact-form estimate; it makes no assertion about approximate geometry, quadrature, polynomial-degree-independent constants, or a rate without a separate numerator approximation theorem.

1.1 The operator bound on $A$ and Cauchy--Schwarz give $|a(v,w)|\le\beta\|v\|_V\|w\|_V$. The lower coefficient bound gives $a(v,v)\ge\alpha\|v\|_V^2$. Hence $a$ is bounded with $M=\beta$ and coercive with $\alpha_0=\alpha$. [given, algebra]

2.1 By [F3], $V$ with the gradient norm is a real Hilbert space. Its data functional $F$ is bounded by the definition of $V'$, and $V_h$ is finite dimensional and conforming by [F1] (with [F2] verifying the interface condition when needed). Thus all hypotheses of [F4] hold with $M=\beta$ and $\alpha_0=\alpha$. Applying [F4] gives both solutions and its estimate is exactly the displayed inequality. Its hypotheses concern the exact form only, so the conclusion carries no geometry or quadrature defect term and no approximation rate beyond the best-approximation infimum. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, given, step 1.1] ∎
cases.evidence: A finite conforming subspace may be the zero space, whose only discrete solution is zero; the best-approximation infimum still contains that element and is never over an empty set.

cases.input_text: No zero-valued input is a boundary case of this claim.
cases.review_reason: For zero load coercivity gives zero continuous and discrete solutions, so the error and best-approximation bound vanish; a zero comparison vector is also always admitted.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the exact finite-control coefficient hypotheses of
[[def-na-periodic-diagonal-controlled-diffusion-hjb-problem]], in any dimension
$d\ge1$. Let $u$ be bounded upper semicontinuous and $v$ bounded lower
semicontinuous on $\mathbb T^d\times(0,T)$; assume their interior
$C^{1,2}$-test inequalities are those of
[[def-na-second-order-parabolic-viscosity-solution]], using the local
maximum/minimum contact convention of
[[def-viscosity-subsolution-and-supersolution]]. Suppose the raw relaxed initial
traces are ordered at every $x\in\mathbb T^d$:
$$\limsup_{\substack{(y,t)\to(x,0)\\t>0}}u(y,t)\le\liminf_{\substack{(y,t)\to(x,0)\\t>0}}v(y,t).$$
Then $u\le v$ on $\mathbb T^d\times(0,T)$. In particular this applies to the
model's common continuous initial datum and its two relaxed initial
inequalities. Defining the values at $t=0$ by their respective raw upper and
lower envelopes gives the same order there. No continuity, spatial Lipschitz
bound, or differentiability of $u,v$ is assumed.

1.1 For any fixed lifts, a lattice minimizer exists: only finitely many integer vectors can give a norm no larger than the norm at $k=0$. If a minimizing difference $r$ has $|r|=D(x,y)<1/2$, then for every nonzero $k\in\mathbb Z^d$, $|k|\ge1$ and $r\cdot k\ge-|r||k|$: for $r\ne0$ this follows by expanding $\bigl||k|r+|r|k\bigr|^2\ge0$, and for $r=0$ it is immediate. Consequently $$|r+k|^2-|r|^2=|k|^2+2r\cdot k\ge |k|(|k|-2|r|)>0.$$ Thus that minimizing difference is unique. Choose continuous local lifts near $x,y$ and keep the minimizing lattice vector fixed; their resulting difference $r^{\prime}$ stays of norm less than $1/2$ in a sufficiently small neighborhood. The same inequality for every nonzero $k$ shows that this difference remains the unique minimizer throughout that neighborhood. Hence there $D^2=|r^{\prime}|^2$, a smooth quadratic in the local coordinates, justifying [F5]. [F5, algebra, construct]

1.2 Define $u(x,0)$ as the raw upper trace and $v(x,0)$ as the raw lower trace. Boundedness makes them finite. For example, if $x_k\to x$ and $u(x_k,0)$ approaches its limsup, the raw upper-trace definition and [A1] let us select interior $(y_k,t_k)$ with $|y_k-x_k|+t_k<1/k$ and $u(y_k,t_k)>u(x_k,0)-1/k$. Thus $y_k\to x$, $t_k\to0$, and $\limsup_k u(x_k,0)\le u(x,0)$. The lower-trace argument is dual. For a sequence with positive times tending to zero, the raw trace definition gives the USC/LSC inequalities directly; splitting a mixed sequence into positive-time and initial-edge subsequences proves the extensions are USC/LSC on the closed initial edge. The assumed order gives $u(x,0)\le v(x,0)$. Assume for contradiction that $u(x_*,t_*)-v(x_*,t_*)>0$ at some $0<t_*<T$. Choose $S$ with $t_*<S<T$, then choose $\eta,\gamma>0$ sufficiently small that $$m:=u(x_*,t_*)-v(x_*,t_*)-\eta t_*-\gamma/(S-t_*)>0.$$ Put $P(t)=\eta t+\gamma/(S-t)$. If $u(x,t)-v(y,s)-P(t)\ge0$, boundedness bounds $P(t)$ above by $\|u\|_\infty+\|v\|_\infty$, so $t\le S-c$ for some $c>0$. [A1, F4, given, choose, assume-contra]

2.1 Using [F5], define $$M_\varepsilon=\max_{x,y\in\mathbb T^d,\ 0\le t<S}\{u(x,t)-v(y,t)-P(t)-D(x,y)^2/(2\varepsilon)\}.$$ The maximum exists by step 1.2 and [F4]: the expression is USC, and its positive superlevel sets stay in a compact time interval bounded away from $S$. Also $M_\varepsilon\ge m$. Write $M_0=\max_{x,\ 0\le t<S}(u(x,t)-v(x,t)-P(t))\ge m$, also attained. At any maximizing triple $(x_\varepsilon,y_\varepsilon,t_\varepsilon)$, boundedness gives $D(x_\varepsilon,y_\varepsilon)^2=O(\varepsilon)$. Compactness and semicontinuity imply $M_\varepsilon\to M_0$: for every sequence $\varepsilon\downarrow0$, a subsequence of maximizers tends to $(x,x,t)$, and the limsup of the unpenalized expression is at most $M_0$, whereas $M_\varepsilon\ge M_0$. Moreover $$0\le D(x_\varepsilon,y_\varepsilon)^2/(4\varepsilon)\le M_{2\varepsilon}-M_\varepsilon\longrightarrow0,$$ by evaluating the $2\varepsilon$ maximum at an $\varepsilon$ maximizer. These conclusions hold uniformly over maximizing triples, by the same sequential compactness argument. No sequence of these maximizers can have $t_\varepsilon\to0$: then $x_\varepsilon,y_\varepsilon\to x$ along a subsequence and semicontinuity and the initial order give limsup of their maximum values at most $-P(0)<0$, contradicting $M_\varepsilon\ge m$. [A1, F4, F5, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 For fixed sufficiently small $\varepsilon$, introduce independent times and maximize $$\Phi_{\varepsilon,\delta}(x,t,y,s)=u(x,t)-v(y,s)-P(t)-D(x,y)^2/(2\varepsilon)-(t-s)^2/(2\delta)$$ over $x,y\in\mathbb T^d$, $0\le t<S$, $0\le s\le S$. Maxima exist by step 1.2 and [F4] and are at least $M_\varepsilon\ge m$. Boundedness gives $|t-s|=O(\sqrt\delta)$ and $t\le S-c$ uniformly. For fixed $\varepsilon$, compactness shows that as $\delta\downarrow0$ every limit of maximizing quadruples is a synchronized maximizer of $M_\varepsilon$: the limsup of the expression without the temporal penalty is at most $M_\varepsilon$, while the maximum is at least $M_\varepsilon$. Hence the temporal penalty tends to zero too. By step 2.1 and [F5], for all sufficiently small $\varepsilon$ these limiting times are positive and the spatial distance is less than $1/2$. Consequently for each such $\varepsilon$ and all sufficiently small $\delta$, both times are strictly in $(0,S)$ and $D(x,y)^2=|r|^2$ is smooth near the maximizer in local lifts with $r=x-y$ and $|r|=D(x,y)$. Thus all contacts used next are interior in the original cylinder. [A1, F4, F5, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 At such a maximizer apply [F2] to $u(t,x)$ and $-v(s,y)$ with $$\phi(t,x,s,y)=|x-y|^2/(2\varepsilon)+(t-s)^2/(2\delta)+P(t),\qquad\mu=\varepsilon.$$ It gives a closed upper jet of $u$ with gradient $(a,p)$ and Hessian $H$, and a closed lower jet of $v$ with gradient $(b,p)$ and Hessian $K$, where $$p=r/\varepsilon,\quad a=(t-s)/\delta+P'(t),\quad b=(t-s)/\delta,\quad a-b=P'(t)\ge\eta.$$ Negating the jet of $-v$ gives the lower jet of $v$ directly from its defining expansion and witnessing sequence. Let $X,Y$ be the spatial principal blocks of $H,K$. The full Hessian of $\phi$ has no space-time mixed entries. Its spatial block is $\varepsilon^{-1}B$ with $B=\begin{pmatrix}I&-I\\-I&I\end{pmatrix}$ and $B^2=2B$. Restricting the upper matrix inequality in [F2] to vectors with zero temporal components therefore gives $$\begin{pmatrix}X&0\\0&-Y\end{pmatrix}\le(3/\varepsilon)B.$$ The temporal Hessian, including $P''(t)$ and the potentially large $1/\delta$, contributes nothing to this spatial restriction. [F2, F5, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 For each control $c$ write $G_c(x,t,p,X)=\sum_j(\alpha_j^c(x,t)X_{jj}+b_j^c(x,t)p_j)+f^c(x,t)$. By [F3], $a\le\max_cG_c(x,t,p,X)$ and $b\ge\max_cG_c(y,s,p,Y)$. model's common continuous initial datum and its two relaxed initial

bound, or differentiability of $u,v$ is assumed.

Consequently $$|r+k|^2-|r|^2=|k|^2+2r\cdot k\ge |k|(|k|-2|r|)>0.$$ Thus that minimizing difference is unique. Choose continuous local lifts near $x,y$ and keep the minimizing lattice vector fixed; their resulting difference $r^{\prime}$ stays of norm less than $1/2$ in a sufficiently small neighborhood. Thus $y_k\to x$, $t_k\to0$, and $\limsup_k u(x_k,0)\le u(x,0)$. The lower-trace argument is dual. The assumed order gives $u(x,0)\le v(x,0)$. Assume for contradiction that $u(x_*,t_*)-v(x_*,t_*)>0$ at some $0<t_*<T$. ## Statement

Let $x_0<\cdots<x_n$ and $0\le d<n$, and use the $\mu_i$ and
$s=\sum_{i=0}^{n-d}\mu_i$ of
[[lem-floater-hormann-weight-and-blend-identity]]. For
$x_\alpha<x<x_{\alpha+1}$, partition the indices into
$$I_1=\{i\le\alpha-d\},\quad I_2=\{\alpha-d+1\le i\le\alpha\},\quad I_3=\{i\ge\alpha+1\},$$
intersecting each set with $\{0,\ldots,n-d\}$. Each nonempty partial sum
$\sum_{i\in I_k}\mu_i(x)$ is positive. More precisely, if $I_3$ is nonempty,
its terms alternate starting positive with strictly decreasing magnitudes; if
$I_1$ is nonempty, its terms have the same property when read backward from
$i=\alpha-d$. If $d\ge1$, every term in $I_2$ is positive.

1.1 If $i\in I_2$, every factor in $\mu_i(x)$ is positive: left indices lie strictly below $x_\alpha<x$, and right indices lie strictly above $x<x_{\alpha+1}$. Thus all terms in a nonempty $I_2$ are positive. If $d=0$, $I_2$ is empty. [given, F1, algebra]

1.2 If $I_3$ is nonempty, its first index is $\alpha+1$ and $\mu_{\alpha+1}(x)>0$. For $\alpha+1\le i<n-d$, $$\frac{\mu_{i+1}(x)}{\mu_i(x)} =\frac{x-x_i}{x_{i+d+1}-x}<0,\qquad \left|\frac{\mu_{i+1}(x)}{\mu_i(x)}\right|<1.$$ The numerator is negative and its magnitude is smaller than the positive denominator because $x_i<x_{i+d+1}$. Consecutive terms therefore alternate with strictly decreasing magnitudes. Pairing from the first positive term gives a positive sum, including when one positive term remains. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 If $I_1$ is nonempty, its last index is $\alpha-d$ and $\mu_{\alpha-d}(x)>0$. Read backward. For $i\le\alpha-d$ with $i>0$, $$\frac{\mu_{i-1}(x)}{\mu_i(x)} =\frac{x_{i+d}-x}{x-x_{i-1}}<0,\qquad \left|\frac{\mu_{i-1}(x)}{\mu_i(x)}\right|<1.$$ Here $x_{i+d}\le x_\alpha<x$ and $x_{i-1}<x_i\le x_{i+d}$, so the numerator is negative and its magnitude is smaller than the positive denominator. Pairing backward from the first positive term proves the $I_1$ sum is positive. [given, F1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let a periodic rectangular cell be discretized by a uniform Cartesian Yee grid with spacings $h_x,h_y,h_z$, $h=\max_jh_j$, and constant scalar coefficients $\epsilon,\mu>0$. Let $(E,B)$ be a source-free smooth periodic Maxwell solution on $[0,T]$, with the spatial derivatives of $E$ through total order four, $\partial_t^4E$, and $\partial_t^3B$ bounded. Sample $E(t_n)$ by exact oriented edge line integrals $e_*^n$ and $B(t_{n+1/2})$ by exact oriented face fluxes $b_*^{n+1/2}$. Define
$$r_h^n=M_e\frac{e_*^{n+1}-2e_*^n+e_*^{n-1}}{\Delta t^2}+C^TM_bCe_*^n,\qquad s_h^n=b_*^{n+1/2}-b_*^{n-1/2}+\Delta t\,Ce_*^n.$$
With the homogeneous diagonal Hodge weights of [[def-maxwell-discrete-cochain-and-yee-grid]], there is a constant $C_T$ independent of the cell counts such that, whenever $\Delta t\le t_n\le T-\Delta t$,
$$\|r_h^n\|_{M_e^{-1}}\le C_T(h^2+\Delta t^2),\qquad \|s_h^n\|_{M_b}\le C_T\Delta t^3.$$
Here $\|r\|_{M_e^{-1}}^2=r^TM_e^{-1}r$. This is a smooth homogeneous periodic consistency result; it asserts no Taylor estimate across coefficient jumps or a PEC boundary closure.

1.1 Let $u_x=e_x/h_x$ denote the line average of the $x$ component on an $x$-edge; define $u_y,u_z$ cyclically. For values on the corresponding staggered locations, define $\delta_i\delta_j f(r)$ by the four-corner formula $[f(r+\frac{h_i}{2}e_i+\frac{h_j}{2}e_j)-f(r+\frac{h_i}{2}e_i-\frac{h_j}{2}e_j)-f(r-\frac{h_i}{2}e_i+\frac{h_j}{2}e_j)+f(r-\frac{h_i}{2}e_i-\frac{h_j}{2}e_j)]/(h_ih_j)$. Expanding the four signed face incidences around an $x$-edge and inserting [F1] gives the normalized electric operator $h_x^{-1}(M_e^{-1}C^TM_bCe)_x=c^2\bigl(-\delta_y^2u_x-\delta_z^2u_x+\delta_x\delta_yu_y+\delta_x\delta_zu_z\bigr),\qquad c^2=(\epsilon\mu)^{-1},$ where $\delta_j^2f=(f(x+h_je_j)-2f(x)+f(x-h_je_j))/h_j^2$ and $\delta_i\delta_j$ is the corresponding centered staggered mixed difference. The $y$ and $z$ components follow by the same cyclic incidence expansion. [F1, given, algebra]

1.2 For every face, the exact circulation cochain $Ce_*^n$ equals the face flux of $\operatorname{curl}E(t_n)$ by [F4]. Taylor’s formula in time around $t_n$ gives $\int_{t_n-\Delta t/2}^{t_n+\Delta t/2}\!\!\!\int_F\operatorname{curl}E(t)\cdot n\,dS\,dt=\Delta t\int_F\operatorname{curl}E(t_n)\cdot n\,dS+O(|F|\Delta t^3\|\partial_t^2\operatorname{curl}E\|_\infty).$ Faraday’s equation in [F3] identifies the left side with $-\int_F(B(t_n+\Delta t/2)-B(t_n-\Delta t/2))\cdot n\,dS$. Thus each face entry of $s_h^n$ is bounded by $C|F|\Delta t^3$ times the derivative bound. The face weights in [F1] turn the sum of their squared entries into at most $C_T\Delta t^6$ times the fixed box volume, so $\|s_h^n\|_{M_b}\le C_T\Delta t^3\le C_T'\Delta t^2$ on the stated time range. [F1, F2, F3, F4, algebra]

2.1 Taylor’s formula with integral remainder gives $\delta_j^2f=\partial_j^2f+O(h_j^2\|\partial_j^4f\|_\infty)$ and $\delta_i\delta_jf=\partial_i\partial_jf+O((h_i^2+h_j^2)\|D^4f\|_\infty)$. Averaging along the edge changes the midpoint value of each needed derivative by at most $O(h^2)$ by the same symmetric Taylor estimate. Therefore the stencil in step 1.1 differs from $\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}E$ by at most $C h^2$ pointwise. The centered time second difference of the exact edge integrals differs from the edge integral of $E_{tt}$ by at most $C\Delta t^2$ times the stated fourth time-derivative bound. The continuous equation [F3] cancels the leading terms. For an $x$-edge, the resulting electric covector entry is bounded by $C\epsilon h_yh_z(h^2+\Delta t^2)$, with cyclic area factors for the other orientations. Summing squared entries with the reciprocal edge masses in [F1] contributes a factor proportional to $h_xh_yh_z$ per edge, so $\|r_h^n\|_{M_e^{-1}}\le C_T(h^2+\Delta t^2)$, since the dual cell volumes sum to the fixed box volume. [F1, F3, step 1.1, algebra]
3.1 The electric bound from step 2.1 and the separate face bound from step 1.2 give the two asserted residual estimates. [step 2.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎
cases.evidence: A valid periodic Yee cell has positive spacings and actual edge and face cochains; the time-index window can be empty when the step is too large, in which case the residual estimates assert nothing at an inadmissible time.

## Statement

For every valid input to [[alg-positive-tube-forward-euler-for-compressible-sbp]] with finite budget $N$, the loop returns after at most $N$ candidate evaluations. Its accepted-step count is between $0$ and $N$, and every returned nodal state lies in the specified compact tube $\mathcal C$.
1.1 If $N=0$, branch 4 of [F1] returns the input immediately, with zero evaluations and zero accepted stages. [F1, given]

1.2 Suppose $N>0$. At each visited stage $n<N$, branch 3 returns immediately if the candidate fails, so no rejected stage repeats; the algorithm reports $n$ accepted steps because $U^n$ follows exactly $n$ earlier acceptances. Otherwise branch 2 accepts one candidate, so the next stored iterate follows one more acceptance. If all $N$ candidates are accepted, branch 4 returns `completed` with count $N$. Thus the loop has at most $N$ evaluations and the accepted count lies in $[0,N]$. [F1, given]

2.1 The initial nodal vector is in $\mathcal C$ by the algorithm input. Each later vector becomes the stored state only after every node passes membership in $\mathcal C$; branch 3 returns the preceding stored vector. Therefore every returned nodal state lies in $\mathcal C$. [F1, step 1.2, given] ∎

For every valid input to [[alg-positive-tube-forward-euler-for-compressible-sbp]] with finite budget $N$, the loop returns after at most $N$ candidate evaluations. Its accepted-step count is between $0$ and $N$, and every returned nodal state lies in the specified compact tube $\mathcal C$.
1.1 If $N=0$, branch 4 of [F1] returns the input immediately, with zero evaluations and zero accepted stages. [F1, given]

1.2 Suppose $N>0$. At each visited stage $n<N$, branch 3 returns immediately if the candidate fails, so no rejected stage repeats; the algorithm reports $n$ accepted steps because $U^n$ follows exactly $n$ earlier acceptances. Otherwise branch 2 accepts one candidate, so the next stored iterate follows one more acceptance. If all $N$ candidates are accepted, branch 4 returns `completed` with count $N$. Thus the loop has at most $N$ evaluations and the accepted count lies in $[0,N]$. [F1, given]

2.1 The initial nodal vector is in $\mathcal C$ by the algorithm input. Each later vector becomes the stored state only after every node passes membership in $\mathcal C$; branch 3 returns the preceding stored vector. Therefore every returned nodal state lies in $\mathcal C$. [F1, step 1.2, given] ∎
cases.evidence: A candidate failing even one tube membership test is rejected immediately and the previous accepted state is returned, so no degenerate or inadmissible candidate is promoted to stored state.

cases.input_text: The claim has no separate endpoint case beyond its stated boundary convention.
cases.review_reason: Accepted counts include both zero and the full budget; the proof distinguishes immediate rejection from acceptance of the final allowed candidate and proves tube membership for both returns.

## Statement

Let $r>0$ and use the scalar Fisher–KPP reaction $F(u)=ru(1-u)$ on $R=[0,1]$, followed by exact no-flux TPFA diffusion with any diffusivity $d\ge0$. For a nonnegative step $\tau$, the forward-Euler reaction map preserves $[0,1]$ for every starting value $u\in[0,1]$ exactly when $0\le\tau r\le1$; after that step, exact no-flux TPFA diffusion also preserves the interval. For $\tau>0$, on any finite grid with positive cell weights, the reaction strictly increases the discrete mass if at least one cell value lies in $(0,1)$ and leaves it unchanged if every cell value is a reaction equilibrium $0$ or $1$. At $\tau=0$ the reaction map is the identity. This example makes no mass-conservation claim.

1.1 On $[0,1]$, $F(0)=F(1)=0$, so the field points inward at both endpoints. Also $|F'(u)|=|r(1-2u)|\le r$, giving the coordinate Lipschitz constant $L=r$ and Euler restriction $\tau\le1/r$. [F1, A1, algebra]

2.1 For $u\in[0,1]$, set $\alpha=\tau r\in[0,1]$. The Euler value is $u^+=u+\alpha u(1-u)\ge0$, while $ 1-u^+=(1-u)(1-\alpha u)\ge0 $ because both factors are nonnegative. Thus the reaction step preserves $[0,1]$. [A1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 If $\alpha=\tau r>1$, choose $u$ with $1/\alpha<u<1$. Then $1-u^+=(1-u)(1-\alpha u)<0$, so the Euler map leaves $[0,1]$. Together with step 2.1 this proves the stated necessary-and-sufficient bound for the reaction map. [A1, step 2.1, choose, algebra]

4.1 The reaction map satisfies the hypothesis of [F3] by step 2.1; applying [F2] and then [F3] proves that the full TPFA Lie update also remains in $[0,1]$. For a grid state $U=(u_i)_i$ with positive weights $m_i$, its Euler reaction mass increment is $\sum_i m_i\tau r u_i(1-u_i)$. This is strictly positive for $\tau>0$ exactly when some $u_i\in(0,1)$, and is zero when every $u_i\in\{0,1\}$; for $\tau=0$ it is zero for every state. Thus the mass claim in the Statement holds, and no mass-conservation claim is made. [F1, F2, F3, step 2.1, algebra] ∎
cases.evidence: The scalar interval of admissible values is nonempty, while a finite grid with no interior-valued cell has zero reaction mass increment; the strict increase assertion is conditional on at least one interior-valued cell.

## Statement

Fix $0<a<R$, $k>0$, and let $\mathcal V_{a,R}$ and $\mathfrak a_{k,a,R}$ be as in [[def-pe18-spherical-dtn-truncated-variational-problem]]. There is $C=C(a,R,k)$ such that for every $u,v\in\mathcal V_{a,R}$,
$$\sum_{\ell\ge0}(1+\ell)\bigl(\|u_\ell(a)\|_2^2+\|u_\ell(R)\|_2^2\bigr)\le C\|u\|_{\mathcal V}^2,\qquad |\mathfrak a_{k,a,R}(u,v)|\le C\|u\|_{\mathcal V}\|v\|_{\mathcal V}.$$
In particular, the defining traces and boundary pairing are finite, the form is continuous, $\mathcal V_{a,R}$ is a Hilbert direct sum, and finite-degree truncations converge in its norm.

1.1 Each $H^1((a,R);\mathcal H_\ell)$ is complete because $\mathcal H_\ell$ is finite dimensional. A Cauchy sequence in the weighted square-sum norm is Cauchy in each coordinate; take its coordinatewise $H^1$ limits. For every finite number of coordinates the squared norm of the limit is bounded by the liminf of the sequence norms, so the coordinatewise limit has finite total norm; applying the same argument to differences shows convergence in the sum norm. Tails of the defining convergent nonnegative series tend to zero, so finite-degree truncations are dense. For any scalar or finite-dimensional Hilbert-valued $w\in H^1(a,R)$, absolute continuity and $|w(R)|^2-|w(t)|^2=2\operatorname{Re}\int_t^R\langle w'(s),w(s)\rangle ds$ give, after averaging $t$ over $[a,R]$ and applying Cauchy–Schwarz, $\|w(R)\|^2\le(R-a)^{-1}\int_a^R\|w\|^2dr+2\left(\int_a^R\|w\|^2dr\right)^{1/2}\left(\int_a^R\|w'\|^2dr\right)^{1/2}.$ Using $2(1+\ell)AB\le A^2+(1+\ell)^2B^2$, $(1+\ell)^2\le2(1+\ell(\ell+1))$, and $a^2\le r^2\le R^2$, this yields $ (1+\ell)\|w(R)\|^2\le C_{a,R}\int_a^R\left(r^2\|w'\|^2+(1+\ell(\ell+1))\|w\|^2\right)dr.$ Replacing $r$ by $a+R-r$ proves the same inequality at the inner endpoint. Summing with $w=u_\ell$ proves the weighted trace estimate. [F1, algebra]

2.1 The volume terms of $\mathfrak a$ are bounded by a constant times $\|u\|_{\mathcal V}\|v\|_{\mathcal V}$ because $r$ lies in $[a,R]$ and $k$ is fixed. By [F2], $|\tau_\ell|\le C_{k,R}(1+\ell)$. Cauchy–Schwarz over degrees and the trace estimate from step 1.1 give $\sum_\ell |\tau_\ell\langle u_\ell(R),v_\ell(R)\rangle|\le C\left(\sum_\ell(1+\ell)\|u_\ell(R)\|_2^2\right)^{1/2}\left(\sum_\ell(1+\ell)\|v_\ell(R)\|_2^2\right)^{1/2}\le C\|u\|_{\mathcal V}\|v\|_{\mathcal V}.$ Thus the boundary series is absolutely convergent and the whole form is continuous. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎
cases.evidence: The annulus has strictly ordered positive radii and the energy space contains zero; finite harmonic truncations may have zero tails, but the full trace sum is over all nonnegative degrees.

cases.review_reason: The completeness argument takes the uniquely determined coordinate limits of a Cauchy sequence, while the trace estimate and finite-degree truncations are explicit; no arbitrary basis choice is used by these calculations.

## Statement

Whenever [[alg-certified-airy-evaluation]] returns `success`, its interval or
rectangle contains the requested $\operatorname{Ai}(z)$ or
$\operatorname{Bi}(z)$ and passes the requested absolute-radius test. Any
relative certificate is valid only when the enclosure excludes zero. No
success guarantee is made for every input or finite cap. Every execution with finite
caps terminates.

1.1 The initial coefficients used by the procedure enclose the exact Airy initial values by [F3], with the Gamma calls sound by [A1] and the powers of 3 sound by [A2]. Arithmetic on these intervals is sound by [A3]. The series definition and recurrence determine all later coefficients, so the resulting partial sums enclose their exact finite series sums. [A1, A2, A3, F3]

2.1 By [F2], each nonzero omitted class tail lies within its computed absolute tail bound; the third class is zero because its initial coefficient is zero and the recurrence preserves zero. Therefore the exact Airy value lies in the partial-sum enclosure enlarged by the sum of the two tail bounds. [A3, F2, F3, step 1.1]

3.1 The algorithm reports success only when that containing rectangle passes the requested radius test, and its relative flag obeys [F1]. If its finite caps do not allow that test, the result is inconclusive; no claim of universal success is made. [A1, A2, F1, F3, step 2.1]

4.1 The stage loop is finite; each Gamma and elementary-range subcall has finite caps and truncation index, and the residue-class sums have at most the capped number of terms. Thus every capped execution terminates. [given, A1, A2, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the contractible Lipschitz domain and shape-regular mesh-family hypotheses of [[thm-na-uniformly-bounded-commuting-cochain-projection]], with matching affine tetrahedra and the PEC edge space of [[def-maxwell-edge-fem-semidiscretization]]. Assume Countable Choice as in that projection interface. Let $B_0\in H(\operatorname{div};\Omega)$ be piecewise smooth, have matching normal traces, and satisfy $\operatorname{div}B_0=0$. Let $\pi_h^2$ be the degree-two cochain projection in that interface, let $X_h=\operatorname{range}C\subset N_h^2$, and let $P_{X_h}$ be orthogonal projection onto $X_h$ for $(u,v)_{\mu^{-1}}=\int_\Omega u^T\mu^{-1}v\,dx$. Define
$$B_h^0=\pi_h^2B_0+P_{X_h}(B_0-\pi_h^2B_0).$$
Then $B_h^0\in N_h^2$, $D B_h^0=0$, and
$$(B_h^0-B_0,\operatorname{curl}v_h)_{\mu^{-1}}=0\quad(v_h\in V_h),\qquad \|B_h^0-B_0\|_{\mu^{-1}}\le C h\,M_B,$$
where $V_h=N_h^1\cap H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$ and $M_B$ is the maximum of the piecewise first-derivative bounds for $B_0$ and $\operatorname{div}B_0$ used by the smooth interpolation estimate. The error constant is uniform over the shape-regular family when the commuting projection norms are uniformly bounded.

1.1 The subspace $X_h$ is finite dimensional. In a basis of $X_h$, its $\mu^{-1}$ Gram matrix is symmetric positive definite, so the normal equations have one solution for each $B_0-\pi_h^2B_0$; this defines $P_{X_h}$. Its value lies in $X_h\subset N_h^2$, and the definition of orthogonal projection gives $B_h^0-B_0=-(I-P_{X_h})(B_0-\pi_h^2B_0)\perp_{\mu^{-1}}X_h$. Orthogonal decomposition yields $\|B_h^0-B_0\|_{\mu^{-1}}\le\|B_0-\pi_h^2B_0\|_{\mu^{-1}}$. [A1, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Since $I_h^2B_0\in N_h^2$ and $\pi_h^2$ is a projection, $\pi_h^2 I_h^2B_0=I_h^2B_0$. Thus $B_0-\pi_h^2B_0=(I-\pi_h^2)(B_0-I_h^2B_0)$. Uniform boundedness of $\pi_h^2$ on $H(\operatorname{div})$, norm equivalence from the coefficient bounds, and [F3] imply $\|B_0-\pi_h^2B_0\|_{\mu^{-1}}\le C h M_B$. Combining with step 1.1 gives the asserted approximation estimate. [F1, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The projection identity and [F1] give $D\pi_h^2B_0=\pi_h^3(\operatorname{div}B_0)=0$. Every element of $X_h$ is a discrete curl, so [F2] gives $D P_{X_h}(B_0-\pi_h^2B_0)=0$. Adding the two terms proves $D B_h^0=0$. [F1, F2, given, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $\Omega=\prod_{j=1}^d(0,L_j)$ and let $u\in C^1([0,T];C^4(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^m))$ solve $u_t=D\Delta u+F(u)$ with $D=\operatorname{diag}(d_r)$, $d_r\ge0$, and range in a compact reaction-inward rectangle $R$. Assume $F\in C^2$ near $R$, homogeneous Neumann data hold, and the coordinatewise even reflection of $u$ across every face extends to a $C^1_tC^4_x$ function on the doubled torus $\prod_j(\mathbb R/2L_j\mathbb Z)$. On the uniform cell-centered grid of [[def-cell-centered-rectangular-no-flux-tpfa-grid]], start the exact reaction-then-diffusion Lie step of [[alg-exact-lie-reaction-diffusion-step]] from cell-center samples and use uniform $\tau=T/N$. Then a constant $C_T$, independent of the mesh widths and $N$, satisfies
$$
\max_{0\le n\le N}\|U^n-P_hu(t_n)\|_\infty\le C_T(\tau+h_{\max}^2),\qquad t_n=n\tau.
$$
This result is for rectangular Cartesian TPFA grids and solutions with the stated even $C^4$ boundary compatibility; it does not assert mesh-uniform accuracy for general admissible polyhedral meshes.

1.1 For each coordinate define $r_j(k_j)=k_j$ if $0\le k_j<N_j$ and $r_j(k_j)=2N_j-1-k_j$ if $N_j\le k_j<2N_j$. Then $(E_hU)_k=U_{(r_j(k_j))_j}$. At an interior original index, the doubled periodic stencil uses the same two neighbors as $A_h^N$. At the left boundary, the doubled neighbor $k_j=-1$ is represented by $2N_j-1$, whose reflected index is $0$, so its value is $U_i$; the right-boundary ghost similarly equals the last cell value. Therefore $ A_{2h}^{\rm per}E_hU=E_hA_h^NU $ for every array $U$. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 From step 1.1, $(A_{2h}^{\rm per})^kE_h=E_h(A_h^N)^k$ for every integer $k\ge0$, by induction. The exponential power series [F6] then gives $e^{-\tau d_rA_{2h}^{\rm per}}E_h=E_he^{-\tau d_rA_h^N}$ for each species. The nodewise reaction flow also commutes with $E_h$: reflected copies start from identical values and solve the same IVP, so uniqueness [F5] keeps them identical. [F4, F5, F6, step 1.1, induction, algebra]

3.1 At time zero, $E_hP_hu(0)$ is exactly the sample of the even-reflected continuous initial data on the doubled torus. Step 2.1 shows that the periodic split update of this array is the even extension of the no-flux TPFA split update. Induction over $n$ therefore identifies the periodic numerical iterates with $E_hU^n$. [F1, F2, F4, step 2.1, induction]

4.1 The even-reflected function is $C^1_tC^4_x$ by [A1]. On every reflected open subrectangle, reflection preserves the Laplacian and acts only by coordinate sign changes on first derivatives; since the PDE has constant diagonal diffusion and pointwise reaction, the reflected function satisfies the same equation there. The equality extends across each interface by continuity of the function and its time and second spatial derivatives. Thus the doubled function solves the periodic problem covered by [F3]. Its samples are $E_hP_hu(t_n)$, and step 3.1 plus reflection gives $ \|E_hU^n-E_hP_hu(t_n)\|_\infty=\|U^n-P_hu(t_n)\|_\infty. $ Apply [F3] on the doubled grid, whose counts $2N_j$ are at least four, to obtain the bound. [A1, F1, F2, F3, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Definition

**Inputs.** A finite list of input basis contractions $\phi_a=\sum_{i=1}^{q_a}d_{ai}g_{ai}$, $1\le a\le n$, from [[def-cartesian-gaussian-primitives-and-contractions]], represented by finite dyadic intervals for real centers and positive exponents and finite dyadic intervals or complex rectangles for coefficients; a finite nuclear list; positive integral and energy tolerances for the requested outputs; an optional positive gradient tolerance, defaulting to the energy tolerance when absent; optional positive screening tolerance; finite positive integer work and precision caps $W,P$; and a dyadic format of precision $2\le p\le P$ with exponent bounds and fixed elementary truncation index $K\ge1$. A primitive request is the singleton-contraction case. An energy/gradient request additionally requires $n,r\ge1$, real basis coefficients, real nuclear data, real matrices $C\in\mathbb R^{n\times r},D\in\mathbb R^{r\times r}$ given by dyadic boxes (exact matrices are singleton boxes), and uniform finite bounds $B\ge\sup\|C\|_F$, $M_D\ge\sup\|D\|_F$ from [[def-finite-gaussian-basis-variational-energy-and-gradient]]. Internal primitive labels $(a,i)$ are distinct from the input basis labels $a$; $C$ is a subsequent transform of the input basis.

**Outputs.** A status `success`, `inconclusive`, `domain`, or `range`; outward real intervals or complex rectangles for the requested overlap, kinetic, nuclear-attraction and two-electron Coulomb integrals; when requested, an energy interval, a gradient center and a Frobenius gradient-error bound; and a separately accumulated discarded-energy bound. Success encloses every parameter value in the input boxes. No status declares an omitted integral zero.

**Finite calls and accounting.** Use [[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]] for arithmetic. Every real elementary call means a typed DAG call to [[alg-certified-elementary-range-evaluation]] at the supplied format and $K$. Enclose $\pi$ by the $K$-term Machin/arctangent certificate in [[lem-trigonometric-identities-machin-and-range-reduction]], with exact rational tail endpoints before final outward conversion. A shared counter charges each conversion, comparison, loop update, arithmetic operation, recurrence update and summand, including every primitive operation executed by a child. Check the counter before executing an operation and interrupt any child at exhaustion. A required Boys call receives remaining work $R$ as its finite work cap, precision cap $P$, the same format and $K$, absolute tolerance $\varepsilon_I/2$ where $\varepsilon_I$ is the integral tolerance, and no relative request; its actual work is charged to the parent. A required child non-success propagates its status, except that a rounded intermediate failing a domain certification on valid original data yields `inconclusive`. Overflow yields `range`; cap exhaustion yields `inconclusive`. These choices are conservative and need not permit success under every cap or tolerance.

1. Validate positive exponent lower endpoints, finite input boxes, indices in $\mathbb N_0^3$, supported format and positive tolerances/caps. Invalid original data return `domain`. For energy/gradient verify realness and dimensions and certify the norm bounds by outward Frobenius upper bounds on the complete boxes. If this sufficient norm test cannot certify the supplied bounds, return `inconclusive`; do not claim that an unknown represented matrix violates its bound. Form finite requested primitive-pair and quartet lists lexicographically. Include all shifted overlap pairs required by the kinetic raising/lowering formula; a negative index contributes zero.

2. For each ordered primitive pair with exponents $a,b$, indices $\alpha,\beta$ and centers $A,B$, compute $p=a+b$, $P=(aA+bB)/p$, and $K_{ab}=\exp(-ab\|A-B\|^2/p)$ by outward arithmetic and the real elementary call. Compute the Hermite coefficients by [[thm-cartesian-pair-hermite-expansion-and-coefficient-recurrence]], raising the first primitive in x,y,z order and then the second, storing each intermediate degree table until its successors have been formed. The final table has $\prod_{j=1}^3(\alpha_j+\beta_j+1)$ entries; every intermediate table update is also charged. Compute overlap by the finite shifted polynomial expansion and the moments in [[lem-cartesian-gaussian-moments-and-parameter-derivatives]], and kinetic by [[thm-cartesian-gaussian-raising-lowering-and-kinetic-recurrences]]. Certified square roots and integer powers evaluate all half-integer factors in those moment formulas.

3. To evaluate an attraction primitive pair, put $L=|\alpha|+|\beta|$ and use exponent $\eta=p$ and center difference $P-C_{\rm nuc}$. To evaluate a primitive Coulomb quartet, including any diagonal self quartet, put $L=|\alpha|+|\beta|+|\gamma|+|\delta|$, $\eta=pq/(p+q)$ and center difference $P-Q$, where the second pair has exponent $q$. Form the nonnegative Boys argument interval $\mathcal T=\eta\|P-Q\|^2$, with the evident attraction substitution, using interval squaring and the positive exponent bounds. Request Boys orders $0,\ldots,L$ from [[alg-certified-boys-finite-budget-branch-evaluation]]. If rounding prevents certification of a required positive denominator, return `inconclusive`.

4. Initialize $R^j_{000}=(-2\eta)^jF_j(\mathcal T)$ for $0\le j\le L$. For total derivative degree $d=1,\ldots,L$, enumerate $(t,u,v)$ lexicographically with $t+u+v=d$, choose its first nonzero coordinate in x,y,z order, and apply that coordinate's recurrence in [[thm-gaussian-coulomb-hermite-recurrences-and-integral-formulas]] for $0\le j\le L-d$. Negative-index terms are zero. For example, when $t>0$, use $R^j_{tuv}=(P_1-Q_1)R^{j+1}_{t-1,u,v}+(t-1)R^{j+1}_{t-2,u,v}$. Each predecessor is at a smaller derivative degree and within its stored Boys-order range. Contract the finite Hermite sums in that theorem to get each primitive integral.

5. Contract primitive integrals to input-basis integrals by the finite coefficient sums. For overlap, kinetic and attraction the coefficient is $\overline{d_{ai}}d_{bj}$. For the defined pair-density Coulomb convention, the primitive quartet coefficient is $d_{ai}\overline{d_{bj}}\overline{d_{ck}}d_{dl}$: expand $\overline{f_{ab}(x)}f_{cd}(y)$ in [[def-cartesian-gaussian-primitives-and-contractions]]. In the real energy branch these are the four real contraction coefficients. Cache only identical ordered parameter boxes, angular indices, format and truncation context; an $R$ cache record also stores its cutoff $L$. Reuse a table only if its stored cutoff is at least the needed cutoff; otherwise compute the larger table under the counter.

6. Optional Coulomb-energy screening applies to whole input-basis quartets, before their off-diagonal primitive quartets are evaluated. First compute every required contracted diagonal $G_{ab,ab}$ without screening by steps 2–5, including all coefficients $d$. Obtain finite nonnegative upper endpoints $U_{ab}$ from their real projections, justified by [[thm-positive-coulomb-bilinear-cauchy-schwarz-screening]]. Form the outward real interval $W_{ab}=\sum_{p,q}C_{ap}D_{pq}C_{bq}$ and its upper absolute bound $A_{ab}=\max(|\inf W_{ab}|,|\sup W_{ab}|)$. Compute nonnegative outward upper bounds $Q_{abcd}\ge\sqrt{U_{ab}U_{cd}}$ and $w_{abcd}\ge\tfrac12A_{ab}A_{cd}Q_{abcd}$. Enumerate all ordered candidate basis quartets lexicographically, with no unrecorded symmetry compression. Skip a quartet only if the outward accumulated sum after adding $w_{abcd}$ is at most the screening tolerance; otherwise compute its primitive sums. Store a skipped real entry as $[-Q_{abcd},Q_{abcd}]$ and report the actual accumulated weighted sum. Thus entrywise radius uses $Q$, while the discarded-energy bound uses $w$. Even a skipped integral must pass its requested integral-tolerance test. No screening is required or performed when this optional real-energy branch is absent.

7. Form the one-body matrix $H$ with its specified finite nuclear weights and the Coulomb tensor $G$ on the input basis. For real energy/gradient output use their midpoint tensors $\widetilde H,\widetilde G$ and largest entrywise radii $\varepsilon_2,\varepsilon_4$, including every screened interval. Evaluate the finite polynomial $E(C;D,\widetilde H,\widetilde G)$ by outward arithmetic over the full $C,D$ boxes, and enlarge its interval by $\delta_E=M_DrnB^2\varepsilon_2+\tfrac12M_D^2r^2n^2B^4\varepsilon_4$ from [[thm-gaussian-contraction-error-energy-gradient-bounds]]. Evaluate every formal partial derivative of this same finite polynomial by differentiating its two and four factors of $C$ and using outward finite sums. If their intervals have midpoints $c_{a\mu}$ and radii $\rho_{a\mu}$, return gradient center $c$ with outward upper Frobenius error bound $\sqrt{\sum_{a,\mu}\rho_{a\mu}^2}+\delta_\nabla$, where $\delta_\nabla=2nrBM_D\varepsilon_2+2n^2r^2B^3M_D^2\varepsilon_4$. This includes uncertainty in $C,D$ as well as integral error; nuclear and contraction-coefficient uncertainty was already included in the integral boxes. Count all these operations. Return `success` only when every requested integral radius, energy radius and gradient-error bound meets its own declared tolerance; otherwise return `inconclusive`.

An $R$ table with cutoff $L$ stores $\sum_{d=0}^L(L-d+1)\binom{d+2}{2}$ entries. All input, pair, primitive-quartet and auxiliary tables are finite. Every update and child evaluation is also subject to the shared finite work counter, so valid inputs may return `inconclusive` when their tolerance or work requirement cannot be certified.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice required by the weak Poisson supplier. Let $f\in L^2(\Omega)$ on a bounded connected Lipschitz polygon, and let $(\sigma,u)=(-\nabla u,u)$ be the unique weak Dirichlet solution. The exact functional $J_h$ has a unique minimizer in the conforming RT0/P1 family, and that minimizer is the orthogonal best approximation in the residual inner product. Its scalar component remains in $H^1_0(\Omega)$.

1.1 The weak solution supplier in [A1] applies because a bounded polygon is open and bounded in one direction, and $v\mapsto(f,v)$ is bounded on $H^1_0$ by Cauchy–Schwarz and Poincare. It gives $u\in H^1_0$; the distributional equation gives $\sigma=-\nabla u\in H(div)$ and $div\sigma=f$. [A1, given, algebra]

2.1 For any $(\sigma_h,u_h)$ in the trial family, the residual of its difference from $(\sigma,u)$ equals $(\sigma_h+\nabla u_h,div\sigma_h-f)$ by [F3]. Thus $J_h=\|R((\sigma_h,u_h)- (\sigma,u))\|^2$. By [F2], $(z,w)_R=(Rz,Rw)_{L^2\times L^2}$ is an inner product on the ambient error space. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 By Gram–Schmidt choose an orthonormal basis $e_1,\ldots,e_N$ of $R(X_h)$, and define $Pq=\sum_{j=1}^N(q,e_j)e_j$. Then $q-Pq$ is orthogonal to every $e_j$, so $Pq$ uniquely minimizes distance to $R(X_h)$ by Pythagoras. The finite-dimensional image is closed; injectivity in [F2] pulls $P(R(\sigma,u))$ back to a unique minimizer and the same identity gives best approximation. The scalar component stays in the stated H1_0 trial factor. [F1, F2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice and the real form and spaces of [[def-na-ultraweak-poisson-dpg-formulation]] on a finite conforming triangular mesh. For every admissible local input to [[alg-na-practical-dpg-finite-riesz-solves]], the exact factorization terminates after $O(N_K^3)$ scalar arithmetic operations once its Gram entries and right-hand side are formed; it returns `singular-test-matrix` exactly for a dependent input family, and on an independent family it returns the unique finite Riesz representative. Let $U_h\subset U$ consist of volume fields $\sigma_h|_K\in P_1(K)^2$, $u_h|_K\in P_1(K)$, continuous scalar traces $\widehat u_h|_{\partial K}\in\widetilde P_2(\partial K)$, and conservative normal traces $\widehat\sigma_{n,h}|_{\partial K}\in P_1(\partial K)$. This is finite-dimensional. Let $V_r=\prod_K(P_3(K)^2\times P_3(K))$, presented cellwise by fixed ordered bases, and let $T_r:U_h\to V_r$ be the assembled finite Riesz map. On each fixed basis the unique local Riesz representatives assemble to a bounded linear map satisfying $\|T_rw_h\|_V\le\|b\|\|w_h\|_U$. Now assume the continuous primal and adjoint graph inf-sup constants have minimum $\beta>0$. Let $\Pi:V\to V_r$ be the bounded Fortin map of [[lem-na-practical-dpg-fortin-p1-r3]], with $b(U_h,(I-\Pi)V)=0$ and $\|\Pi\|\le C_\Pi$. Then for every bounded load $F\in V'$, the practical DPG system tested with $T_r(U_h)$ has a unique solution $x_h$, and
$$\|x-x_h\|_U\le(1+\|b\|C_\Pi/\beta)\inf_{z_h\in U_h}\|x-z_h\|_U,$$
where $x$ is the exact continuous solution.

1.1 On an arbitrary local input family, its Gram matrix is positive semidefinite. As long as the preceding vectors are independent, the next unpivoted $LDL^{\mathsf T}$ pivot is the squared norm of that vector's residual after orthogonal projection onto their span; this follows by solving the preceding Gram equations. Hence every pivot is positive exactly while the vectors remain independent, and the first dependent vector gives a zero pivot, so the algorithm returns `singular-test-matrix` exactly for a dependent family. If the family is independent, the finite loop and triangular solves terminate, the resulting coefficients solve $Gc=g$, and the returned vector is therefore the unique finite Riesz representative. The factorization and solves use $O(N_K^3)$ exact scalar operations after entry formation. For each cell this representative satisfies $(T_{r,K}w_h,v_K)_{V(K)}=b_K(w_h,v_K)$; summing over cells gives $(T_rw_h,v_r)_V=b(w_h,v_r)$ for every $v_r\in V_r$. For the fixed bases of $V_r$, local uniqueness and linearity of $b$ show that the assembled $T_r$ is linear. Its Riesz identity and [F2] give $\|T_rw_h\|_V\le\|b\|\|w_h\|_U$. [F2, F5, F6, given, algebra]

1.2 By [F7], $U,V$ are real Hilbert spaces; boundedness [F2] and Riesz [F5] define $A:U\to V$ by $(Aw,v)_V=b(w,v)$. The primal inf-sup gives $\|Aw\|_V\ge\beta\|w\|_U$, so $A$ is injective and its range is closed: if $Aw_n$ converges, the lower bound makes $w_n$ Cauchy, and its limit maps to the range limit. The adjoint inf-sup gives $\|A^*v\|_U\ge\beta\|v\|_V$, so $\ker A^*=\{0\}$. By the defining adjoint identity, $v\perp\operatorname{ran}(A)$ iff $(Aw,v)_V=0$ for every $w$, iff $(w,A^*v)_U=0$ for every $w$, iff $A^*v=0$. Hence $\operatorname{ran}(A)^\perp=\ker A^*$, the closed range is dense, and therefore all of $V$. Riesz represents $F\in V'$, so it has a unique preimage $x\in U$. [F1, F2, F5, F7, given, algebra]

1.3 For $w_h\in U_h$, the continuous primal bound gives $\beta\|w_h\|_U\le\sup_{v\in V}b(w_h,v)/\|v\|_V$. Fortin orthogonality in [F3] gives $b(w_h,v)=b(w_h,\Pi v)$ and $\|\Pi v\|_V\le C_\Pi\|v\|_V$, so the restricted inf-sup on $V_r$ is at least $\gamma=\beta/C_\Pi$. [F3, given, algebra]

2.1 On $V_r\times U_h$, put $a(r,v)=(r,v)_V$ and $c(v,w_h)=b(w_h,v)$. The first form is coercive on all of $V_r$, and [F4]’s constraint inf-sup is $\gamma$ by step 1.3. Applying [F4] with datum $F|_{V_r}$ and zero constraint gives a unique pair $(r_h,x_h)$ with $(r_h,v)+b(x_h,v)=F(v)$ and $b(w_h,r_h)=0$. The first equation makes $r_h$ the Riesz representative of the restricted residual; the second is orthogonality to $T_r(U_h)$, exactly the practical DPG equations by [F6]. [A1, F2, F4, F6, step 1.3]

3.1 Give $V_r'$ the inner product transported from $V_r$ by its Riesz map. The second mixed equation makes $F-B_rx_h$ orthogonal to every $B_rw_h$ in this inner product. For any $z_h$, $F-B_rz_h=(F-B_rx_h)+B_r(x_h-z_h)$, so Pythagoras gives $\|B_r(x_h-z_h)\|_{V_r'}\le\|F-B_rz_h\|_{V_r'}=\|B_r(x-z_h)\|_{V_r'}\le\|b\|\|x-z_h\|_U$. Apply the discrete inf-sup $\gamma$ to $x_h-z_h$, then the triangle inequality and infimize over $z_h$ to obtain the displayed estimate. [F2, F5, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. On $D=(0,1)^2$, let $c=(1/2,1/2)$ and split the square into the four triangles joining $c$ to consecutive corners. The continuous P1 vector space with zero boundary values has no nonzero elementwise divergence-free field. Choose a nonzero smooth compactly supported divergence-free displacement $u$ and set $f=-\operatorname{div}(2\varepsilon(u))$. Then $u$ solves the continuous model with $\mu=1$ for every finite $\lambda\ge0$, but the P1 displacement Galerkin solutions on this fixed mesh tend to zero as $\lambda\to\infty$, so their $V$-norm error tends to $\|u\|_V>0$. The mini mixed pair on the same mesh retains the $\lambda$-uniform best-approximation estimate of [[thm-nearly-incompressible-elasticity-mini-uniform-stability-and-error]]. This is a fixed-mesh obstruction, not a mesh-uniform P1 rate.

1.1 Set $\eta(t)=\exp(-1/((t-1/4)(3/4-t)))$ for $1/4<t<3/4$ and $\eta(t)=0$ otherwise. At each endpoint every derivative from the interior is a finite sum of reciprocal-distance powers multiplied by $\exp(-c/\text{distance})$ for some $c>0$, hence tends to zero; so $\eta\in C_c^\infty(0,1)$. Put $\psi(x,y)=\eta(x)\eta(y)$ and $u=(\partial_y\psi,-\partial_x\psi)$. Equality of mixed derivatives gives $\operatorname{div}u=0$. Since $\eta(1/2)>0$ and $\eta(1/4)=0$, the mean value theorem gives $y\in(1/4,1/2)$ with $\eta'(y)>0$; hence $u_1(1/2,y)=\eta(1/2)\eta'(y)>0$. Thus $u\ne0$ and is compactly supported in $D$. [given, construct, algebra]

1.2 Let $f=-\operatorname{div}(2\varepsilon(u))\in C_c^\infty(D;\mathbb R^2)$. For $v\in C_c^\infty(D;\mathbb R^2)$, integration by parts and symmetry of $2\varepsilon(u)$ give $2(\varepsilon(u),\varepsilon(v))=(f,v)$. By [A1, F5], choose such tests converging to any given $v\in V$ in $H^1$; [F4] makes both pairings continuous under this convergence, so the identity holds for every $v\in V$. [A1, F4, F5, given, algebra]

1.3 A P1 vector field in this mesh vanishes at every boundary vertex and is determined by its center value $z=(a,b)$. On the bottom triangle the edge vectors from the center to its corners are $(-1/2,-1/2)$ and $(1/2,-1/2)$; its affine gradient $G$ maps both to $-z$. Subtracting gives the first column of $G$ zero, and adding gives the second column $(2a,2b)$, so divergence is $2b$. On the right triangle the edge vectors are $(1/2,-1/2)$ and $(1/2,1/2)$; subtraction gives the second column zero and addition the first column $(-2a,-2b)$, hence divergence is $-2a$. On the top triangle the edge vectors are $(1/2,1/2)$ and $(-1/2,1/2)$; subtraction gives the first column zero and addition the second column $(-2a,-2b)$, hence divergence is $-2b$. On the left triangle the edge vectors are $(-1/2,1/2)$ and $(-1/2,-1/2)$; subtraction gives the second column zero and addition the first column $(2a,2b)$, hence divergence is $2a$. If all four divergences vanish, then $a=b=0$, so the elementwise divergence-free subspace is exactly $\{0\}$. [given, algebra]

2.1 Since $\operatorname{div}u=0$, the volumetric term vanishes and step 1.2 gives $\mathcal E_\lambda(u,v)=f(v)$ for every $v\in V$ and every finite $\lambda\ge0$. By [F1], this identifies the same nonzero $u$ as the unique continuous solution for each such $\lambda$. [F1, step 1.1, step 1.2, given, algebra]

3.1 Let $u_{h,\lambda}$ be the P1 Galerkin solution, which exists uniquely by [F1]. Testing with $u_{h,\lambda}$, using [F6] with $\mu=1$, and applying [F4] gives $\|u_{h,\lambda}\|_V\le\|f\|_{V'}$ and $\lambda\|\operatorname{div}u_{h,\lambda}\|_2^2\le\|f\|_{V'}^2$. Thus along every sequence $\lambda_n\to\infty$ the discrete solutions are bounded in the finite-dimensional P1 space and have a convergent subsequence; the divergence of its limit is zero because the divergence norms tend to zero and convergence in $H^1$ implies convergence of divergence in $L^2$. The limit is zero by step 1.3. If the full family did not converge to zero, a sequence bounded away from zero would have such a zero-convergent subsequence, a contradiction. Hence $u_{h,\lambda}\to0$ and the reverse triangle inequality gives $\|u-u_{h,\lambda}\|_V\to\|u\|_V>0$. [F1, F4, F6, step 1.3, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The mini mixed comparison is exactly the scoped result [F2] under the spaces [F3]; its estimate keeps the best-approximation term and its constant is independent of $\lambda$ on this mesh family. No conclusion about a P1 rate as $h\to0$ is used. [F2, F3, step 3.1] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice, Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Let
$\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded contractible Lipschitz
polyhedral cavity with connected boundary. Let $\epsilon,\mu>0$ be constant
scalar coefficients and let $\{\mathcal T_{h_n}\}_{n\ge1}$ be a
shape-regular refining family of matching affine tetrahedral meshes, with
$h_n\to0$. Use the full continuous and discrete curl-kernel quotient gauges
$X$ and $X_{h_n}$ of
[[def-na-pe11-maxwell-cavity-eigenproblem]]. Suppose the three PE09
supplier statements on regular decomposition,
[[thm-na-discrete-compactness-and-poincare-lowest-order-nedelec]], and
[[thm-na-uniformly-bounded-commuting-cochain-projection]] hold for this exact
domain, boundary convention and mesh family. Then the continuous PEC curl-curl
problem has isolated positive eigenvalues of finite multiplicity. For every
isolated continuous eigenvalue $\lambda>0$ of multiplicity $m$, choose
$\delta>0$ so that $I=(\lambda-\delta,\lambda+\delta)$ has
$\lambda-\delta>0$ and its closure contains no other continuous eigenvalue.
Then $I$ contains exactly $m$ discrete eigenvalues for all sufficiently large
$n$; these converge to $\lambda$ and their eigenspaces converge to the
continuous eigenspace in symmetric $L^2$ gap. If positive discrete eigenvalues converge to a finite
limit, that limit is a continuous eigenvalue. Thus the method has no nonzero
spectral pollution. No claim selects convergent individual eigenvectors
inside a repeated eigenspace.

The positive coefficients in this theorem are homogeneous scalars. A
variable or tensor-valued coefficient requires a weighted compactness and
projection interface; it is not covered by the unweighted PE09 statements.
The quotient removes the entire curl kernel, so topology-dependent zero modes
are not counted as positive eigenvalues.

1.1 Put $Y=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ with inner product $b(u,v)=\epsilon(u,v)_{L^2}$, and let $H_X$ be the $Y$-closure of $X$. The graph of distributional curl is closed: convergence of a field and its curl in $L^2$ passes to the distributional identity in [[def-na-hcurl-space]]. Thus $H(\operatorname{curl})$ is Hilbert by [F6], and $H_0(\operatorname{curl})$ is a closed subspace by its closure definition. ## Statement

Assume Countable Choice and the hypotheses of
[[cor-na-mini-element-pressure-mass-schur-bounds]]. Precondition the steady
MINI saddle system symmetrically with
$P=\operatorname{diag}(A_h,\nu^{-1}M_Q)$, using the convention of
[[def-na-symmetric-saddle-point-system-and-block-preconditioners]]. Put
$$ c_-=(C_FC_{\rm div}(D))^{-2}/(1+d),\qquad c_+=d, \qquad \lambda_\pm(s)=\frac{1\pm\sqrt{1+4s}}2. $$
Every eigenvalue of the Cholesky-symmetrically preconditioned matrix lies in
$$ [\lambda_-(c_+),\lambda_-(c_-)]\;\cup\;\{1\}\;\cup\; [\lambda_+(c_-),\lambda_+(c_+)], $$
where $1$ has multiplicity $\dim V_h-\dim Q_h$ (zero when the dimensions
are equal). This interval is for the steady Stokes scaling $\gamma=1/\nu$;
it is not an iteration-count or solver-speed guarantee.

1.1 The finite mesh contains a simplex, so [F3] gives $N_K\ge1$ and $N_v\ge d+1$; therefore both $V_h$ and $Q_h$ have positive dimensions as required by [F1]. Congruence of [F2] by $(\nu^{-1}M_Q)^{-1/2}$ shows that the normalized Schur eigenvalues $\mu_j$ lie in $$ \left[(C_FC_{\rm div}(D))^{-2}/(1+d),\ d\right]=[c_-,c_+]. $$ Since $Q_h$ is nonzero and $M_Q$ is positive definite, [F2] also forces $c_-\le c_+$; both endpoints are positive. [A1, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 The derivative formulas $\lambda_-'(s)=-(1+4s)^{-1/2}<0$ and $\lambda_+'(s)=(1+4s)^{-1/2}>0$ for $s>0$ show that the two eigenvalue branches map $[c_-,c_+]$ onto the two stated intervals. Applying [F1] therefore yields the displayed spectral enclosure and multiplicity. [F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice and the hypotheses of
[[cor-na-mini-element-pressure-mass-schur-bounds]]. Precondition the steady
MINI saddle system symmetrically with
$P=\operatorname{diag}(A_h,\nu^{-1}M_Q)$, using the convention of
[[def-na-symmetric-saddle-point-system-and-block-preconditioners]]. Put
$$ c_-=(C_FC_{\rm div}(D))^{-2}/(1+d),\qquad c_+=d, \qquad \lambda_\pm(s)=\frac{1\pm\sqrt{1+4s}}2. $$
Every eigenvalue of the Cholesky-symmetrically preconditioned matrix lies in
$$ [\lambda_-(c_+),\lambda_-(c_-)]\;\cup\;\{1\}\;\cup\; [\lambda_+(c_-),\lambda_+(c_+)], $$
where $1$ has multiplicity $\dim V_h-\dim Q_h$ (zero when the dimensions
are equal). This interval is for the steady Stokes scaling $\gamma=1/\nu$;
it is not an iteration-count or solver-speed guarantee.

1.1 The finite mesh contains a simplex, so [F3] gives $N_K\ge1$ and $N_v\ge d+1$; therefore both $V_h$ and $Q_h$ have positive dimensions as required by [F1]. Congruence of [F2] by $(\nu^{-1}M_Q)^{-1/2}$ shows that the normalized Schur eigenvalues $\mu_j$ lie in $$ \left[(C_FC_{\rm div}(D))^{-2}/(1+d),\ d\right]=[c_-,c_+]. $$ Since $Q_h$ is nonzero and $M_Q$ is positive definite, [F2] also forces $c_-\le c_+$; both endpoints are positive. [A1, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 The derivative formulas $\lambda_-'(s)=-(1+4s)^{-1/2}<0$ and $\lambda_+'(s)=(1+4s)^{-1/2}>0$ for $s>0$ show that the two eigenvalue branches map $[c_-,c_+]$ onto the two stated intervals. Applying [F1] therefore yields the displayed spectral enclosure and multiplicity. [F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Assume the continuous trial-to-test operator is boundedly invertible with lower inf-sup constant $\beta>0$, and let $\Pi:V\to V_r$ be the bounded Fortin map with $b(U_h,(I-\Pi)V)=0$. For any exact solution $x=B^{-1}F$ and any $\widetilde x_h\in U_h$, define the practical residual estimator $\eta=\|F-B\widetilde x_h\|_{V_r'}$ and Fortin data oscillation $\operatorname{osc}(F)=\|F\circ(I-\Pi)\|_{V'}$. Then
$$\beta^2\|x-\widetilde x_h\|_U^2\le\eta^2+(\|\Pi\|\eta+\operatorname{osc}(F))^2,\quad \eta\le\|b\|\|x-\widetilde x_h\|_U,$$
$$\operatorname{osc}(F)\le\|b\|\|I-\Pi\|\inf_{z_h\in U_h}\|x-z_h\|_U.$$
For the stated P1/R3 Poisson Fortin map, $\operatorname{osc}(F_f)\le C(\sum_Kh_K^2\|f-f_K\|_{L^2(K)}^2)^{1/2}$, where $f_K=|K|^{-1}\int_K f$; it vanishes for cellwise constant $f$.

1.1 Let $e=x-\widetilde x_h$ and let $\epsilon\in V$ represent $F-B\widetilde x_h$ by Riesz. Choose an orthonormal basis $e_1,\ldots,e_N$ of the finite-dimensional polynomial space $V_r$ and set $\epsilon_h=\sum_{j=1}^N(\epsilon,e_j)_V e_j$. Then $\delta=\epsilon-\epsilon_h$ is orthogonal to $V_r$, $\eta=\|\epsilon_h\|_V=\|F-B\widetilde x_h\|_{V_r'}$, and $\|\epsilon\|^2=\eta^2+\|\delta\|^2$. Continuous inf-sup gives $\beta\|e\|\le\|\epsilon\|$. [A1, F2, F3, F4, given]

1.2 Riesz gives $\eta\le\|Be\|_{V'}\le\|b\|\|e\|$. For any $z_h\in U_h$, Fortin orthogonality gives $F((I-\Pi)y)=b(x-z_h,(I-\Pi)y)$; take the dual norm and infimum to obtain the oscillation approximation bound. [F1, F2, F4, given, algebra]

2.1 Since $\Pi\delta\in V_r$, $\|\delta\|^2=(\delta,\delta-\Pi\delta)$. Substitute $\epsilon-\epsilon_h$ for $\delta$; Fortin orthogonality kills $b(\widetilde x_h, (I-\Pi)\delta)$, leaving $F((I-\Pi)\delta)+(\epsilon_h,\Pi\delta)$. Hence $\|\delta\|\le\operatorname{osc}(F)+\|\Pi\|\eta$. Combine with step 1.1 to get the reliability inequality. [F2, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For the Poisson load, mean preservation gives $\int_K(v-\Pi^{grad}_3v)=0$, so $F_f((I-\Pi)(\tau,v))=\sum_K(f-f_K,v-\Pi^{grad}_3v)_K$. By [F2], each difference is bounded by $Ch_K\|\nabla v\|_K$. Cauchy–Schwarz over cells yields the stated data oscillation; it is zero if every $f|_K=f_K$. [F1, F2, step 1.2, algebra] ∎
cases.evidence: The finite test projection can have an empty orthonormal sum in a zero test subspace, but a nontrivial stable trial space then requires the assumed Fortin property and continuous inverse; the ordinary trial competitor set contains zero.
